en: Volume II, Part II:
Prāyaścitta Kāṇḍa [1]
The Twelfth Chapter.

Now, this twelfth chapter is commenced for the purpose of prescribing certain remaining rules of conduct (*ācāra*) and penances (*prāyaścitta*) that have not been included among those set forth in the three chapters of the *Ācārakāṇḍa* and the eight chapters of the *Prāyaścittakāṇḍa*.
Among these, he first describes bathing occasioned by such causes as bad dreams.

"If one should see a bad dream, or after vomiting, or after undergoing the rite of shaving, or after sexual intercourse, or [exposure to] the smoke from a funeral pyre, bathing alone is prescribed. (12.1) Thus, sleep is of two kinds: good sleep and bad sleep. Among these, that which produces happiness for the dreamer at the time of seeing it and indicates future prosperity is a good dream. An example of this is what the Chandogas record:

"When one sees a woman in dreams while engaged in rites for the fulfillment of desires, one should know that there will be success in that dream-vision" (ChU 5.2.8). By contrast, a bad dream (*duḥsvapna*) is that which produces distress at the time of seeing it and indicates some impending misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) for a person. Regarding this, the followers of the Ṛgveda recite an example. For there, after describing many portents of death occurring while awake and concluding with the statement "these are direct observations," the following dream-portents are then recorded in the tradition: [The list of bad dreams follows... ...and so forth. These are the bad dreams. Now, the following is said regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for them: "One should offer an oblation of ghee in the fire with the verse beginning 'Agni, you are the expiation for sin' (*agne vratapate*). This is the expiation for these. Furthermore, it is said: "If one sees a bad dream, one should recite the *Sāvitrī* verse, the *Puruṣasūkta*, or the *Śivasaṃkalpa* hymn. This is the expiation for these. Moreover, it is said: "One should bathe at dawn, offer water libations, and give gifts. This is the expiation for these. And finally, it is said: "One should fast for a day and night, or for three days, or for seven days. This is the expiation for these. Thus, the expiation for bad dreams has been explained. One who knows this and acts accordingly is freed from the evil effects of bad dreams. He attains long life, fame, strength, and the world of heaven. He becomes prosperous. Therefore, one should indeed know this. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Thus it is said. Now, regarding dreams: one sees in a dream a black man with black teeth; he kills him. A boar kills him. A monkey leaps upon him. A swift wind carries him away. Having eaten gold, he vomits it up. He eats honey. He eats lotus stalks (*bisas*). He wears a single white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) on his head. Yoked to donkeys and boars, he travels. Wearing a garland of *nalada* grass, he walks toward the south, leading a black cow with a black calf. [3] And so forth. Those who know the science of dreams state that a dream is a signifier of what is to come.
Mounting bulls, elephants, palaces, mountain peaks, and trees;
being smeared with excrement; weeping; seeing a corpse; and sexual intercourse with a forbidden woman in a dream—these are auspicious.
"A woman wearing black garments, with black perfumes and ointments, who embraces one in a dream—one should declare death for him. Thus [it is said].

Intending all this, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa composed the following aphorism in the section concerning dreams: "For it is indicative, according to scripture, and those who know it declare so" (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.4). In that regard, when a bad dream is seen that indicates a future misfortune, one should rise in the morning and perform a bath for that reason. Likewise, if food has been vomited after eating, one should bathe immediately. Similarly, one should practice bathing after shaving, sexual intercourse, or smelling the smoke from a funeral pyre. In the same way, bathing should be understood as necessary upon touching a wicked person and so forth. Yama says thus:

"When indigestion has occurred, after vomiting, after shaving, after sexual intercourse, following a bad dream, or upon contact with a wicked person, bathing alone is prescribed. Thus says Vṛddha-Parāśara as well.

"One should perform a bath after a bad dream, sexual intercourse, vomiting, purging, shaving, or touching a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, or a cemetery. Regarding sexual intercourse, however, the bath refers specifically to the period following menstruation; as Śātātapa says:
"For it is traditionally taught that bathing after sexual intercourse during the fertile period is prescribed because of the suspicion of pregnancy;
however, when one engages in intercourse outside the fertile period, the purification is like that for voiding urine or excrement.
Regarding specific cases such as vomiting and so forth, Manu says:
"One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then perform the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*);
one who has eaten food should simply sip water; bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse" (MDh 5.144).
[5] Thus, the meaning is that one who has vomited immediately after eating food should sip water. 12.1.
Now, he states the causes for the re-initiation of those who require penance:
"Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or that which has been touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve re-initiation" (12.2).

And this rite occurs immediately after the performance of the vow; regarding that, the scriptural statements have already been cited in the preceding chapter in connection with the topic of expiation. 12.2.

Furthermore, regarding the case where one who already possesses the primary consecration undergoes a secondary consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), [the author] refutes [the necessity of certain items] even when the deerskin and so forth are obtained:
"The deerskin, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born during the rite of secondary consecration" (12.3).

Even shaving the head is excluded, as in the case of the wearing of deerskins and other such items. Thus Viṣṇu says: “In all these cases, at the conclusion of the penance for the twice-born, one should perform the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again; however, in the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), shaving, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging, and the vows (*vrata*) are to be avoided” (ViDh 51.4–5). The “vows” refer to the *saumya*, *prājāpatya*, and others, as well as the prohibitions against honey, meat, collyrium, and so forth.

At the beginning of the previous chapter, it was stated that for consuming impure substances, semen, beef, excrement, urine, or the like, one must perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance (11.1); that refers to cases where the act is committed intentionally. For this very reason, eating together with a woman who has recently given birth (*bālāpatyā*) was cited there as an illustration of such an act. However, in the present context, he declares the expiation for consuming excrement, urine, and so forth unintentionally: "One who has consumed excrement or urine shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance for the sake of purification;
having bathed, he should consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and thus he shall become pure. (12.4)

Having performed the *prājāpatya* penance, and subsequently having bathed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and consumed that *pañcagavya*, one becomes pure. Furthermore, this must be done prior to the *punaḥsaṃskāra* (re-consecration), according to the statement of Viṣṇu: "At the conclusion of the penance, one should perform the *saṃskāra* once again" (ViDh 51.4). Regarding water defiled by feces, urine, and the like, one should refer to what is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "When water is polluted by urine, feces, and so forth, and one should drink it, then the *sāntapana-kṛcchra* vow is the purification for that sin" (KūPu 1.2.33.38).
Regarding anyone among the four castes who, having raised a weapon for the purpose of suicide, somehow desists even before death, the author states the penance for him by way of a question:

"And in the case of falling into water or fire, as well as in the case of renunciation and fasting unto death—for those of the castes who have fallen back [into a lower state], how is purification ordained? (12.5)
By performing two Prājāpatya penances, by visiting sacred fords,
and by the gift of eleven bulls, those three castes are purified.
I shall declare the penance for a Brāhmaṇa: having gone to a forest at a crossroads and shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should perform two Prājāpatya penances.
"Śvāyaṃbhuva has declared that one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee for purification;
by that, one is released from that sin and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa. (12.8) Thus it is said.

There are five causes of death: water, fire, and so forth. People die by entering rivers, lakes, and the like; by entering fire; by falling from a precipice; by embarking on the Great Journey (*mahāprasthāna*); and by fasting (*anāśaka*). Among these, death by water and the other means is threefold: prescribed (*vihita*), prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*), and permitted (*anujñāta*). Prescribed death is also twofold: that in the form of asceticism for the sake of a desired goal (*kāmya-tapas*) and that in the form of penance (*prāyaścitta-tapas*). Regarding the latter, the form of asceticism is demonstrated in the *Narmadāmāhātmya* of the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "O King, he who should enter the fire at the Somatīrtha..."
"Whether in water or by fasting, that mortal is not born again. Thus it is said.
In that very same [work], regarding the greatness of Prayāga, it is stated:
"He who enters a fire of dried cow-dung between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā..."
For he is not deficient in limb, free from disease, and endowed with the five sense faculties.
As many as are the pores on his limbs,
for so many thousands of years is that man honored in the heavenly world.
[9] He who should enter the water at a world-renowned confluence when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu shall be liberated from all sins.
"He attains the world of Soma and rejoices together with Soma. (KūPurāṇa 1.1.37.6–7)

This death, which takes the form of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), is as follows: dying in water or by other means out of anger and the like is prohibited. Accordingly, in the section on impurity (*aśauca*), a Smṛti passage beginning with "death through anger" (*krodhāt prāyam*) has been cited. Furthermore, the death in water or similar means of one afflicted by a severe disease is neither prescribed nor prohibited; rather, it is merely permitted by the scripture. In that same context, this is illustrated by the statement beginning with "by incurable great diseases. Since that which is permitted is optional, its result is merely the non-attainment of the [desired] fruit; however, such a person is not subject to expiation. Even for one who, having prepared to die for the sake of expiation, desists from it, his prior sin is simply not removed; yet there is no further expiation to be performed by him. This being the case, only the prohibited [forms of death] remain. Even in that case, although death after having prepared to die constitutes a "bad death" (*durmaraṇa*), this expiation does not apply to one who actually dies therein, because such a person no longer exists [to perform it]. However, for one who prepares to die and then turns back from death, this expiation is indeed required.
[Objection: But surely this is not appropriate even for him, because suicide is prohibited by the scriptures and its cessation is scripturally enjoined.

[Reply: Certainly. We do not say that this penance has the cessation [of the act] as its cause; rather, the effort toward the performance of the prohibited act is the cause. It is precisely because the mere effort is the cause that the smallness of the penance is justified.

"Those who have turned back after attempting to die by water, fire, and so forth, are called *pratyavasita*s. The meaning of the question is that a specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be stated for each of these four castes. In this regard, for a Kṣatriya there is a double *Prājāpatya* penance; for a Vaiśya, a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*); for a Śūdra, the gift of ten cows along with a bull; and for a Brāhmaṇa, a vow such as retiring to the forest (*vanagamanavratam*). By the attempt to commit suicide, his status as a Brāhmaṇa is lost and the state of a Caṇḍāla is attained. Upon the cessation of that Caṇḍāla-hood through the performance of the vow, he regains his previously established Brāhmaṇa-hood. Thus says Vṛddha-Parāśara: [The text continues with the citation from Vṛddha-Parāśara.]
But one who desists from fasting and remains established within the system of the four castes is to be known as a Caṇḍāla; he must be avoided with great effort.
[11] But those who have fallen away from their dharma— Caṇḍālas, wandering mendicants, and ascetics— one should cause the offspring born of them to dwell together with the Caṇḍālas.
And likewise for those who have fallen from their caste (pratyāvasita-varṇas) through such acts as entering water or fire, embracing asceticism, or fasting unto death— how shall their expiation be?
Through the favor of Brahmins, by visiting sacred fords,
and by the gift of a hundred cows, those three castes are purified.
I shall declare for the Brahmin: having gone to a forest crossroads, he should shave his head including the top-knot and perform ablutions at the three junctions of the day.
One should recite the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times day after day;
thus one is liberated from all sins and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
"Seeking alms, one dwelling in the forest should wander through the village for seven houses;
having consumed that alms-food, he is purified within half a year.
Regarding this very matter, Vasiṣṭha states other vows:
One who abandons his life while still living shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights,
or fast for three nights, always wearing an oily garment;
restraining his vital breaths within himself, he should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
"Or else, according to this procedure, one should recite the *gāyatrī*;
or, having kindled the fire, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses" (VaDh 23.19–21).

In that regard, the recitation (*japa*) and the oblation (*homa*) are to be treated as alternatives depending on the specific qualifications of the learned person. As for the twelve-night and three-night periods, they are to be established as applicable based on the distinction between the presence or absence of capacity in an unlearned person.

In the root text, by the word *pravrajyā*, the undertaking of the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*) was previously explained; alternatively, it is intended here as *parivrajyā* (the life of a wandering mendicant). This being the case, an expiation is stated for a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen away from the state of a wandering mendicant (*parivrajyā*). This should be understood as applying to one who, being full of faith, desires to take up the life of a wandering mendicant again, preceded by a re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) and other rites. However, for one who does not desire to take up the life of a wandering mendicant again, there is servitude to the king and so forth until death. As for what Nārada says in this regard:
"But a twice-born man who has fallen from the mendicant order shall become the slave of the king alone;
there is no re-initiation for him, nor any purification whatsoever.
(NSm 5.35). This refers to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, as Kātyāyana says:
In a place where the three twice-born castes have abandoned the life of renunciation,
the king shall banish the Brāhmaṇa and enslave the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.

[13] Thus says Dakṣa: "But one who, having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, does not abide by his own duty, the king shall brand him with the mark of a dog's foot and banish him immediately. (DaSm 7.34)
Yājñavalkya says: "One who has fallen from the life of a wandering mendicant shall become the king’s slave until death. (YDh 2.183) || 12.5–8 ||
Now, as a supplement to the section on conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*), he describes the different types of bathing:
"The wise have proclaimed five meritorious baths:
the fiery (*āgneya*), the watery (*vāruṇa*), the brahmic (*brāhma*), the windy (*vāyavya*), and the celestial (*divya*). (12.9)
Thus [ends the ninth].
He explains the nature of the five [types of bathing] taught, beginning with that of Agni, in their proper order: "The *āgneya* is bathing with ashes; the *vāruṇa* is by immersion;
the *brāhma* is with the mantra 'āpo hi ṣṭhā'; and the *vāyavya* is declared to be the dust raised by cows. (12.10)
But that which occurs during a shower of rain is called a twice-born bath;
having bathed there, a human being becomes as one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā. || 12.11 ||

[14] Thus it is said. The ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) is of two kinds: that beginning from the feet and that beginning from the head. Among these, the one beginning from the feet pertains to those who are dispassionate toward sense-objects, because it follows the order of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*). This is shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"The smearing of the body with fiery ashes from the feet to the head. (KūPu 1.2.18.13).
The [ash-bath] beginning from the head is shown in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
O you of excellent vows, one should worship the region of the head with Īśāna, the face with Tatpuruṣa,
the region of the chest with Aghora, and the private parts with Vāma.
"One should purify the feet with the *sadyojāta* mantra and the entire body with the *praṇava*. (Liṅga Purāṇa 1.26.37–38).

The *vāruṇa-snāna*, which consists of immersion in water, has been explained in detail in the first chapter under the verse: "Sandhyā, bathing, recitation (*japa*), and fire-offering (*homa*)" (Parāśara Smṛti 1.39). And that [bathing] should be performed three times during the [three] baths. The procedure for this has been shown by Baudhāyana: "On the ground, on the head, and likewise in the sky; on the head, in the sky, and likewise on the ground."

"Mantra-bath is prescribed [to be performed] in the sky, on the earth, and upon the head. (BDh 1.2.10.21). Standing in the dust raised by the wind from the hooves of cows returning on their paths in the evening is the *vāyavya* (wind-bath). Bathing the body with rainwater accompanied by sunshine is the *divya* (celestial) bath; this is superior to those previously mentioned. By this, the two other baths—the *yaugika* (conjunction-bath) and the *sārasvata* (Sarasvatī-bath)—are also implied. The *yaugika* consists of meditating upon Viṣṇu through yoga. Regarding that, Vyāsa says: "The *brāhma*, *āgneya*, *vāyavya*, and *divya* [baths] have been described..."
Likewise, the Vāruṇa and the Yaugika; thus, in brief, the sixfold bath is complete.
The Brāhma bath, however, consists of sprinkling with drops of water using *kuśa* grass and sacred mantras.
[16] Bathing with ashes is known as the fire-bath (āgneya); bathing with the dust raised by cows is remembered as the wind-bath (vāyavya);
and that which is performed under rain falling from the sun is called the divine bath (divya).

"The Vāruṇa bath consists of immersion [in water], while the Mānasa bath is the realization of the Self; the Yogic bath is declared to be the contemplation of Viṣṇu through yoga. Thus, the Sārasvata bath is accomplished by the benediction of the learned. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"The dust raised by cows is said to belong to Vāyu when the Lord of Rays [the Sun] is setting;
the bath obtained through the Sarasvatī of the learned is remembered as Sārasvata. (Bṛhad-Śrāddha-Mayūkha 3.49).
Vyāsa states the manner of the learned's utterance:
One who knows the ritual should himself perform the ceremonial bath with due decorum for a twice-born man who has arrived spontaneously, as well as for a disciple or a son.
May there be a bath for those who desire it with jars made of gold, filled with the waters of the Ganges accompanied by mantras, and performed with auspicious and meritorious rites—
at first, at Prabhāsa, or at Madhuma, or at Puṣkara, where the waters possess manifold virtues. (VyāSm 1.14–15)
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, in the waters of Kanakhala, at Bhadrakarṇa, and at Gayā;
[17] And when the Moon is eclipsed by Rāhu while conjoined with the Sun at Sannihatī—
especially at these renowned sacred fords (tīrthas) known throughout the three worlds— may my ritual bath be rendered complete and flawless.

Thus end the baths. Among these seven baths, the *vāruṇa* (water-bath) is primary, while the other six baths are secondary. The statement of Śaṅkha regarding the distinction between the primary and secondary is cited in the very section on conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*). Therein, the secondary baths are intended for those who are incapable [of the primary one]. As it is said in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "When impurity has arisen, one should perform a bath; likewise, the wise have declared that when one is unable [to bathe in water], the Brāhma and other baths [should be performed]. (KūPu 1.2.18.11)

|| 12.10–11 || The king, having heard that speech of his, spoke these words to him: "O Brahmin, I shall give you whatever you desire. The Brahmin said: "O King, grant me this boon: that my son may not die before he has reached the age of one hundred years. The king said: "O Brahmin, even if I were to give up my own life, I would not grant you such a boon. The Brahmin said: "O King, if you do not grant me this boon, then I shall depart from here for the forest. The king said: "O Brahmin, I shall grant you another boon; choose whatever else you desire. The Brahmin said: "O King, if you will grant me another boon, then let my son live for five hundred years. The king said: "O Brahmin, I shall grant you yet another boon; choose whatever else you desire. The Brahmin said: "O King, if you will grant me yet another boon, then let my son live for a thousand years. The king said: "O Brahmin, I shall grant you yet another boon; choose whatever else you desire. He establishes, with supporting reasoning, that the libation (tarpaṇa) must precede the Varuṇa-bath and the wringing out of the garment must follow it:
"All the gods, together with the hosts of ancestors, travel in the form of wind behind the twice-born man going to bathe, afflicted by thirst and seeking water. (12.12)
"They return disappointed once the wringing out of the garment has been performed;

therefore, one should not wring out the garment without having performed the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa). (12.13). Thus, those who follow one going to bathe all depart disappointed when the garment has already been wrung out—this is the logical conclusion. Regarding this matter, the statements from the *Yogiyājñavalkya-smṛti* and other sources have already been cited above.

|| 12.12–13 || The king, having heard that speech, was filled with wonder; he spoke these words to his ministers who were seated nearby. "O ministers, listen to this matter, for it is not something easily understood. How could there be such a thing as a son born from a woman who has been enjoyed by another? || 12.12–13 ||

At the time of libation, sesame seeds should be placed on the palm in the area where the hair grows outwards, or in another vessel, but not on the back of the hand where the hair grows downwards—with this in mind, he states the sin incurred by placing them there: "Whoever offers libations to the ancestors with sesame seeds while placing them in the pores of the skin, by him the ancestors are satisfied with blood and filth. (12.14)
On this point, the statement of Devala has already been cited previously. || 12.14 ||
At the time of bathing, he prohibits the shaking of the hair and similar acts:
"He who shakes his hair after bathing, or who voids excrement, or even sips water while still standing in the water—he is excluded from the rites for the ancestors and the gods. (12.15)

[19] Thus: the word "having bathed" (*snātvā*) is connected to both sides, like the eye of a crow. This being so, that man who—immediately after bathing—shakes his hair while still wet; or he who, immediately after bathing, voids excrement or urine while wearing wet clothes; or he who, at a time when he is not supposed to bathe, stands in the midst of water in a river or similar place and sips water (*ācāmet*); all three such types of men are excluded by the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and the gods (*daivatās*). The meaning is that they are unfit to perform ancestral rites (*paitṛka*) or rites for the gods (*daivika*). || 12.15 ||
At the time of sipping water (ācamana), he prohibits covering the head and so forth:

"Having covered the head or the neck, or even with the lower garment or the topknot hanging loose, one remains impure even if one has sipped water, provided one is without the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). (12.16) Thus it is said.

One should not sip water for purification after wrapping one's head or neck with a garment; likewise, one should not sip water while the lower garment is loose, or while the top-knot is untied, or while devoid of the sacred thread. 12.16.
He states another rule regarding sipping water (ācamana):
"One standing on dry land should not sip water while in the water, nor one standing in the water while on dry land;
having touched both, one who has sipped water becomes pure in both places. (12.17)

For he who, without touching water with his feet, sits on pure ground and performs *ācamana* while slightly stooping, letting drops fall only into the water, is purified neither by the water nor by the ground. And he who, conversely, places both feet in the water and performs *ācamana* while letting drops fall onto the ground, is likewise not purified in either case. Therefore, one should not perform *ācamana* in that manner. Rather, one should perform *ācamana* while touching the ground with one foot and the water with the other; in this way, one becomes pure in both respects. This rule applies specifically to one who has bathed and whose clothes are still wet. (12.17)
He states the occasions for the second sipping of water (ācamana):
"Having bathed, having drunk, having sneezed, having slept, having eaten, upon entering a road, and after putting on a garment—one who has already sipped water should sip again. (12.18)
He states the occasions for touching the ear as a substitute for sipping water (ācamana):
"Upon sneezing, upon spitting, likewise upon being defiled by food particles from the teeth, upon speaking untruth, and upon conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear. (12.19)
He establishes the purity of the sound of the ear by means of an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda):
"The sacred sites such as Prabhāsa and the rivers such as the Gaṅgā reside in the right ear of the Brahmin," so Manu has declared. (12.20)
"Agni, the waters, the Vedas, as well as Soma, the sun, and the wind—
all these indeed abide in the right ear of the Brahmin. [12.21] Thus it is said.
It prohibits bathing before the dawn:
"Bathing during the day, purified by the rays of the sun, is praised;
bathing at night is not recommended, except upon the sighting of Rāhu [during an eclipse]. (12.22) Thus it is said.

Having intended to provide an exception to the rule regarding bathing at night within the context of bathing during an eclipse, it was stated [in verse 12.20]: "except upon seeing [the moon] other than Rāhu. (12.22)
By means of the example of bathing, he states the counter-exception for giving and other acts as well:
"Bathing, giving, recitation, and fire-offerings should be performed during an eclipse of Rāhu;
otherwise, however, the night is impure, therefore one should avoid it. (12.23) Thus.

Although the prohibition against giving and other acts at night was not introduced in the root text, this [verse] should be understood as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) made with the prohibition established in other treatises kept in mind. At other times—specifically at a time when there is no eclipse—the night is impure for bathing and similar rites; therefore, one desiring to perform bathing or other such acts should avoid that night. (12.23)
He establishes the suitability of giving gifts and so forth at the time of the Soma-draught:
"The Maruts, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas—indeed, all these deities dissolve into the Soma; therefore, one should give when it is being taken. (12.24) Thus.
Just as in the case of an eclipse of Rāhu, he permits the giving of gifts at night even during the sacrifice of the threshing floor and similar occasions:
"At the threshing-floor sacrifice, at a wedding, at the sun's passage into a new sign, and likewise during an eclipse—giving at night is indeed permitted; it is not ordained otherwise. (12.25)
Furthermore, citing the appearance of Rāhu as an illustrative example, he approves of the giving of gifts at night on occasions such as the birth of a son:
"At the birth of a son, at a sacrifice, likewise during a funeral rite, and at the sight of Rāhu, giving at night is praised; not otherwise. (12.26)
[23] Thus: "Death is the act of passing away. When that has occurred, the giving of gifts such as a cow, sesame seeds, and a vessel must be performed even at night. (12.26)

Having accepted that this prohibition—"not at other times, nor at night"—applies to bathing just as it does to giving, [the author] states an exception regarding bathing during the first and last watches of the night:
"But the 'great night' (mahāniśā) should be known as the middle watch; one should perform the bath during the first and last watches as one would during the day. (12.27)

The prohibition regarding the night pertains to the *mahāniśā* (the dead of night). The term *mahāniśā* denotes the second and third *yāmas* (watches of the night). This being the case, the first and fourth *yāmas* are suitable for bathing and other such acts, just as during the day; therefore, one should perform bathing and so forth at those times. However, this applies only to times of distress (*āpad*). Otherwise, it would contradict the rule: "by the rays of the sun" (Parāśara Smṛti 12.22). But in the case of optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) bathing, there is no prohibition even during the *mahāniśā*. As Devala says: "The *mahāniśā* should be known as the two middle watches."
"One should not perform a bath in that [river] except for rites performed for specific desires or occasional observances. (12.27)
[24] Previously, the sighting of Rāhu was mentioned as a cause for bathing at night; now he states another cause:
a sacred tree, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, a Caṇḍāla, and a seller of Soma.
"But having touched these, a Brāhmaṇa shall enter the water with his clothes on" (12.28).

A *caitya* is a cremation ground suitable for a funeral pyre (*citi*). A tree planted there is a *caityavṛkṣa*. The *citi* and other such things are well known. Touching them is a cause for bathing. The intention is that if, by some chance, this occurs at night, one must bathe even then. (12.28)
He states another occasion for bathing:

"One should perform a bath after weeping before the collection of the bones; for within ten days of a Brahmin's death, there is indeed bathing, but after that, there is merely sipping water (ācamana). (12.29)

“Among the days prescribed by scriptural injunctions beginning with ‘on the first day’ (VyāSm 59), when the collection of bones is performed, crying prior to that time is a cause for bathing; however, crying after the collection of bones is a cause only for sipping water (ācamana), not for bathing. (12.29)
Now, an objection: it was stated that one should bathe even at night during a lunar eclipse (*somagrahaṇa*), but that is incorrect because water lacks purity at that time. To this, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"At that time, water is undrinkable during the two middle watches of the night;
likewise, bathing must not be performed, nor the act of sipping water (*ācamana*)."
Anticipating the objection, "Therefore, how can bathing at night be accepted? he states that this impurity applies to occasions other than an eclipse of the moon and so forth:
"All water is equal to the Gaṅgā when the sun is seized by Rāhu; the same is declared regarding an eclipse of the moon for rites such as bathing and giving gifts. (12.30)
Since the mention of the lunar eclipse (*somagraha*) is illustrative, there is no fault of impurity even during the transits (*saṃkrānti*) and other such occasions. || 12.30 ||
Just as the *soma* vessel and other items serve as causes for the excellence of water, he likewise speaks of *kuśa* grass:
"A bath purified by *kuśa*, a twice-born man who sips water with *kuśa*,
and water drawn up with *kuśa*— these become equal to the drinking of *soma*" (12.31).

Having performed the sprinkling with *kuśa* grass, the ritual bath (*mantrasnāna*) that is performed is the "bath purified by *kuśa*" (*kuśapūta-snāna*). Holding *kuśa* blades on the ring finger while performing the sipping of water (*ācamana*) constitutes the "touching with *kuśa*-water" (*kuśodakopasparśana*). The drops of water drawn up with the tips of *kuśa* grass for the purpose of sprinkling during the morning and evening prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and other rites are "water drawn up with *kuśa*" (*kuśoddhṛtatoya*). That water is as praiseworthy as the drinking of Soma. (12.31)
Now, in order to permit the study of a single portion for one who is unable to perform the study of the entire Veda, he censures the absence of such study:

"Those who have fallen away from the fire-ritual, those who are devoid of the twilight devotions, and those who do not study the Veda at all—all these are declared to be *vṛṣalas* (outcasts). (12.32) Thus it is said.

At both twilights, the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) must perform the fire-ritual by placing fuel on the fire. By this, the domestic fire (aupāsana) of householders is also implied. For those who are devoid of the fire-ritual and other such duties, there is the state of being a *vṛṣala*, which is equality with the *śūdras* and others. || 12.32 ||
[27] He permits the study of a single portion;
therefore, a Brahmin who is especially afraid of a Śūdra [should do so].

"Even a single portion may be studied if the whole cannot be mastered. (12.33) Furthermore, one should not suspect that the performance of even a single part of the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) or the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) is permissible by the same logic applied to Vedic study; for since these two require no great exertion, incapacity is impossible. In some cases, the omission of them is rooted in atheism, laziness, and so forth. "Fearing a *vṛṣala*" means fearing [the loss of status] due to being a *vṛṣala*. (12.33)
Now, he prohibits the food of a Śūdra:
"Even for one who is constantly studying, chanting, or offering oblations, if he is nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food, no upward path is found" (12.34).

The *dharmaśāstras* proclaim with the beat of a drum that study, recitation, and burnt offerings (*japa-homa*) bring about purity by being the cause for the destruction of all sins without exception. Thus says Manu:
"Daily study of the Veda according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices, and forbearance quickly destroy even those evils born of mortal sins. (MDh 11.245)
[28] Thus it is said. Bṛhaspati also says:
"Just as fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees, so too does one who knows the Vedas burn away the defects of his own karma."
Vasiṣṭha also says: "Just as fire, fanned by the wind and fed with oblations, blazes up, even so a Brāhmaṇa who is constantly devoted to the muttering of prayers shines forth intensely. (VaDh 23.16)
Also in the Caturviṃśatimata: "By performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice at each and every season, one purifies ten generations of one's lineage."

However, for that man who eats the food of a Śūdra continuously and is nourished by its essence, even the aforementioned practices such as Vedic study are not capable of purifying him; therefore, the intention is that one should avoid the food of a Śūdra with great effort. (12.34)
Taking the food of a Śūdra as an illustration, he likewise prohibits contact with Śūdras and similar acts:
"The food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting together with a Śūdra,
and even receiving knowledge from a Śūdra— these cause even one who is blazing [with merit] to fall" (12.35).

The food of a Śūdra has been explained. Dwelling in the same house with a Śūdra is "contact with a Śūdra. Sitting together—such as occasionally sitting in the same cart or vehicle—with Śūdra farmers who are making them perform agricultural work and the like, is "sitting together. Acquiring knowledge from a Śūdra who is eloquent and wise due to his discernment of dharma and adharma arising from listening to the Purāṇas and other sources is "acquisition of knowledge. These things, beginning with the food of a Śūdra, cause even a man renowned for his blazing *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) to fall into hell; therefore, they must be avoided. (12.35)
He states another thing to be avoided:

"That twice-born man who constantly causes food to be cooked by a Śūdra woman, and whose housewife is a Śūdra woman, is excluded from the rites for the ancestors and the gods; he goes to the Raurava hell. (12.36) Thus [it is said].

That Brahmin who, residing in another land or elsewhere for some reason, has his own food cooked by a Śūdra woman; and he whose wife, whether married or unmarried, is a Śūdra—even while living in his own village—both such types of Brahmins are unfit to perform rites for the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya), and they fall into hell. (12.36)
He censures the food of one in a state of birth-impurity as being like the food of a Śūdra:
"A twice-born man whose body is nourished by the food of a Śūdra during a period of death or birth-impurity—I do not know what various wombs he shall go to. (12.37)
"A vulture for twelve births, a pig for ten births, and he shall be in the womb of a dog for seven births—thus Manu has declared. (12.38) Thus it is said.

Whether during the impurity caused by death (*mṛtāśauca*) or that caused by birth (*jātāśauca*), if another Brāhmaṇa eats the food of one who is thus impure and nourishes his body during even those ten days, that Brāhmaṇa—whose limbs have been nourished by the impurity of the dead—is born into many miserable wombs. Having said, "I do not know which specific womb he will go to," the extreme misery of those wombs is described; however, his own knowledge is not revealed. Otherwise, the illustration of birth as a vulture and other such creatures would be contradicted. Nor should it be suspected that his own knowledge was described based on Manu’s statement because the words "Manu said" appear in the passage concerning the vultures, for there is no purpose in describing his personal knowledge. The citation of the word "Manu" is intended to strengthen the authority [of the teaching]. This being the case, since the misery of eating the food of a Śūdra and the food of one in a state of birth-impurity is extremely well-established, it follows that both of these must be avoided under all circumstances.

|| 12.37–38 || The king, having heard those words, spoke these words to his son: "Do not act thus; it is not right for you to abandon your father. || 12.37 || Then the prince, having bowed down to his father’s feet, spoke these words: "I shall go forth; do not obstruct me, O King. || 12.38 ||
He prohibits the performance of fire-offerings for the sake of a Śūdra:
"If a Brahmin should offer oblations as a sacrificial fee for a Śūdra, the Brahmin becomes a Śūdra, and the Śūdra becomes a Brahmin. (12.39)

[31] Thus: if a Brahmin, having accepted a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) from a Śūdra, offers his oblation with Vedic mantras for the sake of achieving peace, prosperity, and so forth, the transgression belongs to that Brahmin alone; the Śūdra, however, shall obtain the fruit of the oblation. || 12.39 ||
Now, at the time of eating, he observes silence.
"Having undertaken the vow of silence, the twice-born man should not speak while seated;
for if one who is eating should speak, that food must be rejected" (12.40). Thus it is said.

He who, having undertaken the vow of silence as a form of austerity with the thought that "one must eat in silence," remains seated and does not utter a single word until he rises to leave; if, through negligence, he should speak some sentence in the midst of his meal, he must then discard the remaining food and not eat it. (12.40)
"He prohibits drinking water from the food bowl:
'If a Brahmin drinks water from that same bowl when half his meal is consumed, he destroys the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and brings harm upon himself. (12.41) Thus it is said.

If one eats food placed in a vessel of bell-metal or similar material and drinks water from that very vessel before the meal is finished, the *havya* and *kavya* offerings performed by him will not satisfy the gods and the ancestors. By that fault, he causes himself to fall into hell and brings about his own destruction. (12.41)
[32] He prohibits causing [others] to eat from a single row or leaving food as remnants: "But he who, while the brahmins are eating, releases his leaf-plate first..."
"He is a fool, he is most sinful, he is a slayer of Brahmins; he is called defiled" (12.42).

When people are seated in a single row and eating, if someone among them discards his own vessel before the others have finished their meal and rises after drinking a mouthful at the end of the meal, his censure is very great. It is for this reason that words such as "fool" and so forth are employed [in the verse]. (12.42)
It prohibits the recitation of the *svastivācana* before the movement of the food vessels at the time of the *śrāddha*:
"If those twice-born ones pronounce the blessing while the vessels have not yet been set down,
the gods do not attain satisfaction, and likewise the ancestors depart in despair" (12.43).
It prohibits eating without bathing and so forth:
"One should never eat without having bathed, nor without having muttered prayers, nor without having invoked the fire;
one should not eat from the back of a leaf, nor likewise at night without a lamp. (12.44) Thus.

Although bathing, recitation, and burnt offerings (*japa-homa*) are prescribed for a time prior to the mealtime, such that eating without having bathed and so forth is not applicable; nevertheless, if at some point due to a certain cause these duties are not performed at their respective times and the time for eating arrives, one should not eat without first performing the bathing and other rites. Likewise, while eating from a leaf-plate (*patrāvalī*), one should eat on the inner side of the leaves and not on the back. Furthermore, one should not eat at night in the dark. (12.44)
Now he prohibits the acquisition of wealth through theft and other such means:

"But the householder, endowed with compassion, should reflect only upon dharma; being of sound intellect and abiding by justice, he should act for the sake of accomplishing the needs of those whom he must support. (12.45)
"One must indeed protect oneself with wealth acquired through righteous means;
however, he who lives by unrighteous means is excluded from all ritual acts. (12.46) Thus it is said.

A householder, though possessed of compassion such that he feels his sons, friends, wife, and others must be protected in every way, should nevertheless contemplate only the scripturally sanctioned means of acquiring wealth—such as officiating at sacrifices—for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of supporting those dependent upon him. And this being so, by conducting himself according to justice, he becomes wise through his primary focus on the concerns of the next world. Therefore, one should provide for oneself and one’s family using only wealth acquired through just means, such as officiating at sacrifices. However, he who lives on wealth obtained unjustly through theft, denial of debts, and the like, is unfit for rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*) or the ancestors (*pitrya*). As for the statement of Manu:

"Manu has declared that aged parents, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be maintained even by committing a hundred improper acts"— this [rule] refers to a situation of distress. (MDh 11.11) 12.45–46.
Now he prescribes the sight of meritorious objects:

"The fire-piler, a tawny cow, one who has performed a sacrificial session, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify by the mere sight; therefore, one should look upon them constantly. (12.47) Thus.

One who is endowed with the fire consecrated by the piling of bricks is an *agnicit*. A *kapilā* is a cow of tawny hue. A *sattrī* is a performer of any sacrificial session (*sattra*), beginning from the twelve-day rite up to those lasting a thousand years. A king is a protector of subjects according to the scriptural path. A mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is one who properly maintains the fourth stage of life (*āśrama*). The great ocean refers to the salt sea and so forth. These, when seen, purify the seer. Although specific objects such as *kuśa* grass, gold, and the like are purifying, they depend upon being held or other such actions; they do not purify by mere sight alone. Therefore, to distinguish them from those, it is said "merely seen. (12.47)
He states that certain objects bestow purity merely by being kept as protection:
"An araṇi fire-drill, a black cat, sandalwood, a fine jewel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, a black antelope skin, and a goat—one should keep these in the house. (12.48)

The *araṇi* is a specific piece of wood consecrated by mantras such as "the *aśvattha* tree within the womb of the *śamī*" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.2.8.8), used for producing fire by friction. A *sumaṇi* is a fine gemstone, such as a ruby (*padmarāga*) and so forth. (12.48)
Now, in order to prescribe the gift of a *gocarma*, he provides a definition of a *gocarma*:
"That field where one hundred cows and one bull can stand without restraint, multiplied tenfold, is proclaimed as a *gocarma*. (12.49)

A hundred cows together with one bull constitute "one hundred cows with a bull. The extent of ground that this herd of a hundred cows occupies when unrestrained for the sake of rest—this area multiplied tenfold—is designated by the term *gocarma*. Manu, however, states another method: "The measure of a finger (*aṅgula*) is said to be eight barley-corn widths across, or three rice grains placed vertically; twelve fingers make a span (*vitasti*)."
Svāyambhuva declared that two vitastis constitute one hasta;
and thirty daṇḍas, measured by a staff of ten hastas, constitute one nivartana.
"And having added five more, this is proclaimed as a *gocarma*. (MDh 12.7–8). Vṛddha-Manu states:
"A *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas* measured by a staff of seven cubits (*hasta*)."
"By giving those very ten [cows], the giver is liberated from sins. (MDh 12.10) || 12.49 ||
For those desiring the destruction of evil, he prescribes the gift of a cowhide:
"A mortal [tainted] by the killing of a Brahmin or other [sins] born of the actions of mind, speech, and body—by this gift of a cowhide, one is liberated from all taints. (12.50) Thus it is said.

Mental, vocal, and physical actions are "activities"; those born from them are "born of mental, vocal, and physical activities. It should not be said that it is illogical for there to be a common cause for the cessation of these three when they are established with slight or greater degrees [of obscuration], because equality is possible among those mental [actions] that are completely obscured, those vocal [actions] that are slightly obscured, and those physical [actions] performed only once. 12.50

[37] He states the specific recipient who is the cause for the excellence of the fruit of giving: "Whatever gift is given to a poor householder, and especially to one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), that gift brings about auspiciousness. (12.51) Thus it is said.

The word "especially" (*viśeṣataḥ*) is connected individually with each of the three qualifiers of the excellence of a worthy recipient (*pātra*), namely, being a householder and so forth. This being the case, that which is given to one who has a large family, who is in great poverty, and whose status as a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) is preeminent due to the extensive recitation of many Vedas, becomes the cause of an excellence of auspicious fruit. || 12.51 ||
He states that there is a greater transgression in seizing the land belonging to another:
"A stealer of land is not purified by [the merit of] constructing ponds, wells, and tanks, nor by performing hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, nor by the gift of ten million cows" (12.52).

It is well known in other scriptures that each of these, such as tanks and the like, is a cause of purification. From the statement that one is not purified even by many such means, it is understood that there is an excess of sin (pratyavāya). Nor is this statement intended to mean that purification does not exist at all; for if that were the case, its mention among the rules for stealing gold—where purification is possible—would be inconsistent. (12.52)
Now, he states a certain specific rule regarding a woman in her menses:
"The woman in her menses must bathe for eighteen days;
after that, she should observe a three-night period," so said the sage Uśanas (verse 12.53).

If a woman, having bathed on the fourth day from the onset of her menses, becomes menstruating again within eighteen days from that point, she should simply perform a bath; she need not observe the three-night period of impurity. However, if the appearance of the menses occurs after eighteen days, the three-night period of impurity must be observed. (12.53)
In connection with the discussion on a woman in her menses, he states the measurement of space required when there is an intervention by *caṇḍālas* and others who have come to mind:

"A *yuga*, two *yugas*, three *yugas*, and four *yugas*, [are the distances] for *caṇḍālas*, those born of a birth-impurity, a menstruating woman, and an outcaste, respectively. (12.54) Thus it is said.

"Downwards" means in reverse order. Therefore, it should be applied as follows: for one who has fallen [from caste], the period of impurity lasts for one *yuga*; for a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), for two *yugas*; for a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), for three *yugas*; and for a *caṇḍāla*, for four *yugas*. The measurement of a *yuga* is to be understood from common worldly usage. (12.54)
[39] Having stated the absence of an intervening period, he now describes the purification:
"Then, by mere proximity, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on."
"Having bathed, one should look at the sun [if one] touches [it] through ignorance.

(12.55). By the word *mātra*, touching is excluded. In the absence of touching, there is only the bath. Even in the case of touching, if it was done unintentionally (*akāmakṛta*), there is both the bath and looking at the sun; if done intentionally (*kāmakṛta*), a doubling of the penance or another means of purification is to be understood. In cases such as a narrow pass (*saṅkaṭa*) and so forth, even though [the sun] is present, there is no bath in the absence of touching, because Saṃvarta accepts an intervention according to what is possible: "Especially in a narrow pass, on uneven ground, and in a difficult terrain..."
"And on the road to the market town, one should proceed according to the circumstances that may arise.

Now, he prohibits drinking water from a pond or similar body of water with the mouth, as one would do like an animal: "A Brāhmaṇa who, though his hands are available, drinks water with his mouth due to weakness in knowledge, will certainly be born in the womb of a dog" (12.56).

Beginning with the words, “The five meritorious baths” (ParSm 12.9), and ending with the passage, “He is certainly born into the womb of a dog” (ParSm 12.56), this entire body of text sets forth what remains of the rules of conduct (*ācāra*). A detailed exposition of almost all of this has already been provided in the first section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*); therefore, it is not elaborated upon here again. Nor should a charge of redundancy be suspected in this case, because what was summarized there in the root texts is explained here in detail. (12.56)
Now follows the remainder of the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta*).
In that regard, he states the expiation for one who, due to some cause, has violated an oath:
"But if a man, being angry, should say to his wife, 'You are unapproachable [to me],'..."
If he desires her again, however, he should cause her to hear it in the midst of Brahmins.
One who is exhausted, angry, blinded by darkness, or afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fear,
having failed to perform a meritorious gift, must observe a three-day penance.
He should perform ablutions at the three daily sessions at the confluence of great rivers;
and upon the completion of the vow, he should give a cow and feed ten Brahmins.

Thus: suppose someone, having become angry for some reason, should declare to his own wife that she is off-limits, saying, "From now on I will not have intercourse with you; you are my mother or my sister. Later, when his anger has subsided and he desires to go to her again, he should then confess his transgression before the assembly.

“At the time of my oath and vow, I was exhausted by traveling to another village or by household duties. When my word was transgressed, I became angry. Even though she was free from fault, I was blinded by the confusion of darkness and devoid of discernment. I was also tormented by hunger, thirst, or fear of the king and others. Therefore, this vow of unapproachability was prompted by such defects and not preceded by discrimination. For this reason, may you graciously grant me penance for this sin.”

Thus it is said. However, he who makes a vow preceded by an oath, saying "I shall give a gift," yet does not give anything to the Brāhmaṇa who has arrived with that very intention; or likewise, having resolved upon a pilgrimage to Kāśī or the like, goes some distance however it may be, and subsequently, having fallen into lack of faith, does not perform that meritorious act—in these three circumstances, this expiation prescribed by the Brahmins must be performed. Having gone to the confluence of two great rivers, one should observe a fast for three nights preceded by bathing at the three periods of the day (triṣavaṇa). On the fourth day, one should give a cow and feed ten Brāhmaṇas. Regarding these initial circumstances, Yama states the expiation according to the distinction of social classes (varṇa):
But when one says out of anger that his own wife is "unapproachable," a Brahmin shall perform the Prājāpatya penance, and a Kṣatriya for nine days.

"A Vaiśya shall perform it for six nights, but a Śūdra shall perform it for three nights" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 6.13). Regarding one who, having made an oath—"I have killed someone belonging to any one of the four castes in this matter"—does not carry out that task, Yama himself has declared the penance: "But having made an oath concerning the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, O King..."
A killer of a Brahmin shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow while subsisting on barley gruel.

For killing a Kṣatriya, a twice-born man shall perform a Parāka penance; for killing a Śūdra, he shall observe the Prājāpatya vow; and for killing a Śūdra, a Śūdra himself shall perform the three-night vow.
Some say that the killing of a *vṛṣala* is not a sin, [claiming it is] false;
this is not my opinion, because he becomes [the killer] by means of his hand. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.206–208) Manu also has stated the expiation for falsehood.
They should worship Sarasvatī with sacrificial porridges (caru) dedicated to the deities of speech,
thereby effecting the supreme expiation for that sin of falsehood.

[43] Or one should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the rule with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, or with the verse beginning "ud" addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses addressed to the Waters. Thus [says] Prajāpati. (MDh 8.105–06)
"One who has drunk Soma but speaks untruth should perform the supreme penance for three nights,
or he should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with ghee using the *saptavatī* verse.
Thus says Hārīta regarding the speaking of falsehood after having made a promise.
"Having made a promise, if one speaks falsely, whether it be a lie or even a truth,
he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow accompanied by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Regarding the student (brahmacārin), Garga says:
For speaking untruth, one should observe a vow for three nights or one night;
having eaten [impure food] for a month, a celibate student (brahmacārī) should undergo the rite of re-consecration again.
[44] For practice, the Aindava penance is prescribed; one who is lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) should perform it twofold;
one living in the forest (vānaprastha) should perform it threefold, and an ascetic (yati) should perform it fourfold.
"In the eating of meat, in speaking untruth, and likewise in carrying out a corpse.
However, on certain specific occasions, even an untruth may be spoken intentionally. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"In a case where there is the execution of those belonging to the [four] castes, a witness should speak an untruth."

"To purify that [lie], the *sārasvata* oblation (*caru*) must be offered by the twice-born" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.83). If one were to speak only the truth, it would follow that the killing of a member of the twice-born—a much more serious sin—would become the cause [of the lie]. To prevent that sin, even a small falsehood may be spoken. For its purification, the *sārasvata caru* is to be offered. Even when the killing of oneself would result from speaking the truth—as in the case of the killing of a member of the twice-born—one should speak a falsehood. Thus Vyāghra says: "If, upon speaking, there would be extreme suffering for oneself..."
In this regard, it must be said that his speech is false, like the words of a tiger. Thus it is said.

|| 12.57–59 || The king, having heard that speech, was filled with joy; he spoke these words to his ministers: “Let the city be adorned for the festival of the daughter of the mountain. || 57 || Then the ministers, having heard those words, quickly decorated the city, which was like the city of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera). || 58 || At that time, the city appeared like Amarāvatī, with its houses and palaces made of gold and jewels, and its streets lined with banners and garlands. || 59 ||
[45] He states the penance for eating at the house of a wicked Brāhmaṇa: "In the case of a Brāhmaṇa of evil conduct who practices forbidden acts..."
Having eaten food, a twice-born man should observe one day of fasting.

Thus [it is said]. "Bad conduct" (*durācāratva*) consists in the non-performance of what is enjoined. Having eaten in the house of a Brahmin who does not perform what is enjoined but practices what is forbidden, one should fast for one day. (12.60)
He states another expiation for that inability:
"By eating the food of a brahmin who is of virtuous conduct and likewise a knower of the Vedānta, a man is released from sin within the interval of a day and night. (12.61)

Thus: the sin committed by eating even once or repeatedly in the house of a wicked Brāhmaṇa on a single day is purified by eating at the house of a well-conducted Brāhmaṇa who is a Vedāntin; or rather, whatever collection of minor sins such as the killing of ants has been incurred on a single day, all that is purified by eating distinguished food. Baudhāyana also states that purification from sin occurs through eating food from a pure household: "One who subsists on alms from Agnihotra-observers is purified in one month."
To those who dwell as forest-dwellers following the Yāyāvara tradition, [it is given] in ten or five days.
"One who possesses wealth for a single day is purified by food on one day;
one who is devoted to the *kapota-vrata* is purified by drinking water for three days. (BDh 4.5.27–28) || 61 ||
He states the expiation for being defiled at the time of death:

"In the case of contamination by food-leavings from above, leavings from below, [contamination] in the intermediate space, or likewise during one's menstrual period, as well as in the event of death while in a state of impurity, one should perform three *kṛcchra* penances. (12.62) Thus it is said.

At the time of death, "vomiting and so forth" refers to impurity discharged upward, while "urine and so forth" refers to impurity discharged downward. When either of these occurs, the performer of the funeral rites—such as a son—should perform three *prājāpatya* penances as a substitute for the wealth [that would otherwise be required]. Death on a tree or similar structure is "death in the intermediate space" (*antarikṣamṛti*). Death of a woman in her courses or a woman who has recently given birth is "death involving ritual impurity" (*aśaucamaraṇa*). In both these types of death, one should perform three *kṛcchra* penances. (12.62)
He states four substitutes for the *prājāpatya-kṛcchra*:

[47] "A *kṛcchra* penance, ten thousand recitations of the Goddess (*devī*), two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and bathing with the head unwet at a sacred pilgrimage site (*puṇyatīrtha*) twelve times. (12.63)
"For a pilgrimage of two yojanas, one kṛcchra penance is prescribed. Thus it is said.

The goddess is Gāyatrī. Ten thousand recitations (*japa*) of her constitute one "ten-thousand" (*ayuta*). This is the first substitute (*pratyāmnāya*). Two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) are the second substitute. One whose head is not wet is "one with a dry head" (*anārdraśiras*); bathing for such a person is "bathing with a dry head. Having bathed once and performed the ancillary rites, one should dry the hair and then perform a second bath. Twelve such baths performed at a sacred pilgrimage site (*puṇyatīrtha*) constitute the third substitute. Traveling two *yojanas* toward a sacred pilgrimage site is the fourth. Likewise, staying in water (*udakavāsa*) and other such practices should be understood as substitutes. This has been stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
The Kṛcchra penance, ten thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, likewise staying in water,
and the gift of a cow to a Brahmin— these four are equal.
One should perform a thousand oblations of sesame seeds and the study of a chapter of the Veda;
likewise, twelve Brahmins should be fed, as well as the Pāvaka sacrifice.
Or other purifying things, the wise say are equal [in efficacy]. (12.63)
Now he states the penance for the emission of semen:
"If a householder should intentionally cause the emission of semen upon the ground... (12.64).
"One should recite the mantra of the Goddess a thousand times along with three breath-restraints.
Regarding an act committed unintentionally, Yājñavalkya says:
"With these two [verses], 'Whatever semen of mine today... and so forth, one should consecrate the spilled semen."

“He should touch [the area] between the breasts and between the eyebrows with that [semen] using the nose. (YDh 3.278). This is the opening of a single verse: “Whatever semen of mine today... (TaitĀ 1.30.2). The subsequent mantra is: “May my virility return to me” (TaitĀ 1.30.2). With these two mantras, having taken up the semen with the nose, he should touch the space between the two breasts or the two eyebrows. Regarding the emission of semen by ascetics (*yatins*) and forest-dwellers (*vanavāsins*), the rule stated by Kaṇva should be observed:
“Having intentionally emitted semen, a householder (*gṛhastha*) should touch [water] with the *vāruṇī* verses.”
Both the forest-dweller and the ascetic should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
[49] Thus it is said. Regarding dreams, however, Kāśyapa says:
"Having discharged semen in a dream, one should perform three prostrations to the Sun;
a forest-dweller and an ascetic likewise should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite three times. (KāśSm 6.11)

Regarding the religious student (*brahmacārin*), Manu says: "If a twice-born religious student should involuntarily emit semen during sleep, he shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with 'punar mām'. (MDh 2.181)

Regarding fear and other such circumstances, Prajāpati said: "If one has emitted semen unintentionally during a state of fear, illness, or in a dream, one should worship the Sun and then mutter the verse beginning with 'punar mām'. (PraSm 3.19)

Regarding the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*), Hārīta says: "Whatever a temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*) might do, whether intentionally or unintentionally, the lifelong celibate student (*brahmacārī naiṣṭhikaḥ*) must perform that very same act twice over. (12.64)
Now he states the expiation for the great sin of killing a Brahmin:
"But toward one who has killed a Brahmin, [the king], endowed with the four branches of knowledge, [should act] according to the rule. (12.65)

"One should prescribe the journey across the ocean bridge as the expiation. Thus [it is said]. The four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, are the "fourfold knowledge" (*caturvidyā*). One who is "endowed with them" is one who possesses their study and performance. By this, the entire assembly (*pariṣad*) proclaimed by Aṅgiras—beginning with the phrase "one learned in the four Vedas and a dialectician" (AṅgSm 3.19)—is indicated. The "ocean bridge" (*samudrasetu*) is the bridge built over the ocean by the son of Daśaratha. One should prescribe that journey for a man who has killed a Brāhmaṇa as something to be performed according to the prescribed rules. (12.65)
It was stated [above] that this should be done "according to rule. Out of the desire to know what that rule is, he describes its procedure:
"On the path of the bridge, he should practice begging for alms from the four castes. (12.66)
"Excluding those who persist in forbidden acts, [the mendicant] should be without umbrella or shoes.

(12.66) Those acts which are contrary to the duties prescribed by the scriptures for the four castes are "forbidden acts" (*vikarma*); those who remain intent upon such acts are "those who persist in forbidden acts" (*vikarmastha*). Excluding them, one should beg for alms on the path to the Setubandha from among the four castes who abide according to the scriptures. The phrase "without umbrella or shoes" should be understood to apply not only at the time of begging, but also while traveling on the road. (12.66)
[51] Regarding the manner of speech to be uttered by one who is begging for alms, he says:
"I am indeed a doer of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins. (12.67)

"I stand at the doors of houses seeking alms, a slayer of a Brahmin. Since the public confession of one's sin is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the penance, he should proclaim his own sin at every house where he begs for alms with such words as "I am a doer of evil deeds. Regarding the harm that results from failing to confess, Aṅgiras says:
"Having committed a sin, one should not conceal it; if it is concealed, it increases" (AṅSm 1.47).

Regarding the three terms "one who has performed evil deeds," "one who commits a great sin," and "a slayer of a Brahmin": there is no tautology because they express, respectively, a great generality, an intermediate generality, and a specific instance thereof. || 12.67 ||
He states a specific location for one who is weary from travel to rest:
"And he should dwell in cow-pens, as well as in villages and cities. (12.68)

"In penance groves, at sacred fords, or by rivers and springs. Since it is impossible to station many cows within a village, the term *gokula* refers to a pasture area established in the forest for their placement—where, due to the fear of tigers and other predators, dwelling outside the village is impractical. In such cases, having entered a village or a city, one should reside in a meritorious spot such as a cow-pen or a temple. However, if there is no danger from tigers and the like, one may dwell in penance groves and similar places. Sacred fords (*tīrtha*) other than those near rivers and springs include Pampā Lake and others. (12.68)

The disclosure of one's sins occurs not only in the houses of mendicants, but also in one's own dwelling places; thus he says: "Having disclosed his sin in these [places], he goes to the ocean for merit. (12.69)
Ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long,
it was constructed by heaps of earth gathered under the command of Rāmacandra.

"Having seen the bridge of the ocean, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin. Thus, when the pilgrimage has been performed according to the stated method, preceded by the confession of the sin, and the bridge is seen, that sin is destroyed. (12.69–70)
He states what must be done immediately after seeing the Setu: "Having seen the Setu, one whose self is purified should plunge into the ocean. (12.71)
[53] Thus; the meaning is clear. 12.71.
For the king who is unable to see the bridge, he states an alternative:
"Or the king, the lord of the earth, should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice."

Even for one incapable of performing the Aśvamedha sacrifice, its meditative worship (upāsana) should be understood as the alternative. Thus it is heard in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa: “By this indeed the gods crossed over all evil; by this they even crossed over the murder of a Brahmin. He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice and he who knows it thus crosses over all evil; he crosses over the murder of a Brahmin” (TS 5.3.12.1–2). And that meditative worship is elaborated upon in the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, beginning with the passage: “The Dawn, verily, is the horse’s... (TS 7.6.25.1). || 12.72 ||
He describes what must be done by one who has returned after completing the pilgrimage to Setu:
"Having returned once more, he approaches for the purpose of dwelling in his home. (12.72)
Together with his sons and servants, he should provide a feast for the Brahmins;
he should also give one hundred cows as a sacrificial fee to those learned in the four Vedas.

"By the grace of Brāhmaṇas, even a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa is liberated. Here, "the grace of Brāhmaṇas" refers to such statements as, "You are free from sin; you are purified. And this vow is to be understood as applying to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of virtuous qualities. Regarding this very subject, Yājñavalkya states another vow:
"Or, by giving sufficient wealth to a worthy recipient, one may attain purification. (YDh 3.250)

One should give to a worthy recipient (*pātra*) endowed with knowledge and austerity cows, land, gold, and so forth, sufficient for the means of livelihood. By the word "or" (*vā*), it is implied that one may give one's entire property or a house together with its furnishings. As Manu says:
"Or one should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
or wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings. (MDh 11.76)
The settled rule is that for one who has no son, there is the gift of all his possessions; for one who has a son, there is the gift of his house along with its furnishings. 12.72–73.
Now we shall describe the regulations for the specific vows prescribed by other sages. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"Bearing a skull as his banner and subsisting on alms while proclaiming his deed, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall attain purification after twelve years of restricted diet. (YDh 3.243)

He must carry the skull-bowl of the Brāhmaṇa he himself killed as his banner, in accordance with the traditional law of Manu: “Having made a skull-banner” (MDh 11.72), and the traditional law of Śātātapa: “A Brāhmaṇa, having caused a Brāhmaṇa to be slain, shall take that very man’s skull-bowl and wander among the sacred fords” (ŚāSm 5.26). Both of these must be held in the hand, according to the traditional law of Gautama: “With a skull-bowl and a *khaṭvāṅga* in his hand” (GDh 22.4). By the word *khaṭvāṅga*, a banner consisting of a skull-bowl mounted on a staff is understood. For the purpose of begging, however, a different earthen bowl must be taken, according to the traditional law of Gautama: “With an earthen bowl in his hand, he shall enter the village for alms” (GDh 22.6). Likewise, Śaṅkha says: “The slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, permitted by the assembly, carrying a *khaṭvāṅga*, wearing the skin of a donkey, eating the remains of food fallen into an earthen vessel, proclaiming his own deed, shall subsist on alms, eating only once a day; making his dwelling in an empty house, by a river, at the foot of a mountain, under a tree, or in a cave—he thus attains purification in twelve years” (ŚaṅSm 16.9). He must be a dweller in the forest and so forth, as Manu has said: [Manu 11.78–80] “Let him always dwell in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, practicing austerities, sleeping on the bare ground, and wearing matted hair and a garment of bark. Let him carry a skull-bowl and a staff, and let him always proclaim his deed. Let him remain chaste, avoiding the houses of all, and seeking alms only once a day at the proper time. By this conduct, a killer of a Brāhmaṇa becomes purified in twelve years. [Manu 11.73] “Or, if he desires to perform a sacrifice, he may offer a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) or other sacrifices accompanied by many gifts; by such a sacrifice, he is immediately purified from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. [Manu 11.74] “Alternatively, having shaved his head and beard and putting on a red garment, he may walk toward the south-west, subsisting on water alone, until his body collapses. [Manu 11.75] “Or, if he desires to live in the forest, he may dwell there, subsisting on air, practicing austerities, and remaining chaste, until his body is released. Let him carry a skull-bowl and a staff, and let him always proclaim his deed. Let him remain chaste, avoiding the houses of all, and seeking alms only once a day at the proper time. By this conduct, a killer of a Brāhmaṇ
"A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having built a hut;
or, having shaved his head, he may dwell at the edge of a village, in a cow-pen, in a hermitage, or at the root of a tree, devoted to the welfare of all beings. (MDh 11.72, 78)

In the phrase “or having shaved his head,” the word “or” (*vā*) should be understood as indicating an option with respect to wearing matted hair (*jaṭā*). For this very reason, Saṃvarta states: “The killer of a Brāhmaṇa, for twelve years, shall wear hair-cloth, have matted hair, and carry a banner” (SaṃSm 109). Alms must be accepted in a reddish earthen bowl made of a broken shard. Thus says Āpastamba: “[58] He should enter the village for alms with a reddish earthen bowl made of a broken shard” (ĀpDh 1.9.24.14). In this regard, he should practice begging without forming the intention that he will obtain something refined. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: “He should go for alms to seven houses without prior selection, eating only once a day” (VaDh 21.9). And this practice of begging applies to one who is incapable [of the full penance]. Thus says Saṃvarta:
But the slayer of a Brahmin shall go to dwell in the forest, wearing matted hair and carrying a staff,
subsisting only on wild fruits and renouncing all desires.
If he cannot subsist on forest produce, he should wander the village seeking alms;
furthermore, being self-restrained and silent, he should beg for food from members of all four castes.
Having taken up alms-food, he should then go to the forest once more;
for as a forest-dweller, he should always touch water without weariness.
"Proclaiming his own sin, the slayer of a Brahmin, the worst of evildoers, shall perform the vow for twelve years according to this rule. Thus [it is said]. Yama states other restrictive rules:
Now, indeed, for the murder of a Brahmin, one should carry a skull-topped staff, eat sparingly,
and likewise proclaim one's own deed with a clay bowl.
He should avoid all dwellings of Brahmins and temples of the gods,
grieving for himself and calling to mind that Brahmin.
One should observe the vow as prescribed, honoring the gods and Brahmins;
thus, being firm in one's vows, always truthful, and having conquered the senses.
He should wander slowly among seven houses that are not previously known and have not been mentally selected— houses where the smoke has ceased and where no food is being consumed.
"O killer of a Brahmin, give me alms!"—having thus proclaimed his sin, he should wander about;
he should beg for food once a day, and if he does not obtain any, he should fast for that day.

"Thus wandering about while constantly confessing the killing of a Brahmin, he removes that sin of Brahmin-killing when the twelfth year is complete. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.21–26). Gautama states the rules regarding celibacy and other observances: "Or, carrying a skull-topped staff in his hand, he shall remain a celibate student for twelve years and enter a village for alms while proclaiming his deed. He should approach a noble person only when seen by him. Subsisting by standing and sitting, and touching water at the three ritual libations, he shall be purified. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 22.4–6). Kāśyapa also says the same.

"Carrying a sacred grass-bundle in his hand, holding a staff, with teeth stained by mud, covered in dust, dwelling at a holy ford, clad in *kuśa* grass, and wearing matted hair—one who kills a Brahmin shall become [purified].

(Kāśyapa Smṛti 3.14) This purification pertains to the case of killing a Brahmin unintentionally. And so, Manu, having introduced this twelve-year penance and described many other vows, concludes at the end:
"This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;

for killing a Brāhmaṇa intentionally, no atonement is prescribed" (MDh 11.89). Furthermore, in the case of repeated Brāhmaṇa-killing, the vow must also be repeated before the fourth instance. On this point, Manu and Devala state:
For the first instance of killing, one should perform the penance; for the second, one should perform double;
for the third, triple; and for the fourth, there is no atonement.
[61] Thus:
"Whatever sinful deed may have been committed once unintentionally—for that, this expiation has been seen by wise sages who know the Dharma. So it is said.

This is because Devala has stated that this [penance] applies to a sin committed once, through the performance of it only once; furthermore, the doubling [of the penance] and so forth is established by the principle that "the occasional rite must be repeated for each occasion. However, regarding one who does not kill a Brāhmaṇa directly, but rather becomes the cause of it through means such as insult, Sumantu says: "When a Brāhmaṇa, devoid of virtues, is insulted and suddenly kills himself out of anger due to causes such as [conflict over] a house or a field..."
