One should observe the Traivārṣika vow, or one should go to the Pratiloma Sarasvatī for the sake of purification from that sin; this is certain.

[62] Thus it is said. Regarding groundless abuse, he himself stated: "A brahmin who is utterly devoid of merit, if he dies out of anger after being groundlessly abused by one who is likewise utterly devoid of merit," [is reborn as a worm].

"One should perform this for three years, and thereafter undergo the *kṛcchra* penance for purification. However, when the person who caused the death is extremely virtuous while the one who committed suicide is utterly devoid of merit, then one should perform the vow for killing a Brahmin for only one year,
without shaving off the hair of the head, beard, nails, and so forth, in the forest.
A Brahmin practicing celibacy becomes purified in one year.

For it has been stated by that very [author]: "Just as the killer is liable for penance, or just as the one who provides the occasion, so too are the consenter and the others partakers of the penance. And thus says Paiṭhīnasi: "The killer, the instructor of the mantra, the facilitator, the instigator, the accomplice, and likewise the guide."
The supporter, the provider of weapons, the provider of food for one who performs forbidden acts,
the indifferent bystander if capable [of intervention], the one who points out the fault, and the one who approves— all these share in the sin.
[63] "One should prescribe an expiation for those who have committed an improper act, and likewise one should prescribe a punishment for them according to their capacity.

Among these, whoever is closer to the act of killing must perform a greater expiation; for one who is further removed from it, a lesser expiation should be prescribed in comparison. Furthermore, even for the direct perpetrator, there is a reduction in the expiation depending on the specific age. Regarding this, Yama says:
"One who is eighty years of age, or a child less than sixteen, as well as one who is diseased or a woman, deserve half of the expiation. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.241).
In some cases, that same author mentions a substitute for the performer [of the rite]:
"For one who is less than eleven years old but more than four years old,
the brother, the father, or another relative shall perform the penance" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 6.3).
As for that which was stated by the same author:
"Therefore, for this most ignorant person, there is neither offense nor sin;

there is no royal punishment for him, nor is an expiation required. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.240) This statement intends to indicate that the expiation is minimal; it does not, however, aim to establish the total absence of such an expiation.

"A quarter [of the penance] should be assigned to children; this is the rule for all sins" (Viṣṇu Dharmasūtra 1.46). By Viṣṇu’s mention of "children" (*bāla*), it is understood that one even younger than a child is even more minor [in fault]. Alternatively, let there be no sin for one younger than a child, since the text provides an explicit prohibition; for indeed, there is no burden too great for a scriptural injunction. As for the statement of Madhyama-Aṅgiras: "One should bestow a thousand cows upon worthy recipients according to the prescribed rule... [the following applies].
"Even a killer of a Brahmin shall be liberated from all sins. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 2.36) [65], and:
"But if the Brahmin is engaged in a Soma sacrifice, one should prescribe double the penance. (Yājñavalkyasmṛti 3.252)

This should be understood as applying to one who is unable to perform the double-vow penance prescribed by that very statement, because the expiation is exceedingly heavy. As for the statement of Śaṅkha: "Having killed [an Ācārya], one should prescribe vows for twelve years, six, three, or one and a half years; at the end of these, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, or half of that again, for all castes in their respective order," that refers to the killing of an Ācārya and others. And so says Dakṣa: "A gift to a non-Brāhmaṇa is equal [in merit]; to one who calls himself a Brāhmaṇa, it is double."
A gift given to a teacher yields a hundred thousandfold merit; that given to a uterine brother is inexhaustible.
"The specific results of giving increase respectively by a factor of two, three, ten, a hundred, a thousand, and infinitely; and it is exactly the same for the case of injury. (DaSm 3.25–26)

Furthermore, regarding that which was stated by Āpastamba: “Having built a hut in the forest, remaining silent, with a dog’s head as his banner and wearing a hempen garment, he should cover himself from the knees upward” (ĀpDh 1.9.24.11), and having begun thus, “Having killed a *śrotriya*, one should observe this very vow until the final breath; there is no restoration to this world for him” (ĀpDh 1.9.24–25)—that refers to the case of [killing] one's mother, father, teacher, and so forth. And likewise in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
“Having killed one's mother, father, or likewise a uterine brother...”
Having killed a guru and a learned brahmin...

Having begun thus, because this very penance (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed; *śāṇī-pakṣaḥ* means a portion of a garment made of hempen thread (*śāṇa-sūtra*). *Ā uttamād ucchvāsāt* means until the final breath, i.e., until death. *Pratyāpattiḥ* means restoration to social intercourse (*vyavahāra*). Regarding one who is incapable [of performing the full penance], Śaṅkha says: “Having killed [a Brahmin], one should prescribe vows for twelve years, six, three, and one and a half years respectively. At the end of these, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, half of that, and half of that again, for all castes in their respective order. “One should perform this very vow until the final breath. In this case, one who is incapable [of the full penance] should, after completing the twelve-year vow, make a gift of a thousand cows. For one incapable even of that, after completing the six-year vow, half of a thousand cows (five hundred). For one incapable even of that, after completing the three-year vow, two hundred and fifty cows. For one incapable even of that, the one-and-a-half-year vow; thereafter, one hundred and twenty-five cows. Thus, for all castes, according to their capacity, there is a cumulative sequence (*samuccaya*) of the twelve-year vow and the gifts of a thousand cows and so forth, following the order of precedence. And this should be applied only to the cases previously mentioned, because of the extreme gravity of the penance.

Now, one might object: since the four sets of vows, such as the twelve-year penance and so forth, have been described together with the four gifts, such as the gift of a thousand cows, and because of the statement, "in the sequence of all the castes," why should there not be an injunction for the four castes—beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—to perform these four vows respectively?
Do not say so; for [the text continues]: "The assembly for Brāhmaṇas shall be as prescribed, but for kings it shall be double."
"For Vaiśyas, it is declared to be threefold, and the penance is remembered to be like that of the assembly.
Likewise:
"Or a Śūdra, having killed a Brāhmaṇa, [must perform] four sets of penances."

Thus, according to the sequence of the statements from the *Aṅgiras* and *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇas*, since a greater penance is prescribed for the other castes in comparison to the Brāhmaṇas, the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) stated by us alone is superior. Now, one might object: "Let that be so in cases where a specific arrangement is declared by citing another scriptural statement as witness; but where an arrangement is declared without any other scriptural statement, how can a system devised by one's own imagination be trusted? Do not say so, for the authors of the *Smṛtis* themselves have stated that such [arrangements] must be formulated. And thus says Devala: [Devala’s verse follows...]

"Having ascertained the caste, capacity, and qualities [of the offender], as well as the nature of the offense, its connection, and so forth, one should prescribe the expiation accordingly. Thus it is said.

This twelve-year vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is to be completed either when the twelfth year is fully elapsed or earlier, upon obtaining the means for saving a Brāhmaṇa or similar causes. Thus says Śaṅkha: "He attains purification in the twelfth year; or in the interim, by releasing a Brāhmaṇa, or by rescuing twelve cows, or he becomes pure immediately from bathing in the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. This being the case, as for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"By saving a Brāhmaṇa, or by [saving] a dozen cows..."
Or likewise, one may attain purification by bathing at the final purificatory rite (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice.
Having seen on the road a Brahmin or even a cow afflicted by a long-lasting and severe illness, the slayer of a Brahmin becomes pure by restoring them to health.

"Having brought [the offender], if all the property of a Brahmin has been seized or destroyed, or if he has been killed, or if he has been wounded by weapons for that reason, he does not incur sin even while living"—this statement does not intend to prescribe another penance; rather, it intends to declare the completion [of the current one]. As for other penances, Manu has stated:
Or he may become a target for weapon-wielders at his own will;
or, with his head hanging downwards, he may throw himself three times into a kindled fire.
Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
Or he may travel one hundred yojanas toward Japan or any other [sacred place],
eating moderately and with his senses restrained, in order to expiate the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Or he should bestow his entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
or wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings.
"Or, eating sacrificial food, he should follow the Sarasvatī river against its current; or, with his diet restricted, he should recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times. (MDh 11.73–77).

All these options are to be determined according to whether the act was intentional or unintentional, and whether the person is learned or unlearned. Regarding the excessive repetition of an intentional act, Yājñavalkya says:
"Or rather, one should offer the body, beginning with the hair and ending with the marrow, with these mantras in due order, saying: 'Svāhā to the hairs' and so forth" (YDh 3.247).
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states eight mantras:

"I offer the body hairs to Death; by means of the body hairs, I cause Death to dwell [within me]. This is the first verse. "I offer the skin to Death; by means of the skin, I cause Death to dwell [within me]. This is the second verse. "I offer the blood to Death; by means of the blood, I cause Death to dwell [within me]. This is the third verse.

"I offer flesh to Death; by means of flesh, I cause Death to dwell [within me]. Thus is the fourth [oblation]. "I offer fat to Death; by means of fat, I cause Death to dwell [within me]. Thus is the fifth. "I offer sinew to Death; by means of sinew, I cause Death to dwell [within me]. Thus is the sixth.

[72] "I offer my bones to Death; by means of my bones, I cause Death to dwell [within me]. Thus for the seventh [oblation]. "I offer my marrow to Death; by means of my marrow, I cause Death to dwell [within me]. Thus for the sixth [oblation]. (VaDh 20.26).
Regarding all such vows that terminate in death, Madhyama-Aṅgiras states that they pertain to those who act out of their own will.
That penance which has been declared by the wise to be terminal—that is to say, ending with death—should be understood as pertaining to intentional acts; of this there is no doubt.
"If a man should ever commit a great sin out of desire, no purification for him is prescribed except by leaping from a precipice or falling into fire. Thus it is said.

As for that which was stated by Sumantu: "A killer of a Brāhmaṇa shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year; sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, confessing his deed, subsisting on alms, he shall frequent the sandy banks of divine rivers, confluences, hermitages, cow-pens, mountains, springs, and penance groves, remaining standing or in the *vīrāsana* posture. When the year is complete, by giving gold, gems, cows, grain, sesame, land, and clarified butter to Brāhmaṇas, he becomes purified" [73], that should be understood to apply to the killing of a wealthy fool who is merely a Brāhmaṇa by birth. Furthermore, as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "He shall subsist on water for twelve nights and fast for twelve nights" (VaSm 23.38), that is to be understood as applying to one who has resolved to end the killing of a Brāhmaṇa and has desisted from the intent to kill at that very moment. Moreover, as for the statement in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
But having killed a eunuch who is a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra;
one should also perform a Cāndrāyaṇa and two Parāka penances.

Thus, this should be understood as referring to one whose manhood is irrecoverable when the killing occurs intentionally. But regarding unintentional killing, Bṛhaspati says: "At the world-renowned confluence of the Aruṇā and the Sarasvatī, a twice-born man shall become pure by bathing at the three periods of the day and fasting for three nights."

[74] Thus. These [penances], beginning with the twelve-year penance and ending with the gift of wealth, apply only to a Brāhmaṇa. For a Kṣatriya and others, however, they are double and so forth. As Aṅgiras said:
"The assembly that is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas is considered to be double for kings;
for Vaiśyas it is declared to be triple, and the vow is remembered as being in accordance with the assembly."
Prajāpati also says:
"The vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa by those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes is double, triple, and even quadruple [respectively]."
As for the statement from the Caturviṃśatimata: "Whatever penance has been prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa by the great sages,
a Kṣatriya should perform three-quarters of it, and a Vaiśya should perform half."
A Śūdra shall perform one quarter [of the penance] even for all sins without exception.

Thus, this refers to cases other than the fourfold *sāhasa* offenses committed intentionally (*prātilomya*). For the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others as well, the penance should be determined in accordance with their respective punishments. Regarding the gradations of punishment, Yājñavalkya says:
"The infliction of punishment should be carried out according to the higher or lower status of the caste and class. (YDh 2.206)

This being the case, for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa by a consecrated Kṣatriya (mūrdhāvasikta), the penance is one of twelve and a half years, which is more than that prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa but less than that for a Kṣatriya. By this same method, the penance for those born of inverse unions (prātilomya) should also be inferred. Likewise, Aṅgiras has shown the gradation of penances even for those in the higher stages of life (āśramins): "If those in the other stages of life commit the sins described for householders, they should perform purification according to their degree of purity, until the instruction of a Brāhmaṇa."
Even if death should occur while one has already begun the performance of a penance, the destruction of sin still takes place. Thus says Hārīta:
"If the performer should die after having resolved upon the penance, he shall become purified on that very day, both in this world and in the next. (HārSm 21.9)
Vyāsa also says: "If a man strives for the sake of dharma but is unable [to complete it], he obtains that merit; of this I have no doubt. (VyāSm 3.41)
Even when one has attempted a killing, the expiation for killing must be performed. To this effect Yājñavalkya says:
"One should perform the vow even if he does not kill, provided he approached with the intent to kill" (YDh 3.252).
The phrase "according to the caste" (*yathāvarṇam*) is understood to follow here. For this very reason, another Smṛti states:
"Even without having killed, one should perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa according to the specific class [of the victim]. (Śānkhāyana Smṛti 1.26) || 12.72–73 ||
Intending to show that the killing of a woman engaged in a Soma-sacrifice constitutes a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), he states the penance:
"Having killed a woman engaged in a Soma-sacrifice, one shall observe the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. (12.74)
Thus [it is said]: "The wife of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is devoted to her husband and remains present at the Soma-pressings. For this very reason, Aṅgiras states:

"Having killed the blameless wife of a foremost twice-born man who has established the sacred fires, one should perform the vow for killing a Brahmin; and the same applies to one who kills an *Ātreyī* woman. (AṅSm 3.19)
[77] Having stated the expiation for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, he now states the expiation for the drinking of intoxicants:
"And a twice-born who has drunk intoxicants should go to a river that flows to the ocean and perform [the following]."
Then, when the Cāndrāyaṇa penance has been performed, one should provide a feast for Brahmins.
"And one should give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins.
Thus [it is said]. "Wine" (*madya*) is a liquid substance that causes intoxication, produced from the *panasa* fruit and so forth. Regarding this, Pulastya says:
"The wine made from *panasa*, grapes, *mādhūka*, dates, palmyra palm, and sugarcane..."
That which is produced from honey, *sairika*, *ariṣṭa*, *maireya*, and that which is born from coconut.

[78] “One should know that there are exactly eleven kinds of intoxicants that are equal [in gravity]. (Pulastya Smṛti 1.12–13) Upon drinking any one of these eleven intoxicants, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance on the bank of a great river, feed Brāhmaṇas, and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This rule applies to cases of intentional action. However, regarding unintentional consumption, Bṛhaspati says:
“Having drunk an intoxicant through negligence, a twice-born man should perform the Atikṛcchra penance.”
"One should perform his purificatory rite and feed Brahmins according to one's ability" (BṛSm 4.23).

This expiation for drinking liquor applies only to a Brāhmaṇa, not to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, because the prohibition against drinking liquor is directed specifically at the Brāhmaṇa: "Liquor, meat, *surā*, and *āsava* are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas."
Therefore, a Brahmin who partakes of the oblation for the gods must not eat that.
Thus it is stated in the *Smṛti*. Bṛhad-Viṣṇu also says:

"The liquor made from *mādhūka* flowers, that from sugarcane juice (*aikṣava*), that from *sīra*, *tāla* palm, dates (*khārjūra*), and *pānasa* fruit; likewise, that produced from honey (*madhūttha*), *mādhvīka*, *maireya*, and that derived from coconut."
"These ten intoxicants are impure for a Brāhmaṇa. Thus [it is said].
However, Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya permits the drinking of intoxicants for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya:
"A Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya may, under any circumstances, drink out of desire."
"Having drunk only liquor (madya) that is *surā*, one incurs no fault. Vyāsa also says:
"Both were intoxicated by honey-wine (*madhvāsava*), and both were anointed with sandalwood paste."
I saw Keśava and Arjuna eating together in a single row.
[80] Thus. Prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), if one drinks liquor, that expiation must be performed by the father or others. Regarding this, Jātūkarṇya says:
"If a boy who has not been initiated should drink liquor out of delusion, his mother, brother, and likewise his father, shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances for him. (12.75)
Having stated the penance for drinking intoxicating liquor in general, he now states the penance for drinking *surā*:
"Having drunk *surā* even once, one should drink *surā* that is red-hot like fire. (12.76)
"He shall thus purify himself in this world and in the next.
Surā is a specific liquid substance produced from flour and other ingredients. Thus says Manu:
"Surā should be known as being of three kinds: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that made from honey (mādhvī)."

"Just as one [type of liquor] is so, so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.94). In this context, the term *surā* is used in its primary sense for *paiṣṭī* (liquor distilled from flour), while it is used in a secondary sense for *gauḍī* (rum) and *mādhvī* (liquor made from honey). This is because Pulastya, after enumerating *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* among the eleven types of intoxicants, states: "Upon drinking *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*—which are non-primary forms of *surā*—even once, and upon drinking *surā* repeatedly, a Brāhmaṇa shall drink heated, intensely hot *surā* until his complexion becomes like that of fire and he dies" (PulSm 1.14). And likewise says Bṛhaspati:
"In the case of drinking liquor intentionally, one should cast that [hot] [substance] burning into his mouth;
having been completely consumed by it and died, he shall attain purification" (BṛSm 4.25).
Vyāghra states that death by means of that [substance] applies to the intentional or unintentional habitual drinking of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* liquors.
"Whether intentionally or unintentionally, having drunk liquor, the best of the twice-born, having then drunk that [liquor] while it is fire-colored [hot], shall be purified from that sin upon death.

In the case of intentional, single consumption of *paiṣṭī* liquor, death as stated in the root text (*mūlavacana*) should be understood. But in the case of unintentional consumption, Yājñavalkya says:
He said:
"Either clothed in hair or with matted locks, one should perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin;
or one should eat oil-cake or grain-husks at night for three years. (YDh 3.254)
And this practice of consuming *piṇyāka* and other substances for three years refers to the context of vomiting [the liquor]. Accordingly, Vyāsa says with reference to the vow of three years:
"A drinker of intoxicants shall perform this very vow when vomiting has been effected; and the consumption of *pañcagavya* is prescribed for him every day as a purification of the body. (VyāSm 2.51)
As for that which was stated by Manu:
"Or he may eat grains or oil-cake once at night for a year,
wearing clothes of hair, with matted locks and carrying a banner, in order to remove the sin of drinking liquor" (MDh 11.92).

Thus, that [penance] should be understood to apply when the contact is merely with the palate. Furthermore, as for what Devala stated: "In the case of drinking *surā*, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by drinking one of these—silver, copper, or lead—made red-hot like fire, until he abandons his body"; and also what Manu stated:
"Or he should drink cow-urine the color of fire, or water;
or milk, ghee, or even the liquid of cow-dung, until death. (MDh 11.91)
Thus, both of these [statements] have the same scope as the root text. Regarding one who knows the Veda, Aṅgiras says:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor, having performed the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, shall again attain equality with Brāhmaṇas; such is the Vedic revelation. Thus [it is stated].
Regarding the once-off drinking of secondary (gauṇa) liquor, Aṅgiras says:
"The best of the twice-born who, having drunk liquor, makes a gift of land and never drinks it again, becomes purified after being consecrated."

As for that which was stated by Sumantu: "For a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk *surā*, there is bathing in the waters of the ocean for six months while remaining submerged; he should offer eight thousand oblations of the *Sāvitrī* daily; there is a fast for three nights; he becomes purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance and by bathing at the concluding ceremony (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice"—this should be understood as referring specifically to the case of the *Bṛhaspatisava* sacrifice mentioned previously. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati: "Having drunk *gauḍī*, *mādhvī*, or *paiṣṭī* *surā*, a Brāhmaṇa should perform [the following penance]."
"The Taptakṛcchra, the Parāka, and the Cāndrāyaṇa [are prescribed] in succession" (BṛSm 4.61).

This should be understood as applying to the drinking [of substances] for the purpose of curing a disease that cannot be treated by any other medicine, because the expiation is light. For this very reason, it should be applied to cases where [the act] consists merely of the mental resolve. 12.76.
Now he states the penance for the theft of gold:
"Having himself stolen the gold of a Brāhmaṇa," (12.77).
Taking up a pestle, he should go into the presence of the king for execution;
slain by the king, he attains purification, and he is indeed released from his debt. (12.78)
"But that which is done intentionally deserves death, and not otherwise.
In this context, the word *suvarṇa* refers to gold possessed of a specific weight. And that specific weight has been shown by Yājñavalkya:
"A mote of dust situated in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*."
Eight of those [yūkās] make one *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*.
Three *gaura* make one *yava*; three of those middle-sized *yavas* make one *kṛṣṇala*; five of those *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*. (YDh 1.362–63)

He who steals gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa of the specified measure shall, for his own purification, go of his own accord to the presence of the king, taking up a club as the instrument of striking, in order to bring about his own death at the king's hand. Having gone there, he should announce: "Strike me thus. Then, by this execution at the king's hand using the club as the instrument, he becomes purified. If, however, he does not die from the blow of the club, then, being released by the king, he indeed attains purification. And so says Saṃvarta:
"Then, taking up a club, he himself should strike him once;

if that thief survives, he is then released from the theft. (Saṃsmṛti 120–21). Alternatively, the alternative view—*‘and he is indeed released’*—should be explained as follows: where there are many dependents of the thief, such as his sons, friends, and wife, who must be supported by him, and the king, out of compassion, thinking that if the thief were killed many would perish, does not execute the thief but instead releases him after imposing a fine or other punishment, then even in that case the thief is indeed purified.
Now, one might object: if this were the case, then according to the statement of Gautama, "A king who does not strike is a sinner" (GDh 12.45), the king would incur sin.
This is not so; for since that [statement] is motivated by compassion for those he is obligated to support and the like, it remains applicable even in cases other than those involving a thief.

Furthermore, one might ask: since the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is so utterly reprehensible, why is this alternative view—that he is "already liberated"—not explained as referring specifically to that case?
We say it is because of the contradiction with the words of Manu. And so says Manu:
"A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, shall confess his own deed and say: 'May your majesty punish me.'"
"Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by such execution the thief is purified, or a Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone. (MDh 11.99–100)

In this context, the side of execution applies to a Brahmin who is a mere bearer of the name; whereas the side of penance applies to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with qualities such as being present at a *savana* sacrifice. Nor should it be suspected that theft is impossible for such a person, for it is possible when, due to occasional and localized tamasic tendencies, an excess of greed arises. This being the case, the position that "he is indeed liberated" can also be applied to this subject. As for the theft that would be intentional, in that case this aforementioned execution should be understood to apply. Otherwise, in the case of theft through negligence or the like, one does not deserve execution. Nor should it be suspected that theft rooted solely in greed cannot be accidental; for instance, when one steals gold tied in the hem of a garment without knowing it to be gold, and having stolen it, gives it to another or destroys it rather than returning it to the owner—then even unintentional theft is certainly possible. In the case of such theft, purification through penance should be understood to apply, just as in the case of a Brāhmaṇa present at a *savana*. The specific details of the penance have been shown by Manu.

"But a twice-born man who, desiring to remove the impurity born of stealing gold through austerity, shall wear garments of hair and perform in the forest the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin" (MDh 11.101).
Regarding gold of a quantity less than one *suvarṇa*, the various distinctions of vows are shown in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
If [the skin] is struck even to the measure of the tip of a hair, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
likewise, for striking to the measure of a nit, a wise person should perform three rounds of breath control.
For a sin the size of a black mustard seed, one should perform four breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and recite the Gāyatrī mantra eight thousand times for the purification of that evil.
If [the theft] is the size of a cow- or mustard-seed, one should indeed recite the Sāvitrī mantra for one day;
for gold the size of a barley-corn, the penance lasts for two days.
Having stolen even a single *suvarṇa-kṛṣṇala* of gold, the best of the twice-born should perform the *sāntapana* penance in order to remove that sin.
[88] Having stolen even a single *māṣa* of gold, the lowest of the twice-born becomes purified after three months by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel.

"For the theft of gold, one should drink barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) for a year; beyond that, it should be known as ending only with life, or else the vow of a *brahmahā* (slayer of a Brahmin). Thus, the consumption of barley-gruel for a year pertains to the theft of gold slightly less than a *suvarṇa*; for regarding the theft of a full *suvarṇa*, a twelve-year penance is prescribed. As for that which has been stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
Or he should give gold equal to his own weight after performing a sacrifice;
or else, devoted to the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), he should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six years.
A learned man who wanders to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) is thereby liberated from the theft.

In that context, the gift of gold equal to one's own weight pertains to those who are extremely wealthy; the *kratu* sacrifice pertains to wealthy *śrotriya*s. Regarding the expiation for theft, everywhere the stolen property must first be restored to the owner; this applies especially when the theft involves gold or other property belonging to a *brahmana*.
The thief must restore the stolen property to its owner, but he shall pay an additional eleventh part as a fine.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*). However, when the king, due to incapacity, does not proceed to kill [the thief], then that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: “[99] A thief, with disheveled hair, should supplicate the king. Then the king should give him an axe made of *audumbara* wood. With that, he should take his own life. By dying, he becomes purified” (VaDh 20.31). *Audumbara* means made of copper. When, having stolen gold and consumed it, one returns it immediately out of remorse, then that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed: “Remaining for three years, eating only at every fourth mealtime” (ĀpDh 1.9.25.13). But regarding theft committed through mere mental intent, Sumantu says: “A stealer of gold becomes pure by subsisting on air for twelve nights” (VaDh 20.41). Regarding the repeated theft of a large quantity of the property of a Brāhmaṇa endowed with many virtues—such as being a teacher, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), or one engaged in a sacrifice—Vasiṣṭha’s statement should be observed: “[100] One who has no clothes, anointed with clarified butter, should take his own life starting from the feet by means of a fire of cow-dung. By dying, he becomes purified; so it is known” (VaSm 20.42). Thus, the expiation for the theft of gold has been explained. The expiation for violating the Guru’s bed is elaborated in the tenth chapter, in the passage beginning: “If one should go to his mother or his sister” (ParSm 10.8).
Now, the penance for association with outcasts (*patita*).
Manu has declared the penance for one who, having associated for a year with outcasts such as those who have killed a Brahmin (*brahmaha*), becomes an outcast himself:
"Whatever man enters into association with any one of these outcasts..."
"He should perform that very same penance for the purification of the contact" (MDh 11.181).

However, the Teacher, intending to show that in the Kali age there is no fault in contact [with sinners], did not prescribe a penance for such contact. For this very reason, in another Smṛti, among the things to be avoided in the Kali age, it is stated: "The fault of contact applies to those who are sinful" (SaṃSm 1.53).
He states that even though the fault of association does not necessarily cause loss of caste (*pātitya*), it does indeed result in mere sin:
"From sitting together, from lying down together, from traveling together, from conversing, and from eating together... (12.79).
"For sins indeed spread, like a drop of oil upon water.
(91) Just as a drop of oil cast upon water pervades everywhere, so too does the sin committed through association with one who has fallen pervade the person who associates with them. 12.79.
Under the pretext of the faults arising from association, he now states the general expiations for all those for whom no specific expiation has been previously mentioned:
"The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Yāvaka, and likewise the Tulāpuruṣa. (12.80)

"Following after cows indeed destroys all sins. Thus it is said. The *tulāpuruṣa* is a specific type of *kṛcchra* penance; its nature we shall explain further below. In every case where an explicitly prescribed expiation is not found, there one must perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances—either repeatedly or non-repeatedly—in accordance with the gravity or lightness of the sin. From this, it is established that all sins are destroyed. (12.80)

Thus, in this section on penance (*prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa*), we have explained those penances for sins beginning with miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*) and ending with mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) which were set forth by the Teacher in nine chapters; in doing so, we have cited other Smṛti texts that arose in connection with them and established their systematic application.
This concludes the establishment of the rules based on Smṛti passages not previously cited.
Now, having cited those which were previously not mentioned, we shall establish them;
therein is the nature of the *atipātaka* (grave sins).

In this regard, relying upon the enumeration of sins proclaimed by Viṣṇu, the statements concerning expiations are cited here in their proper sequence. Therein, Viṣṇu, having first enumerated the heinous crimes (*atipātaka*), defined their nature as follows: "Sexual intercourse with one's mother, sexual intercourse with one's daughter, and sexual intercourse with one's daughter-in-law—these are the heinous crimes" (ViDh 34.1). The expiations for these three are determined in the tenth chapter, within the section beginning, "If one should approach his mother... (ParSm 10.8). [Now follows] the nature of the mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*).

Following the *atipātaka* (heinous crimes), the *mahāpātaka* (great crimes) are enumerated, and their specific nature is defined as follows: “Killing a Brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, and violating the teacher’s bed—these are the *mahāpātakas*; and association with those who commit them as well” (ViDh 35.1–2). Among these, for the four [crimes] excluding the violation of the teacher’s bed, penances have been stated in the twelfth chapter by the passage beginning with “In the case of the fourfold knowledge” (ParSm 12.64) and ending with “the destroyer of all sins” (ParSm 12.81). However, regarding the violation of the teacher’s bed, the penance has been declared in the tenth chapter in the verse beginning with “Having approached the wife of his father” (ParSm 10.11).
The nature of secondary sins (anupātaka):
Following the major sins (mahāpātaka), the secondary sins are enumerated, and their nature is specified as follows:

The killing of a Kṣatriya engaged in a sacrifice, a Vaiśya, a menstruating woman, a pregnant woman, a cow of great size, an unknown fetus, or one who has sought refuge—these are equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. Giving false testimony and the killing of a friend—these two are equal to the drinking of liquor. The seizure of a Brāhmaṇa’s land is equal to the theft of gold. Sexual intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle, maternal grandfather, maternal uncle, father-in-law, or a king is similar to sexual intercourse with the wife of one’s guru; as is intercourse with the wives of one’s father or mother, or with the wives of a Śrotriya, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a friend. [94] Likewise, intercourse with one’s own sister, a female friend, a woman of the same lineage, a woman of a higher caste, a maiden, a menstruating woman, a woman who has sought refuge, a female ascetic, or a woman entrusted to one’s care. (ViDh 36.1–7)
Thus [ends the section].
Now follows the expiation for secondary sins (anupātaka).
Regarding that, Viṣṇu himself has stated the expiation.
"But these secondary sinners, like the perpetrators of mortal sins,
are purified by the horse sacrifice or by visiting sacred fords" (ViDh 36.8).

Among these, the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) pertains to a sovereign king (*sārvabhauma*), according to the Vedic injunction: "A sovereign king shall sacrifice with the horse sacrifice. Bathing at sacred fords (*tīrthasnāna*) pertains to others; that is the general expiation (*sādhāraṇaprāyaścitta*). Where a specific expiation is neither expressly stated nor implied, this general one is to be understood as applicable. Regarding the killing of a Kṣatriya engaged in sacrifice or the killing of a Vaiśya in similar circumstances, the expiation has been shown in the commentary on the sixth chapter in the passage: "Whether a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya" (ParSm 6.17). Likewise, the expiation for killing a pregnant woman or a woman of the Atri lineage has been declared in that same place. The expiation for killing an embryo whose sex is unknown has been described in the fourth chapter in the context of the verse: "And she who causes an abortion" (ParSm 4.17). Only the killing of one who has sought refuge remains. Manu, however, mentions other acts equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
"Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, malicious talebearing directed toward the king, and false accusations against one's teacher—these are equal to the killing of a Brahmin. (MDh 11.55).
Yājñavalkya also mentions other [sins]:

"Exceedingly severe abuse of gurus, reviling the Vedas, the killing of a friend, and the loss of what has been studied—these should be known as equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa" (YDh 3.228). In this context, for the killing of one who has sought refuge and similar acts, it should be understood that the penance for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa is reduced by one quarter. This is because the word *sama* ("equal") is seen to be used in the sense of "slightly less," as in expressions such as "the minister is equal to the king. Manu, however, states that the abandonment of what has been studied and other such acts are equal to the drinking of liquor.
"Denying the Vedas, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor. (MDh 11.56)

Regarding that, Vasiṣṭha states the penance for abandoning the Veda (*brahmajjhā*): “One who has abandoned the Veda, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should again receive the Veda from his teacher” (VaDh 20.12). And this penance refers to the abandonment of study through negligence. However, according to the opinion of Manu, if it is abandoned out of atheism (*nāstikatā*), the penance is one less a quarter than that for drinking liquor (*surāpāna-vrata*). Although Vasiṣṭha says: “[97] ‘In the case of falsely persisting against a teacher, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and bathed with one’s clothes on, one becomes purified by the teacher’s grace’” (VaDh 21.28), this should be understood as referring to a single instance committed unintentionally. For giving false testimony (*kauṭasākṣya*), which is enumerated by Viṣṇu, the penance lasts twelve years. And likewise, Śaṅkha speaks regarding the continued practice of that vow.

"Having given false testimony, as well as having misappropriated a deposit, and having abandoned one who has come for refuge—one should perform this very same vow. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 17.5). This refers to cases where the death of a person belonging to a [specific] caste would result from speaking falsely as a witness. Viṣṇu also shows another act equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.

"Whether reviled, beaten, or even deprived of his wealth, he with reference to whom one gives up his life—he is called a slayer of a Brahmin" (ViDh 3.46). Thus, in the absence of causes such as verbal abuse and the like, the fault of killing belongs only to the deceased, and not to the person intended. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:

"But if any twice-born man should abandon his life for no reason, the fault lies with him alone, and not with the person he might have named. Yājñavalkya also enumerated [certain acts] as equal to drinking liquor.

"Eating forbidden food, deceitfulness, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses—these are equal to the drinking of liquor. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.229)

In all such cases where parity is stated, the penance pertaining to that [standard case] should be performed with some reduction. That reduction is to be determined in accordance with the gravity or lightness of the occasion (*nimitta*). However, in the case of seizing land belonging to a Brāhmaṇa—which is equal to the theft of gold—since it is impossible to conceive of a reduction in penances ending in death (*maraṇāntika*), twelve-year vows and the like are to be applied as appropriate. Yājñavalkya mentions other acts equal to the theft of gold:
"The seizure of horses, gems, men, women, land, cows, and likewise..."
"For the misappropriation of a deposit is indeed equal to the theft of gold" (YDh 3.230). Manu also says:
"The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as [the theft] of men, horses, and silver..."
"And stealing gold from those belonging to the [highest] earth-like Vajra-classes is considered equal to stealing gold. (MDh 11.57).

Regarding acts such as sexual intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle and others, which are equal to violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpa*), this has been explained in detail in the tenth chapter within the section beginning with "And likewise in the case of approaching a maternal aunt" (ParSm 10.9).
[Now follows] the nature of minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Immediately after the secondary sins (anupātaka), Viṣṇu, having enumerated the minor sins (upapātaka), defined their nature as follows:

False testimony when it serves to elevate oneself; slander directed toward a king; persistent falsehood regarding one’s teacher; reviling the Vedas; abandoning what has been studied; and [abandoning] the sacred fire, mother, father, son, or wife; eating the food of those whose food should not be eaten or consuming forbidden food; seizing the property of others; adultery with another’s wife; officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom one should not sacrifice; living by a forbidden occupation; accepting gifts from the unworthy; killing a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, or cow; selling what should not be sold; [100] the state of being a *parivitti*—that is, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him—and the act of giving away a daughter in marriage to such a person; officiating at a sacrifice for them; becoming a *vrātya*; teaching for a fee; receiving instruction for a fee; exercising authority over all mines; operating large-scale mechanical works; injuring trees, shrubs, creepers, or medicinal herbs; living off a woman; practicing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*); engaging in root-magic (*mūlakarman*); undertaking actions solely for one’s own sake; failing to maintain the sacred fires; theft; failing to discharge one’s debts to the gods, sages, and ancestors; studying improper treatises; atheism; and immoral conduct. [101] Associating with women who drink liquor. These are the minor offenses (*upapātaka*). (ViDh 37.1–36)

Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya, however, cited certain minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as the non-payment of debts and others not mentioned by Viṣṇu: "Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, the non-payment of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, selling forbidden goods, and superseding an elder brother in marriage."
Receiving instruction for a fee, teaching for a fee, adultery, causing a younger brother to marry before an elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt.
Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of censured wealth;
atheism; the abandonment of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons.
Stealing grain, base metals, or livestock; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice; abandoning one's father, mother, or son; and the sale of a tank or a garden.
Violating a maiden, officiating at a sacrifice for one whose younger brother has married before him,
giving a daughter in marriage to such a man, dishonesty, and the breaking of a vow.
[103] Undertaking actions for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning Vedic study, the sacred fire, and sons, as well as the abandonment of kinsmen;
Cutting down trees for the sake of firewood, living by the killing of women or by medicinal herbs, the construction of lethal machines, vices, and the selling of oneself— these are [prohibited].
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the low-born, consorting with those of inferior birth,
likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), and being nourished by the food of others.
"Studying false scriptures, having authority over mines, and the sale of one's wife—each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka). (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.234–42)

Although this [rule], "And falsehood regarding one's own excellence" (*anṛtaṃ ca samutkarṣe*, MDh 11.55), was classified by Manu among the crimes equal to the killing of a Brahmin, by Yājñavalkya among those equal to the drinking of *surā* liquor, and by Viṣṇu among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), there is nevertheless no confusion whatsoever, because it is possible to state its threefold nature according to the distinction of the subject matter (*viṣaya*). That distinction of subject matter is now stated: If one should speak a falsehood by imputing a great crime—one that does not even exist—to a person who is hateful, in order for him to be killed by the king’s servants and others, that is equal to the killing of a Brahmin, because it results in death. However, if one, desiring gain, honor, or fame, speaks a falsehood in the royal assembly or elsewhere to manifest in oneself a knowledge of the four Vedas that does not actually exist, that is equal to the drinking of *surā* liquor, because of its extreme contemptibility. But if one speaks a false word in vain during a pleasant conversation or the like, without any benefit to another, for him this is a minor offense (*upapātaka*). Regarding the first two cases, the penance has already been stated. As for the third, Yājñavalkya speaks concerning that which is committed intentionally: [The text continues with the citation from Yājñavalkya.]
"Reciting 'May there be splendor in me,' one should mutter [the Sāvitrī] upon seeing one's own reflection in water;
likewise when one has seen something impure, or when there is restlessness, or even when a falsehood has been spoken. (YDh 3.279).
However, for an act committed unintentionally, that which was stated by Manu should be observed.
"Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, and having spoken untruths;
and after drinking water, one who is about to study, even if already pure, should sip water (ācamana). (MDh 5.145)

Speaking of another’s faults before the king, whether directly or indirectly, is calumny directed at the king (*rājagāmi paiśunyam*). There are two types of false persistence (*alīkanirbandha*) toward a guru. Among these, if one who is himself capable creates an obstacle to a guru’s acquisition of wealth and so forth by means of false persistence—such as when the guru is residing in the royal palace or elsewhere—this is the "false persistence" described by Manu as equal to the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). Alternatively, where the guru’s displeasure arises merely through verbal abuse and the like, this is a "false persistence" that constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*). Censure of the Vedas (*vedanindā*) is threefold. One type of censure is the persistent effort to establish the lack of authority of the Vedas after having studied the treatises of the Buddha, the Arhats, and others; this has been described by Yājñavalkya as equal to the murder of a Brahmin. The second type of censure is the disregard for the performance of duties prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, due to an addiction to the sciences of logic such as sophistry (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), even while maintaining the conviction in the authority of the Vedas. With this very point in mind, Manu said: [105] *etad uktaṃ bhavati |* (This is what is meant: *(Note: The provided text ends with the phrase "etad uktaṃ bhavati," which indicates a transition to further commentary.)*

“The twice-born who, relying on the treatises of logic (*hetuśāstra*), would despise both of these—he is an atheist and a reviler of the Veda; he should be excluded by the virtuous. (MDh 2.11) This censure was cited by Manu among those [sins] equal to drinking liquor. However, when someone, even while performing Vedic rites, does not have absolute faith in their fruit—thinking, “What will come of this? I perform it merely out of fear of public reproach”—those who censure him in this way, this censure is recited among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*).

In this manner, having considered the relative gravity or lightness of each of the various types of offenses enumerated—beginning with the abandonment of Vedic study—one must determine their internal subdivisions. In the verse, “Of fire, mother, father, son, and wife” (ViDh 37.6), the word "abandonment" (*tyāga*) also carries over from the previous context. These enumerated minor offenses (*upapātaka*) are designated as such because they are less serious than the previously mentioned heinous crimes (*atipātaka*), mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), and secondary sins (*anupātaka*). As it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
“Those sins which have been declared to be equal to mortal sins... [106]
"Those are designated as *pātaka*s (major sins), and that which is less than those is an *upapātaka* (minor sin).
Now follows the general expiation for an *upapātaka*.
Regarding that class of *upapātaka*s, Viṣṇu has declared the general expiation.
"But these men who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*) shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, or they may perform the *parāka*, or they may sacrifice with the *gosava*. (ViDh 37.35).

In this regard, when these [offenses] are repeated and occur in combination, the *gosava* sacrifice is to be understood as the penance. For each individual case, however, the *parāka* is for one who is capable, while the *cāndrāyaṇa* is for one who is incapable. Yājñavalkya also states a general penance:

"Purification for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) may likewise be achieved by the *cāndrāyaṇa*, or by drinking milk for a month, or again by the *parāka* penance" (YDh 3.265). By the word "likewise" (*evam*), the vow prescribed for cow-slaughter is extended [by analogy] here; for an extension (*atideśa*) has a narrower scope than a direct injunction (*upadeśa*). Certain ancillaries of the cow-vow, such as the cow-hide and so forth, are excluded in other contexts. And this set of four vows should be understood as optional alternatives based on one's capacity when the act was committed unintentionally. However, in the case of intentional (*kāmakāra*) commission:

[107] "Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (*upapātaka*) shall perform this very same vow, excluding that for the student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), or else the *cāndrāyaṇa* for the sake of purification.

Thus, what was stated by Manu should be understood as the three-month penance. And this general expiation is to be observed in the absence of a specifically prescribed expiation or when such a specific one is not found.
The specific expiations prescribed for each case.

We shall cite the specific penances as they occur, according to their applicability. Regarding the minor offense (*upapātaka*) of falsely persisting in a claim against a teacher, Viṣṇu says: “In the case of falsehood regarding one’s own excellence, false persistence against a teacher, or insulting him, one should subsist on milk for a month” (ViDh 54.54). Regarding the abandonment of the sacred fires (*agnityāga*), he says: “One who neglects the Veda and the fires should bathe at the three periods of the day, sleep on the ground, and subsist on alms once a day for a year” (ViDh 54.13). Vasiṣṭha also says: “He who casts away the fires, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should have them re-established” (ViDh 21.27). Manu also says:
A Brāhmaṇa who, out of his own will, neglects the sacred fires of the Agnihotra shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.
"If an Agnihotrin intentionally neglects the sacred fires for more than a month, he must perform both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances without hesitation. (MDh 11.129–30)

Hārīta states: “If the *agnihotra* has been neglected for one year, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance and then re-establish the fires. If it has been neglected for two years, one should perform both the *Sāntapana* and the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. If it has been neglected for three years, one should practice the *Kṛcchra* for one year and then re-establish the fires” (HārSm 3.19–21). Śaṅkha also says: “One who neglects [the fire] for a year should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance and give a cow as a gift” (ŚaṅSm 11.23). Bharadvāja says: “Upon the lapse of twelve days, there is a fast for three days; upon the lapse of a month, a fast for twelve days; upon the lapse of a year, a month-long fast and subsisting on milk. All of this should be applied appropriately according to the context as referring to the abandonment of the sacred fires due to laziness. As for what is stated in the *Bharadvāja-gṛhya*: “For up to ten nights, one should perform one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*; for up to twenty nights, there should be a fast; beyond that, up to sixty nights, one should fast for three nights; beyond that, up to a year, one should observe the *Prājāpatya* vow; and beyond that, as the time increases, so does the gravity of the fault”—that refers to the abandonment of the fires through negligence (*pramāda*). However, regarding abandonment due to atheism (*nāstikya*), Vyāghra says:
"A twice-born man who abandons the sacred fire out of atheism (nāstikya) should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
otherwise, there is the re-establishment of the fire (punarādhāna), as well as the giving of gifts.

Since the Prājāpatya is mentioned as an illustration, other vows should be inferred according to the gravity or lightness of the time of abandonment. Jātūkarṇya states the duty regarding these other vows:
"A Brahmin should offer barley into the fire even when the proper time has passed;
if the fire is lost, the twice-born man should perform the *ādhāna* rite again and offer it according to the rules.

This refers specifically to the *aupāsana* fire. Regarding the abandonment of one's wife, Śātātapa says: "One who abandons a wife from her youth is purified by subsisting on milk for a month. As for the expiation for eating what is unfit to be eaten or consumed, that has been explained in detail in the eleventh chapter.
Now follows the expiation for seizing the property of others.
Regarding the seizure of another's property, Manu says:
"Having committed thefts of grain, cooked food, or wealth out of desire, the best of the twice-born..."
One is purified by a year of penance (kṛcchra) if [the act] was committed in the house of one's own caste.
For the abduction of human beings, women, fields, or houses,
and for [the theft of] water from wells or tanks, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the purification.
Having stolen articles of small value from another's house,
one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of self-purification after returning that property.
For stealing food that is chewed or swallowed, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats,
and for taking flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
clothing, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast of three nights.
For stealing gems, pearls, corals, copper, silver,
iron, brass, or stones, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
"For cotton, silk, wool, cloven-hoofed and single-hoofed animals, birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must drink milk for three days. (MDh 11.162–68).
Among these subjects, a specific penance according to the specific quantity of grain is stated in another Smṛti:
"For one who steals more than ten jars of grain, there is corporal punishment.
As for that which was stated by Jābāli:
"In the case of sesame, grain, food, clothing, beds, and meat..."
One should perform this vow with a concentrated mind for half a year.

Thus, this refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally, because of its minor nature. Regarding, however, the theft of edible food sufficient for a single meal, Paiṭhīnasi says: "In the case of stealing enough food, whether chewed or swallowed, to fill the stomach, one should subsist on *pañcagavya* for three nights. As for those other penances shown by other sages regarding the matters mentioned by Manu, there is no dispute concerning those penances that are identical. The distinction is that those which are lesser apply to unintentional acts, while those which are greater apply to intentional and habitual acts. In this regard, the scriptural authorities are as follows:

For the theft of substances of little value, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance. For the theft of edible foods, drinks, vehicles, beds, seats, roots, flowers, and fruits, one must drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). For the theft of grass, wood, trees, dry food, molasses, clothing, leather, and meat, one should fast for three nights. For the theft of gems, pearls, corals, copper, silver, iron, and bell-metal, one should eat only grain-particles (*kaṇa*) for twelve days. For the theft of cotton, silk, wool, and the like, one should subsist on milk for three nights. For the theft of cloven-hoofed or single-hoofed animals, one should fast for three nights. For the theft of birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, ropes, and bamboo articles, one should fast for one day.
"Having returned the stolen property to the creditor by some means,
one should then perform a penance for the removal of that taint. Thus says Jābāli (ViDh 52.7–14).
Having stolen horses, cattle, land, or a maiden, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
having stolen small animals, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Molasses, cotton, grain, clarified butter,
salt, cooked food, medicine, oil, a bed, clothing, and sandals.
[113] For bronze, iron, copper, or lead, the penance is a *kṛcchra* or even half a *kṛcchra*.
This applies when [these metals] are found in water, or among fruits, roots, flowers, leaves, and fragrant substances.
For the destruction or theft of earthenware, honey, or meat, a quarter-kṛcchra penance is prescribed;
for the destruction or theft of other items, one must satisfy the owner first.
Having confessed his sin to the Brahmins, he becomes fit for expiation; however, a Brahmin who, through negligence, has stolen the wealth of the social classes [must perform penance].
And whatever expiation has been prescribed, one should perform it with the consent of Brāhmaṇas,
in the case of stealing the property of a king, women, or the common people.
"And in the case of the theft of wealth, one should perform the vow for a year.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for approaching the wife of another is set forth in the tenth chapter.
[Next is] the expiation for officiating at a sacrifice for those for whom one should not officiate.
Regarding officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, Manu has said: "By performing sacrifices for *vrātyas*, by performing funeral rites for others,
by practicing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and by performing the *ahīna* sacrifice, one removes the taint through three *kṛcchra* penances" (MDh 11.197).

As for that which was stated by Pracetas, having enumerated those who officiate at sacrifices for Śūdras and others: “These shall perform the penance of the five fires, lying in the open air, and lying in water, respectively during the summer, the rainy season, and the winter; they shall eat barley-gruel mixed with cow’s urine for one month,” that refers to cases of habitual practice committed intentionally. As for that which was stated by Yama:
“If a Brahmin priest engages in service for a person of the Śūdra caste, whether out of affection or for the sake of wealth, the Kṛcchra penance is his purification” (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.287).

Thus, that [rule] refers to the case of one who is incapable [of performing other penances]. As for what was stated by Gautama: “In the case of employing forbidden mantras, one should mutter the *Anuvākas* a thousand times” (GDh 22.33), that refers to the case of intentional repetition. As for what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi: “A priest who officiates for Śūdras becomes purified by renouncing all property, after performing a thousand breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) repeated ten times,” that refers to the case of unintentional repetition. Regarding the acceptance of improper gifts (*asatpratigraha*), Yājñavalkya says: “Dwelling in a cow-pen, a student (*brahmacārī*) shall observe the milk-vow (*payovrata*) for one month.”
"One who is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī is purified from the acceptance of improper gifts" (YDh 3.290).
Regarding this, the number of recitations has been shown by Manu:
"Having recited the Sāvitrī three thousand times with a concentrated mind..."
"By drinking milk in a cow-pen for a month, one is released from the sin of accepting what should not be accepted. (MDh 11.194).
This should be understood to apply when both the donor and the object are [unlawful]; however, when either one is absent, it has been shown in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
By means of the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice, all terrible forms of receiving gifts are purified;
likewise by the Aindava, the Mṛgāreṣṭi, or by some [sacrifice] dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
"By the mere hundred-thousand-fold recitation of the Goddess's mantra, one is purified from the acceptance of improper gifts.
As for the statement of Vṛddhahārīta:
"Having accepted a gift from a king, one should always dwell in water for a month."
Subsisting on milk during the sixth mealtime, he is liberated when the month is complete.
"Having constantly gratified the twice-born with their desires, he who is ever firm in his vows... (Vṛddha-Hārīta-Smṛti 11.71–72).

This refers to the acceptance of a black antelope skin and other such items during times of distress, such as at Kurukṣetra or during an eclipse. Regarding the acceptance of small amounts of wealth, Hārīta states: "Upon accepting gems, garments, cows, and the like, one should mutter the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times" (Hārīta-Smṛti 21.3).
The same is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
"But when even a mere alms-meal has been accepted, one should recite the mantra for the sake of merit. Thus it is said. Also in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"When all [foods] are prohibited, one should assign a sixth part [as permissible]."

The phrase "for the sake of giving" is to be understood as the ellipsis. However, if one lives by improper occupations (*vikarman*), the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is required. Accordingly, Yama, having enumerated actors and others who live by improper occupations, says:
"For all of these, a means of restoration must be sought;
a twice-born man who consumes their food should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 6.13)
Nārada also says:
Wealth that has been acquired solely through censurable action is purified either by its renunciation or by the pursuit of dharma.

"An object that has come into one's possession through unjust means should be cast into the waters; or, having been used, it should be instructed [to be given away], or it should be given to a knower of Brahman. (NSm 14.7–8).
The penance for the killing of a Kṣatriya and others is described in the sixth chapter; however, the penance for the killing of a cow is elaborated upon in the eighth and ninth chapters.
The expiation for the sale of items that should not be sold is shown in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Having committed the sale of liquor, one should perform four Saumya penances."
For consuming lac, salt, or meat, one should perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
For consuming honey, clarified butter, oil, or Soma, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
for milk, milk-rice, or cakes, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
In the sale of curd, ghee, sugarcane juice, jaggery, sugar-candy, and so forth,
as well as all substances cooked in oil or fat, one should perform the Parāka penance.
[118] A Brāhmaṇa who sells prepared food should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
however, for the sale of buttermilk, he should observe a fast, and for the sale of sour gruel, he should eat only at night.
For the sale of betel nuts, madder, grapes, and dates, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance; for the sale of jackfruit, it lasts for three days.
For plantains, coconuts, ginger, and citron,
as well as for jambīra and similar fruits, the *pādakṛcchra* penance shall apply.
One should perform the Kṛcchra penance for selling substances such as musk;
for camphor and the like, it shall be half of that; and for selling asafoetida and similar items, it is for one day.
Having sold sesame seeds, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
however, one may sell those produced from cultivation for the sake of a sacrifice, as well as those obtained through gifts.
For the sale of red or yellow garments, or even a black antelope skin,
one must perform the Kṛcchra penance, according to the words of Garga.
If a twice-born man, deluded by wealth, should sell a cow for the sake of profit, he must perform the Prājāpatya penance;
for elephants, an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa) is prescribed.
In the sale of donkeys, horses, goats, sheep, and young camels, one should perform the Parāka penance; for men, one should practice double that.
Having sold women, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
the wise say that for men, the vow is double.
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for selling the Vedas;
for selling the auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas), the Parāka penance is required, and for selling the Smṛtis, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
A twice-born man should perform the Sāntapana penance for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Rahasyas and Pañcarātras, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance therein.
"For verses, for treatises on ethics (nītiśāstra), and likewise for Prakrit works—
for all such branches of knowledge— one should perform a quarter-pādakṛcchra penance.
Thus says Hārīta as well:

In the sale of molasses, sesame, flowers, roots, fruits, or cooked food, the penance is the *saumyāyana*. In the sale of any one of the following—lac, salt, honey, meat, oil, milk, curd, buttermilk, perfumes, skins, or garments—the penance is the *cāndrāyaṇa*. The same applies to the sale of wool, hair, silk-cotton, land, cows, houses, or weapons. In the sale of fish, meat, sinews, bones, horns, nails, conch-shells, or mother-of-pearl, the penance is the *taptakṛcchra*. This also applies to the sale of asafoetida, bdellium, yellow orpiment, realgar, collyrium, red chalk, alkali, salt, gems, pearls, coral, bamboo, or earthenware. In the sale of groves, tanks, wells, lotus-pools, or one's own meritorious deeds, one becomes purified after one year by bathing at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, eating only at every fourth meal-time, and reciting the *Gāyatrī* ten thousand times. The same applies to the sale of deficient weights and measures or mixed goods. Thus it is said. (Hārīta Smṛti 4.4–10)
In such cases involving multiple vows concerning a single subject, a systematic arrangement should be devised according to the circumstances, following the principle already stated previously.
The expiation for the four [offenses] beginning with *parivitti* has been described in the fourth chapter.
Now, the expiation for the *vrātya*.
A *vrātya* is one who has fallen away from the *sāvitrī*. Regarding his expiation, Manu has said:

"Those twice-born men for whom the *sāvitrī* has not been recited according to the rule—having caused them to perform three *kṛcchra* penances, one should initiate them according to the rule. (MDh 11.191)

[121] Thus it is said. Vasiṣṭha also states: "One whose *sāvitrī* has been lost shall perform the Uddālaka-vow: for two months he shall subsist on *yāvaka*; for one month on milk; for half a month on *āmikṣā*; for eight nights on clarified butter; for six nights he shall eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) obtained unasked; for three nights he shall subsist on water; and for one day and night he shall fast. Alternatively, he may go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), or he may perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice" (VaDh 11.76–79). In this regard, the rule of Manu applies to cases of distress (*āpad*), whereas the Uddālaka-vow applies to cases where there is no distress. As for that which was stated by Yama:
He for whom the Sāvitrī has been lost for fifteen years shall,
having shaved his head including the top-knot, perform the penance with a concentrated mind.
For twenty-one nights, he should drink a handful of barley-gruel,
and he should feed seven or five Brahmins with sacrificial food (havis).
"Then, for one who has been purified by the *yāvaka* penance, the initiation (*upanayana*) is prescribed" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 5.27–29);
this refers to cases where [the offender] is equal to a *manuṣya* (human). For one whose father and ancestors were also uninitiated, that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed:

Now, if one's father and grandfather should both be uninitiated (*anupeta*), they are described as equal to those who have killed a Brahmin (*brahmahatya*). One should avoid their arrival, feeding them, and marriage with them. For those who desire it, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*): just as a single season constitutes an offense in the first case, so does a year. Then follows the initiation (*upanayana*). Thereafter, for one year, there is the ritual touching of water (*udakopasparśana*). This is calculated per person for as many years as there may be uninitiated ancestors. [The purification is performed] with the seven *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "What is near and what is far," with the Yajus-purification, the Sāman-purification, and the Aṅgirasa-purification; or else, simply with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then he may be taught. Now, if the initiation of one's great-grandfather and further ancestors is not remembered, they are described as equal to those at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). One should avoid their arrival, feeding them, and marriage with them. For those who desire it, there is an expiation: he should observe the twelve-year period of Vedic studentship (*traividyaka-brahmacarya*), then the initiation, and then the ritual touching of water with the *pāvamānī* verses and others.
Thus [ends the section] (ĀpDh 1.1.1.32–2.8).
This concludes the penance for studying or teaching for a fee.
Regarding studying and teaching for a fee, Hārīta says:
"He who teaches for wages and he who is taught for wages shall drink milk for three fortnights by way of penance.
Regarding the injury of trees and the like, Manu says:
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
"For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest, one should follow a cow for one day while observing a milk-vow. (MDh 11.142–44).
And this refers to cases other than the cutting of trees for the sake of sacrifice; for this very reason, Yājñavalkya also qualifies it with the word "in vain" (*vṛthā*).
"For cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred *ṛc*s should be recited;
he who cuts medicinal herbs in vain shall subsist on milk for a day and follow a cow.

(YDh 3.276). As for that which was stated by Hārīta: "Upon killing stationary beings such as trees or reptiles, having offered an oblation with the verse 'yasyedaṃ prāṇam' (VS 34.5), one should give a vessel of sesame seeds to a Brāhmaṇa," that refers to meritorious stationary beings such as the *aśvattha* tree. Regarding the repeated cutting of species of trees such as the jackfruit or coconut—which yield great fruit—Śaṅkha says: [text follows].
"One should observe a year-long vow after cutting down a fruit-bearing tree" (Śaṅkha Smṛti 17.49).
There is no fault if [the act] has a visible purpose, for the traditional law states: "One should not harm trees that bear fruit and flowers; one may cut them down for the sake of agricultural work.
Now follows the expiation for atheism (*nāstikya*).
If, however, the atheism is verbal, that is a minor offense (upapātaka). As the authors of the Purāṇas have said:
"The knowers of dharma who perceive the truth have declared that atheists are of three kinds:
those corrupted in action, those corrupted in mind, and likewise those corrupted in speech."
"Minor offenses (upapātaka) are considered [to arise from] corruption of action, while corruption of speech is known as a grave offense (pātaka).
However, through repetition, corruption of action is held to be a major offense (mahāpātaka). Thus it is said.

Regarding minor offenses (*upapātaka*) such as atheism (*nāstikya*), Vasiṣṭha states: “An atheist, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism” (VaDh 21.29). As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha—“An atheist, one who lives like an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who brings false accusations: these five shall subsist on alms in the house of a Brāhmaṇa for one year”—this refers to the case of atheism constituting a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). Regarding the expiation for the violation of a vow (*vratalopa*), Yājñavalkya prescribes the vow of the *avakīrṇin* for one who has violated his vow.
"A celibate student who approaches a woman becomes an *avakīrṇin*;
by sacrificing an ass as an animal to Nirṛti, he is purified. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.280). Manu also says:
But one who has spilled his semen shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, according to the procedure for a *sthālīpāka* offering.
Having performed the fire-oblation according to the rules, and finally with the verse beginning "saṃ meti," one should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Guru, and Agni.
When this offense has been committed, having worn a donkey skin,
he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
"Subsisting on alms obtained from them only once a day, and performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day, he becomes purified in one year. (MDh 11.118–23)

Vasiṣṭha also states: "If a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he shall sacrifice a donkey as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣas in a common fire at a crossroads in the forest; or he shall offer a *caru* oblation to Nirṛti. He should sacrifice from it, saying: 'To Kāma, svāhā! To Kāmakāma, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities who are Rakṣases, svāhā! (VaDh 23.1–3). In this regard, it should be understood that the animal sacrifice applies to one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), while the *caru* oblation applies to one not so learned. Śaṅkha, however, prescribes specific penances according to the distinction of caste: "One who has spilled his seed upon a guarded Vaiśya woman shall perform the three daily ablutions for one year; for a Kṣatriya woman, for two years; for a Brāhmaṇa woman, for three years. Furthermore, there is that which was stated by Aṅgiras:
But for the sake of one who has spilled his seed, he should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin;
wearing clothes of bark for six months, he shall likewise be freed from the sin.

This refers to cases where there is slight deviation [from the rules]. Regarding those women who are completely deviant, Śaṅkha says: “Having had intercourse with a loose Brāhmaṇa woman, one should fast for six nights and give a cow. Having done so with a Kṣatriya woman, one should fast for three nights and give a vessel of clarified butter. With a Vaiśya woman, eating only at every fourth mealtime, one should feed Brāhmaṇas and give a load of fodder to cows. Having had intercourse with a Śūdra woman, one should bathe with one's clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa. Having had intercourse with cows, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance. Having had intercourse with a widow (raṇḍā), one should give a load of straw and a māṣa of lead. In this case, the principle that “the Kṣatriya’s [penance] is half that of the Brāhmaṇa” does not apply; rather, it is the same for all three castes. Thus said Śāṇḍilya.

"A twice-born man who has broken his vow of chastity, as well as a king and a Vaiśya, become pure after performing a sacrifice with a donkey, eating only alms-food constantly, and remaining composed for one year. Regarding repeated practice, Kaṇva says:
On the first night, one who has committed an emission [of semen] should sacrifice with a donkey;
by performing this according to practice for one year, he becomes purified.
