[129] Regarding this, Gautama states the specific rule: “Having put on its skin with the hair facing upward, carrying a red vessel, he shall go for alms to seven houses while proclaiming his deed” (GDh 24.93). Jātūkarṇya defines the characteristics of an *avakīrṇin*: “The wise call him an *avakīrṇin* who, being a student (*brahmacārin*) under a vow, has discharged semen, whether intentionally or unintentionally. (Jātūkarṇya)
Śāṇḍilya, however, states that there is an additional vow for the forest-dweller and the ascetic:
"If emission occurs intentionally, both the forest-dweller and the ascetic shall perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*, conjoined with three *parāka* penances."
Regarding the renunciant’s subsequent acceptance of the householder’s life, Saṃvarta says:
"If some foolish ascetic, having renounced the world, should return to it, he must perform the *kṛcchra* penance without weariness for six months immediately thereafter. (Saṃsmṛti 159)

[130] Thus says Vṛddha-Parāśara as well: "A Brahmin who has fallen from his vows, who has emerged from the life of a wandering mendicant, and who has desisted from fasting unto death, desires to enter the state of a householder."
With self-restraint and concentrated mind, he should perform the six-month Kṛcchra penance;
he should also perform three Kṛcchras and three Cāndrāyaṇas.
"Having been consecrated by all the purificatory rites beginning with the *jātakarman*, one attains purity.

Regarding this, the established rule is that for a Brāhmaṇa there is a six-month *kṛcchra* penance, for a Kṣatriya three *cāndrāyaṇas*, and for a Vaiśya three *kṛcchras*. Others maintain that these three vows, beginning with the six-month one, should be assigned to the Brāhmaṇa alone, depending on whether the act was a single occurrence or a repeated practice. Manu extends the vow prescribed for a *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) even to the omission of other vows:
"Without having performed the begging of alms and without having kindled the sacred fire..."
"One who is not ill shall perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin* for seven nights" (MDh 2.187).
As for that which Yājñavalkya said:
"But having neglected begging for alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill..."
One should offer two oblations with these two [mantras] beginning with "kāmāvakīrṇa."

"Then one should perform the attendance [upon the fire], with the mantra: 'May he sprinkle me with this. (YDh 3.281–82). The two mantras for the *homa* are: "I am one who has spilled his seed through lust; I am one who has spilled his seed. To the one who desires lust, Svāhā! I have fallen into lust; I have fallen. To the one who desires lust, Svāhā! (GDh 25.9–10). And this [penance] is to be understood as applying when [the act] is not performed due to being preoccupied with duties such as service to the teacher.
[Now follows] the penance for the sale of a son and so forth.

Regarding the sale of a daughter and other such acts, the penance prescribed for common minor offenses (*upapātaka*) should be applied. As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha: "Having sold a temple, a shelter, a garden, a grove, an assembly hall, a water-station, a pond, a holy bridge, or a son, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra*," and that which was stated by Vṛddha-Parāśara:

"Having sold a daughter or a cow, one should perform the *sāntapana* *kṛcchra*," these should be understood as applying to cases of unintentional action during times of distress. However, as for that which has been declared in the Caturviṃśatimata:
Having sold women, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
the wise say that for a man, the vow is double.

Thus, that [rule] should be understood in that very context according to the intention. As for what Paiṭhīnasi says: "In the case of selling a grove, a pond, a well, a lotus-pool, a meritorious deed, or a son—one who bathes at the three periods of the day, sleeps on the ground, observes celibacy, and eats only at every fourth meal-time, becomes purified in one year"—that refers to the case of habitual practice.
Regarding the expiation for defiling a maiden:

it should be understood that the general expiation for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) applies to the defilement of a maiden. As for what Śaṅkha says: "One who defiles a maiden and one who sells Soma shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year," and as Hārīta says:

A defiler of virgins, a seller of Soma, a husband of a Śūdra woman, one who abandons his wife from her youth, a drinker of spirituous liquor, a priest for Śūdras, an assailant of his guru, an atheist, one who lives as an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, a slayer of a friend, one who makes false accusations, one who associates with outcasts, a betrayer of friends, a killer of those seeking refuge, and one who lives by counterfeiting—these shall perform the five-fold penance consisting of exposure to heat, staying in the open air, and lying in water during the summer, rainy, and winter seasons respectively; they shall eat barley-gruel mixed with cow’s urine for one month. (Hārīta Smṛti 2.4–5)
Thus, that [penalty] should be understood as applying in the case of defiling a maiden by means of the reverse process.
Now, regarding the expiation for vices such as gambling:
even for vices like gambling, the expiation prescribed generally for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) should be applied. As for that which Baudhāyana states concerning a vow lasting one year:

Now, the acts that cause impurity: gambling, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), living by gleaning for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, begging for alms by one who has returned home from his teacher’s house, staying in the teacher’s house beyond four months, teaching him [the Veda] beyond that period, and the pointing out of constellations. As for the expiation for these: twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, six days, three days, and one day—this is the expiation for those who have committed acts causing impurity. (BDh 2.1.2.15–17)
Thus, that refers to the subject of practice; as Pracetās also said:

A liar, a thief, a king’s servant, one who subsists by planting trees, a poisoner, an arsonist, one who lives by mounting chariots or elephants, a stage-player, a cheat at dice, a teacher of Śūdras, the husband of a Śūdra woman, a maker of musical instruments, one who lives by astrology, one who lives like a dog, one who lives as a Brahmin in name only, a physician, a temple-priest, a domestic chaplain, a gambler, a drunkard, a forger, a seller of his own offspring, and a seller of human beings or cattle—these are the ones he should expel. Having assembled, a Brāhmaṇa should do so according to the law and with due deliberation. When they have renounced all their property, they should eat only at every fourth mealtime, bathe three times a day for a year, and at the end of that period, perform libations to the gods and ancestors and provide daily fodder for cows; in this way, they become fit for social intercourse.
Thus, that refers to the object of repeated practice.

Regarding the penance for living without belonging to an *āśrama*, Hārīta has stated the following penance: "One who lives without an *āśrama* should perform the *Prājāpatya* *Kṛcchra* for one year and then enter an *āśrama*. For a second [year], an *Atikṛcchra*; for a third, a *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and beyond that, a *Cāndrāyaṇa*.
This is the penance for serving a *Śūdra*.

Regarding service to a Śūdra, Baudhāyana says: “Sailing on the ocean; misappropriating the deposit of a Brāhmaṇa; trading in all types of merchandise; false testimony regarding land; serving a Śūdra; being born of a Śūdra woman; having offspring from such a union; and the expiation for these [sins]: they should eat sparingly at the fourth meal-time and enter the water according to the ritual of the *savana*s. By alternating between standing and sitting, they remove that evil in three years. (BDh 2.1.2.2–10). This refers to cases of long-term habitual practice.

Regarding the expiation for sins that cause loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), after the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), Viṣṇu enumerates those that cause loss of caste as follows: "Causing injury to a Brāhmaṇa; smelling things that should not be smelled or food that has been tasted by another; cruelty toward living beings; and engaging in sexual intercourse with animals or with a male—these are the acts that cause loss of caste. Regarding these, Manu and Viṣṇu have declared a general expiation:
"Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste..."
"One should perform the Sāntapana, Kṛcchra, or Prājāpatya penance if the act was unintentional" (MDh 11.124;
VDh 37.7). Among these, the expiation for causing injury to a Brāhmaṇa is set forth in the eleventh chapter, while that for sexual intercourse with cattle is set forth in the tenth chapter.
Regarding the expiation for the sin of causing mixture (*saṅkarīkaraṇa*):

after enumerating the acts that cause loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), Viṣṇu states, "Violence against domestic or wild animals is an act causing mixture" (ViSm 39.1). He himself has stated the general expiation for that:
"Having committed an act causing mixture, one should eat barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) for one month."
"Or else, one should perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance. (ViDh 39.2). This has been stated in detail in the sixth chapter.

Regarding the expiation for sins that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), Viṣṇu enumerates them immediately after those that cause loss of caste (*saṅkarīkaraṇa*): "Accepting wealth from censurable persons, trade, living by usury, speaking untruths, and serving Śūdras—these constitute *apātrīkaraṇa*" (Viṣṇu Smṛti 40.1). Manu has stated the general expiation for this:
"Having committed an act that renders one unworthy of receiving gifts, one becomes pure through the *taptakṛcchra* penance."
"Purification may be achieved either by the Śītakṛcchra or by the Mahāsāntapana penance. (ViDh 40.2) [138] Thus it is said.

Regarding the expiation for sins that cause impurity (*malinīkaraṇa*), Viṣṇu, after enumerating those acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), subsequently listed those that cause impurity: "The killing of birds, aquatic animals, and creatures born in water; [the killing] of worms and insects; and eating food mixed with intoxicants—these are the acts that bring about impurity" (ViDh 41.1–4). Regarding this, he stated the general expiation:
"For acts causing impurity, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification."

"Or else, the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra is the purifying expiation. (ViDh 41.5). Thus, having described the specific expiations, the specific expiations for miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*) are now stated. Regarding that, Manu says concerning the abandonment of one who has sought refuge:
"Having abandoned one who has come for refuge and having caused the Veda to be corrupted, a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year. (MDh 11.198)

Regarding study in the presence of outcasts and others, Vasiṣṭha says: “Upon hearing the cry of an outcast or a Caṇḍāla, they shall remain silent and fasting for three nights; it is known from tradition that by practicing the recitation of a thousand verses, they then become pure” (ViDh 23.34–35). This refers to cases where the act is intentional. However, regarding unintentional acts, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states: “If the recitation of the Śruti or Smṛti occurs within earshot of a Caṇḍāla, there shall be fasting for one night. Regarding the interruption caused by the passage of a snake or similar creatures, Yama says:
Of the snake and the mongoose, as well as of the goat and the cat,
of the mouse and the camel, and of the frog and the woman.
Listen now to this immediate expiation for when a man, a sheep, a dog, a horse, or a donkey passes between [the couple].
"A three-night fast and an ablution three times a day, or one must travel to another village on one's knees; there is no doubt in this matter" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.48–50).
Regarding the expiation for mounting vehicles drawn by donkeys or camels and so forth, Yājñavalkya says:

[140] "One who practices breath control (prāṇāyāma), one who has bathed in water, one who has traveled in a donkey-cart or a camel-cart, one who has bathed naked, one who has eaten, and one who has gone to a woman during the day"—thus it is said (YDh 3.291). And this refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally; however, regarding intentional acts, Yama says:
If a woman or a man mounts a donkey or a camel— both being uneven vehicles—
at a sacrifice or while officiating at a sacrifice, it is a kṛcchra penance, and the sacred fire itself is destroyed.
"Having intentionally mounted a camel-vehicle or a donkey-vehicle, one becomes pure by immersing oneself in water with one's clothes on and performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma). Thus [it is said].
This is the penance for voiding urine or excrement [inappropriately].
Regarding the discharge of urine, feces, and so forth in water, Manu says:
"But one who is afflicted and voids bodily waste either without water or in water, becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on and touching a cow" (MDh 11.203).
This refers to cases where one acts without desire. But regarding intentional action, Yama says:
[141] "If one who has fallen into calamity consumes human excrement when water is unavailable, he shall perform a fast for one day and then bathe with his clothes on. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.26)

And as for what Sumantu said: "For one who urinates in water or in fire, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the purification of the body"—that should be applied to cases involving those who are not afflicted by distress.
Regarding the expiation for the omission of ritual acts, Manu has stated that in the case of the omission of Vedic or Smārta rites and the like:
"Upon the transgression of the obligatory rites ordained by the Vedas..."

"And for the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the expiation is fasting" (MDh 11.203). In this case, there is a combination of the fast with the sacrifices and other rites specifically prescribed [for that occasion]. Regarding the non-performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and so forth, Bṛhaspati says: "The householder who eats every day without having performed the great sacrifices..."
If he is not ill, he is purified by half the penance while his wealth exists.

"One who has maintained the sacred fires shall not fail to perform the ritual attendance during a sacrificial rite, nor shall he fail to approach his wife during her season; he too must perform half a *kṛcchra* penance. (Baudhāyana Smṛti 2.13–14).
This is the penance for giving an unequal gift.
Regarding the injustice in giving and so forth among those seated in a single row, Yama says:
[142] "One should not give unequally in the row, nor should one ask for it, nor cause it to be given.
One is liberated from that act by performing the Prājāpatya penance. Thus it is said.

Regarding conversation with those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) and others, Gautama states: “One should not converse with barbarians (*mleccha*), the impure, or the unrighteous. Having conversed with them, one should meditate mentally upon those who perform meritorious deeds, or else one should converse with a Brāhmaṇa” (GDh 9.19–21). Regarding eating while impure, Śātātapa says:

“If a twice-born person, having voided urine or excrement, eats out of delusion without performing the purification for himself, he must observe a three-night fast; if he does so knowingly, he should perform the *Sāntapana* penance” (ŚāSm 2.64).
Vṛddha-Śātātapa also says:
"If one who has urinated while walking on a path should drink water due to a lapse of memory,
he must fast for a day and night, bathe, and offer oblations of clarified butter."

[143] Thus it is said. A tiger also says: "When a householder eats having touched something that should not be touched, he should observe a three-night penance if it was unintentional, and a six-night penance if it was intentional."
"A renunciant (yati) and one dwelling in the forest (vanastha) should perform that very same [penance]," so it is said. Uśanas also says:
"If touched by Caṇḍālas or Śvapacas, or even by one who has defecated or urinated and remains impure from food remnants..."
"One who has eaten the leavings [of another] shall become purified after three nights; one should perform [the penance] for six [nights]. Bṛhaspati also says:
"When a person observing a vow eats without having bathed after offering a *piṇḍa* to his father..."
Having touched a corpse, a woman in her courses, a Caṇḍāla, or likewise a woman who has recently given birth;

"If [the act is] unintentional, it should last for three nights; if done intentionally, one should perform the Sāntapana penance. Thus, regarding the voiding of urine, feces, and so forth without the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), a penance is stated in another Smṛti:
"If a twice-born man becomes impure while without his sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*)," [he must perform a penance].
"The expiation is a fast for a day and night, or else the recitation of the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times. And this refers to an intentional act. But in the case of an unintentional act:
"For one who drinks, urinates, or eats while not wearing the sacred thread..."
Three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), six [rounds], and three nights, in sequence.
[144] Thus it is said. Regarding the act of rising from one's seat after a meal without having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), an expiation is prescribed in the *Aśvamedhika* section:
"If one who has eaten rises from his seat without having rinsed his mouth, he must immediately perform a bath; otherwise, he remains impure."
Regarding eating in a row where one unworthy of the row (apāṅkteya) is present, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"Any excellent twice-born man who eats in the row of one unworthy of the row becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
Regarding the wearing of garments dyed with indigo, Āpastamba says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa wears a garment dyed with indigo upon his limbs,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
If the juice of indigo should enter anyone through the pores of the skin,
the common purification for those of the three castes is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
The keeping and selling [of such items], as well as making a livelihood by that trade—by these, a Brahmin becomes fallen; he is purified by three *kṛcchra* penances.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors—
all these great sacrifices of such a person are in vain because of wearing indigo-dyed thread.
If a Brahmin should ever enter indigo by mistake,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one should pierce the body of a Brāhmaṇa with indigo wood and blood is seen there, the twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the case of women, there is no fault in sexual enjoyment for the purpose of sport upon a bed.
One who eats while wearing a garment dyed with indigo incurs sin. (ĀpSm 6.1–8) [146] Bhṛgu also says: Indigo worn by a woman on the bed does not cause defilement for a Brāhmaṇa.
Indeed, by wearing [it], the king and the aged Vaiśya [attain their goals] except on festival days.
"Indigo dye does not cause defilement in woolen cloth or silk thread.
Thus says Śaṅkha regarding the use of beds and the like made from the Brahma-tree (palāśa):
"Having occupied a bed, a vehicle, a seat, or likewise sandals..."
A twice-born man who has plucked a leaf from a Palāśa tree must observe a vow for three nights.
But a Kṣatriya who, intent on saving his life, turns his back in battle,
shall perform a vow for one year after cutting down a Pippala tree.

If one should pass between two Brahmins, or between a Brāhmaṇa and the sacred fire, or between a husband and wife, or between a cow and an eminent twice-born, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.

"At the time of the *homa* sacrifice, during milking, while engaged in Vedic study, or when taking a wife—if a twice-born man should pass between these [and his teacher], he shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Thus [it is said].
Regarding bad dreams, the sight of portents (*ariṣṭa*), and so forth, that same author says:

"In the event of seeing bad dreams, ill omens, and the like, one should give ghee and gold. Thus [it is said]. Regarding travel to another country other than on a pilgrimage to a sacred site (*tīrtha*), Devala states the penance:
"The Sindhu, Saurāṣṭra, and Sauvīra regions, as well as those dwelling in the borderlands..."
"Having gone to Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga, he becomes worthy of purification.
(DevSm 61) Regarding the expiation for sleeping at the time of sunrise and so forth, Yama says:
"He who sleeps at sunrise is called 'one who has been awakened by the sun' (*sūryābhyudita*)."
But he who sleeps when the sun has set is called one who is devoid of the sun.
"Both of these stealers of the Veda, having fasted for a full day and night and being pure,
should separately perform ten thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī for one day. So also says Manu:
“If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition, or should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while muttering [the *sāvitrī*]” (MDh 2.220).

Gautama, however, states a specific rule for the student (*brahmacārin*): “A student who has been overtaken by the rising sun should remain standing for the day without eating; and once the sun has set, he should recite the *sāvitrī* throughout the night” (GDh 23.21). Vasiṣṭha states a specific rule for the ascetic (*yati*) and the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).

"If a forest-dweller (*vanastha*) and an ascetic (*yati*) should both be overtaken by the rising sun [without having performed their morning rites], they should subsist on *brahmakūrca* and recite the *praṇava* throughout the day" (VaDh 28.41). Regarding the expiation for the loss of the staff, water-pot, and so forth, Paiṭhīnasi says: "If the wooden staff is lost, one should give food to a Brāhmaṇa and fast for that day; the teacher should provide another. It is exactly the same for the water-pot. If the girdle is lost, one should perform the threefold rite (*trivṛt*). Regarding the omission of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) and the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), Saṃvarta states:

"If one fails to perform the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) due to an emergency, or the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) according to the rules, one should, having bathed and being composed in mind, recite the *Sāvitrī* eight thousand times. (Saṃsmṛti 2.27). Yama states the penance for looking at one's own excrement:
[149] “One should not urinate facing the sun, nor should one look at one’s own excrement;
having seen it, one should gaze upon the sun, a cow, fire, or likewise a Brāhmaṇa. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 5.13).
Regarding impurity at the time of eating, Vṛddhaśātātapa says:
If, however, a twice-born man becomes impure at the time of eating,
he shall place that morsel on the ground, bathe, and the Brahmin becomes purified.
"Having consumed that morsel, one becomes pure after a day and night;
having eaten all the food, one is purified after three nights. (VṛŚāSm 16–17).
Regarding the lapse of time for one invited to a *śrāddha*, Yama says:
If a twice-born man, having caused a ketana to be made, should cause it to be transgressed,
he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and is born into the womb of a Śūdra.
"When this sin has been incurred, a Brāhmaṇa who is firm in his vows, having performed the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*, shall thereafter perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 5.14–15)

Regarding the salutation of Kṣatriyas and others, Hārīta says: “Upon saluting a Kṣatriya, one should fast for a day and a night; the same applies to a Vaiśya. Upon saluting a Śūdra, there is a fast for three nights. Likewise, there shall be a fast for three nights upon saluting one who is seated on a bed, one whose feet are placed on sandals or footstools, one who is impure from eating, one situated in darkness, one performing a *śrāddha*, or one engaged in *japa* or the worship of deities. Furthermore, even if invited elsewhere, if one eats elsewhere [without first informing], there is likewise a fast for three nights. (HārSm 21.7–12)
Regarding the expiation for false accusation, Yājñavalkya states the expiation for making a false charge:
"He who falsely accuses another of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) or a minor sin (upapātaka)..."
"One should subsist on water for a month, performing recitations with the senses restrained" (YDh 3.285).

And the recitation should be of the *Śuddhavatī* verses. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime entailing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or one not so entailing (*upapatanīya*), one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the *Śuddhavatī* verses, or go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice" (VaDh 23.39). Hārīta also says:
"In the case of false accusation, reviling, and backbiting against one's elders..."
"One should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* for twenty-one nights" (Hārīta Smṛti 21.3).

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "An atheist, an ungrateful person, one who practices fraud in business, one who destroys the livelihood of Brāhmaṇas, and one who makes false accusations—these shall beg for alms at the house of a Brāhmaṇa for five years. For one year they shall eat only washed alms-food; or for six months they shall follow cows. The application of these statements should be understood according to their respective contexts.
Regarding the expiation for one who has been falsely accused, Yājñavalkya says:
"One who has been falsely accused should perform the Kṛcchra penance, or indeed the Āgneya penance."
"But one should offer an oblation of earth-eating [grains], or indeed a victim to Vāyu" (YDh 3.287).

As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "By this very [rule], the accused is explained" (VaDh 23.37), that should be understood as referring to one who has not yet performed penance at that time. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi: "One falsely accused should perform a Kṛcchra; for minor sins (pātaka), a month; for mortal sins (mahāpātaka), two months"—that too pertains to the same subject matter as Vasiṣṭha's rule.

Thus, the expiations for the ten types of sins—beginning with the most heinous crimes (atipātaka) and ending with miscellaneous offenses (prakīrṇaka), as enumerated by Viṣṇu—have been set forth both in general and in detail.
Now, the secret expiations are being described.

That sin which has not been known by anyone other than the perpetrator is a secret (*rahasya*). Its expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must also be performed in secret. Thus says Hārīta: [153] “Now we shall set forth the secret [expiations] for a Brāhmaṇa who has studied the Dharmaśāstras: ‘In secret, a secret; in public, a public one’” (HārSm 30.1–2). Yama states: “In secret, a secret; in public, a public one. For a secret offense, only a secret [expiation] should be performed; for a public offense, only a public one should be performed. Because it is secret, there is no requirement for the approval of an assembly (*pariṣad*). This is what Bṛhaspati and Yājñavalkya both declare.
One whose fault is publicly known should perform a vow approved by an assembly;
however, one whose fault is not publicly known should observe a secret vow. (YDh 3.301)

[154] Thus it is said. Nor should it be suspected that "there can be no knowledge of the vow without an assembly," for such knowledge is possible for one who knows the scriptures. Even by another intelligent person, it can be ascertained through some pretext in the company of learned men. If, however, one were to manifest the sin before an assembly to demonstrate that knowledge, then the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) becomes extensive. For impurity produced by sin is of two kinds: pertaining to this world (*aihikī*) and pertaining to the next world (*āmuṣmikī*). Of these two, the worldly impurity prevents one's dealings with the virtuous (*śiṣṭas*), while the other-worldly impurity leads one to hell. In the case of public sins, since both types of impurity exist, a profusion of expiations is required for their removal. But in the case of secret sins, because the worldly impurity is absent and only the other-worldly impurity remains, it is removed even by a small amount of recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth. For this very reason, Manu has stated the rules regarding the vows such as the *Prājāpatya* and the recitations and other rites.
"By these vows, the twice-born who have manifested their sins are to be purified;
however, those whose sins are unmanifested, one should purify with mantras and burnt offerings. (MDh 11.226).
Regarding that, he [Manu] himself stated the general penance for secret [sins]:
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices,
and forbearance quickly destroy sins, even those born of the most heinous crimes.
Just as fire, having reached its fuel, consumes it entirely in an instant by its heat,
so does one who knows the Veda burn away all sin committed through ignorance.

"Sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*, performed day after day, purify even the killer of a learned Brahmin within a month. (MDh 11.245–48). Vasiṣṭha says:

"If even a full hundred improper acts have been committed, yet the Veda is retained, the fire of that person's Veda burns them all away, just as fire consumes fuel. (VaDh 27.1). Thus it is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata.
With no doubt, a twice-born man should recite these two Anuvākas, "brahma pratiṣṭhā" and so forth, for those [deeds] already performed, those being performed, and those yet to be performed.

[156] Thus says Yama: One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī— the goddess who has a thousand as her maximum, a hundred as her middle, and ten as her minimum— which destroys even the most heinous sins.
By reciting the Virāj mantra twice, one becomes purified on that very day;
by repeating the Vāmadevya mantra three times, one becomes purified on that very day.
By reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, one is released from all sins;
by muttering the *Vṛṣabha* hymn a hundred times, one becomes purified on that very day.
"Having recited the Veda once, one is purified on that very day;
having chanted the eleven Rudras, one is purified on that very day. Thus says Viṣṇu.

Now, therefore, follow the purifiers of all the Vedas, by the recitation (*japa*) and the fire-oblations (*homa*) of which the twice-born are purified from their sins: the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Devakṛta*, the *Śuddhavatya* verses, the *Taratsamandīya*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍya* verses, the *Pāvamānya* verses, the *Durgās*, the *Sāvitrī*, the *Abhiṣaṅgas*, the *Padastomas*, the *Sāmans*, the *Vyāhṛtis*, the *Bhāruṇḍas*, the *Candrasāman*, the two *Sāmans* of the *Puruṣavrata*, the *Abliṅga*, the *Bārhaspatya*, the *Gosūkta*, the *Vāksūkta*, the *Aśvasūkta*, the *Madhvarca*, the two *Sāmans* of *Indraśuddha*, the *Śatarudrīya*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Trisuparṇa*, the *Mahāvrata*, the *Nārāyaṇīya*, and the *Puruṣasūkta*.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agner Vrata, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—
these, when recited, purify living beings.
"One obtains the recollection of past births if one so desires" (Viṣṇusmṛti 56.1–27).
Thus it is said. In the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Likewise, the Pāvamānī verses, the Kautsa hymn, and the Pauruṣa Sūkta..."
By reciting the Madhucchandas pavitra, one shall be liberated from sins.
By reciting the Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa, the Rudra-hymns, the Śukriya, the Mokṣaka,
the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat-sāman, one is liberated from sins.
By muttering the Yajñāyajñīya, the Āditya, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Rājana, and the Pārucchepa Sāmans, one is liberated from sin.
By reciting the Atharvaśiras, the Puruṣasūkta,
as well as the Nīlarudra and the Aindra hymns, one is liberated from all sins.
And whatever Atharvan mantras there are that are devoid of desire,
they all destroy sin, according to the word of Yājñavalkya.
A twice-born man should recite this section beginning with "siṃhe me manyuḥ";
having recited it, he shall be liberated from sins, according to the word of Baudhāyana.
He who studies the Rigveda, or likewise the Yajurveda branch,
the Samans along with their secret doctrines, and the Atharvāngirases as well;
By reciting the Brāhmaṇas, the Kalpas, the six Vedāṅgas,
and likewise other narrative accounts (ākhyānas), one is liberated from sins.
"By reciting the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and hymns of praise to the deities, as well as other established bases of dharma, one is liberated from sins. Thus says Baudhāyana.
One should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) according to the procedure seen in the scriptures;
whatever sin has been committed by the genitals or whatever has been committed by the feet [is thereby purified].
"By means of the arms, the mind, speech, the ears, the skin, the nose, and the eyes—
having performed the evening twilight worship (sāyaṃsaṃdhyā)— one is thereby liberated from that [debt]. Thus says Manu (BDh 2.4.7.18).
Even those who have committed great sins, as well as others who have performed forbidden acts,
are liberated from that defilement by means of well-performed austerity alone.
"Whatever sin people commit through thought, word, or deed, those whose wealth is austerity quickly dispel it all by means of austerity alone. (Manusmṛti 11.239–41) [161].
Thus it is also stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
Recitation of mantras, austerity, visiting sacred fords, and the worship of deities and Brahmins at times such as eclipses serve to purify one of great sins.
Visiting sacred fields of merit destroys all sins;
the worship of deities by men eliminates every trace of evil.
Having reached the lunar day of the new moon (Amāvāsyā), he who propitiates Bhava and feeds the Brāhmaṇas is liberated from all sins.
By worshipping the Great Goddess on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and likewise on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight through the mouth of a Brahmin, one is liberated from all sins.
Likewise, by worshipping the three-eyed Lord with offerings during the first watch of the night on the thirteenth day,
one is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the eleventh day and worshipped Janārdana,
one is liberated from all sins on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight with a concentrated mind,
[one should offer oblations] to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, and Antaka.
To Vaivasvata Kāla and to the Destroyer of All Beings,
one should offer seven handfuls of water each, mixed with sesame seeds.
"Having bathed in a river in the forenoon, one is liberated from all sins. Thus [it is said]. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Even one who is addicted to every kind of sin, by meditating for even a moment on Acyuta..."
"Furthermore, he becomes an ascetic, a purifier even of those who purify the assembly. Thus it is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"The Mṛgāreṣṭi, the Pavitreṣṭi, the Trihavis, and also the Pāvamānī [rites]."
"Sacrifices accompanied by the Vaiśvānara [offering] are destroyers of sin.
Thus it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"In this terrible Kali age, people follow after sin."
O mighty-armed one, they will exist devoid of the distinctions of caste and stage of life.
"I see nothing else for living beings in the Kali age that pacifies all sins as an atonement except for the city of Vārāṇasī. Thus end the general atonements.
Now, regarding the specific penances prescribed for these cases, Yājñavalkya says:
"A killer of a Brāhmaṇa, having fasted for three nights, shall mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn."

"One shall be purified within the water by giving a milch cow. (YDh 3.302). Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: "A slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, having fasted for three nights, shall recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water. This refers to an intentional act. Regarding an unintentional act, however, Yama says: "In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, stealing gold, or violating the Guru’s bed, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa, exhausted by breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). Baudhāyana [says]:

Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, bathed, and purified, he should smear a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) at the water’s edge; then, wearing wet clothes once, with a hand purified once, facing the sun, he should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* self-study (*svādhyāya*). He should do so one hundred times in the morning, one hundred times at midday, and one hundred times in the afternoon, or an unlimited number of times. When the stars have risen, he should consume a handful of barley-gruel (*prasṛti-yāvaka*). By doing this for seven nights, he is liberated from minor offenses (*upapātaka*), whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—with the exception of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*), violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), stealing gold (*suvarṇastainya*), and drinking liquor (*surāpāna*). By twenty-one nights, he overcomes even those. Thus it is said. (BDh 3.5.2–7)
Manu also says: "Or, having purified himself with three *parāka* penances, one who is self-restrained recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest; he is released from all sins. (MDh 11.258)

Bṛhadviṣṇu also states: "Having committed the killing of a Brahmin, one should kindle a fire with abundant fuel toward the east or the north and offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter while reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn; thereby he becomes purified from this. These [penances] are to be applied according to the distinctions of intentional or unintentional acts and so forth. Regarding the drinking of liquor, Yama says: "[165] 'A drinker of liquor, having entered water reaching only to his neck, should take [the water] beginning from the Sutasoma cup, consecrate it with the syllable Om, and drink it. Then, submerged in the water, he should mutter the Mānastokīya hymn. Yājñavalkya says:
"Having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, one becomes pure. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.304). Manu says:
"Having recited the *Kautsa* hymn beginning with 'āpaḥ' and the *Vāsiṣṭha* verse beginning with 'prati'..."
Even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified by the Māhitra hymns and the Śuddhavatī verses.
Having offered clarified butter for a year with the mantras used for the Śakala-homa, a twice-born man destroys even a very heavy sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "namaḥ."

"One who is joined with a great sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind; by practicing the Pāvamānī verses for a year, subsisting on alms-food, he becomes purified. Thus says Vasiṣṭha. (MDh 11.249, 256–57) [166]

"Having drunk *surā*, one should immerse oneself in water and recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* three times; Manu has declared that this is equivalent to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice. (VaDh 26.8).

In this regard, the application [of the penance] should be understood according to whether the act was intentional or unintentional, and whether it was habitual or not. Regarding the theft of gold, Śātātapa says:
Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of a guru,
having committed theft, and even having committed the murder of a Brahmin—
one who is covered in ashes and lying on a bed of ashes [is purified].
"One who recites the Rudrādhyāya is liberated from all sins" (Śānti-smṛti 1.71).

Yama states: "A Brāhmaṇa, having committed the theft of gold, shall place the gold in a shed, bathe in water up to his neck, sprinkle himself with the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and thereby becomes purified of this sin. Bṛhaspati says:
"By reciting the *Asyavāmīya* or the *Śivasamkalpa* even once..."
"Or by stealing gold, one becomes stainless in an instant. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has stolen gold, however, shall remain standing in water while reciting the Rudra-mantra. (YDh 3.304)

And the noble recitation (*japa*) should be performed eleven times. Regarding this, Atri says: "One who knows the Dharma, having repeated the Rudra-mantras eleven times, is liberated even when touched by great sins; there is no doubt in this matter."
Regarding the violation of the Guru’s bed, Yājñavalkya states: "One who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated by reciting the *Sahasraśīrṣa* [hymn];
at the conclusion of this rite, a milch cow must be given separately for each of these [offenses]. (YDh 3.305)
Yama also says: "Now, having committed adultery with the Guru’s wife, one becomes purified from this sin by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water. Manu also says:
"By practicing the Haviṣyāntīya and the hymn beginning with 'na tamaṃ ha,' and by muttering the Puruṣasūkta, the violator of the Guru’s bed is released. (MDh 11.251)
One who associates with another shall perform that very same penance as the one with whom he associates, because it was previously stated: "He shall observe the same vow as that person."
Now, regarding the secret expiations for minor offenses (upapātaka), Yama says:
"By means of four hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) conjoined with ten *praṇavas*..."
"One is released from the murder of a Brahmin, how much more so from the remaining sins. Yājñavalkya also says:
"A hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be performed for the removal of all sins."
"Indeed, for those born from minor offenses (upapātaka) and for that which is not specifically prescribed," thus [it is said]. Manu also says:
"Desiring the removal of sins, both gross and subtle..."
"Having understood [the truth], one should mutter for a year the verse beginning with 'yat kiṃcedam' and the one beginning with 'iti'. (MDh 11.252).
In this regard, the application [of the penance] should be observed according to the distinctions of single performance, repeated practice, and so forth.
Now, regarding the characteristics of vows:
Yājñavalkya has stated that the limbs common to all vows are celibacy,
compassion, forbearance, charity, truthfulness, and freedom from guile.
Non-violence, non-stealing, gentleness, and self-restraint are known as the restraints (yamas).

"Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, Vedic study, and restraint of the generative organ; the observances (*niyamas*) are service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.313–14). Here, *brahmacarya* is the restraint of all the senses. *Upasthanigraha* is the suppression of the sexual organ. The repetition of these two is according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). *Akalkatva* is the absence of crookedness. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:
One should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness.
One should enter the water with one's clothes on three times during the day and three times at night.
Furthermore, one should never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.
He should pass his time standing or sitting; if unable, he may lie down on the ground.
He should be a celibate observer of vows, honoring his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
"And one should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to one's ability; in all vows, one who is intent on expiation should act in this manner. (MDh 11.222–25).
Regarding that, Hārīta states the definition of the Prājāpatya vow:

"For three days one should eat in the evening, for three days in the morning, for three days one should not ask for food, and for the final three days one should subsist on air; this is the Kṛcchra of Prajāpati.
Thus [says] Manu as well.

"A twice-born man performing the *prājāpatya* penance should eat food obtained unasked for three days in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should not eat at all" (MDh 11.211). Regarding this very rite, Vasiṣṭha states another application according to the distinction of qualified persons:
One day in the morning, one day by night, and one day without begging;
one day of the *parāka* penance—thus there are four days, and the next two [days] are likewise.
"For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma, has indeed declared the *śiśukṛcchra* for children, the elderly, and the sick. (VaDh 23.42–43).
Yājñavalkya shows that both of these constitute the *prājāpatyakṛcchra*.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for, and observing a single fast— this is proclaimed as the *pādakṛcchra* (one-quarter penance).
In whatever manner it may be, this [offering] consisting of three qualities is called *prājāpatya*. (YDh 3.319–20)

[172] Thus: by *ekabhakta*, meaning eating only once during the day; by *nakta*, meaning eating only once at night; by *ayācita*, meaning that in which no food has been requested—that is, by eating what is obtained unasked. Since no specific time is indicated here, it refers to eating once either by day or by night. By means of one fast (*upavāsa*)—that is, by abstaining from food for one day—the *pādakṛcchra* (quarter-penance) is accomplished. This very *pādakṛcchra*, whether by increasing the duration in its own place or by repetition like a swinging staff (*daṇḍakalita*), when tripled and practiced three times in any manner whatsoever, is called a *prājāpatya*; this is the meaning. Regarding the number of mouthfuls (*grāsa*) in the *ekabhakta* and other observances, Āpastamba has shown them as follows:
"Twenty-two morsels are prescribed for the evening, twenty-six for the morning; twenty-four are for when no food is begged; beyond that is known as fasting.
The measure of those morsels has also been stated by that same author:
"Just as a chick enters its shell comfortably when it is the size of a hen's egg.
However, in the *Caturviṃśatimata*, the number is heard of in another manner:
"In the morning, twelve morsels; in the evening, exactly fifteen."
"And for the *ayācita* [vow], two; and for the one who subsists on air, eight at most.

In this regard, the application should be understood as depending upon one's capacity. Āpastamba, however, having prescribed four types of *pādakṛcchra*, states their application according to the distinction of social classes (*varṇa*): "Three days of fasting is one quarter; three days of eating only what is unasked is another quarter."
Three days in the evening, and likewise one quarter for three days in the morning; and likewise one quarter for three days in the morning.
"A Śūdra should perform [the penance] for one quarter in the morning; a Vaiśya should be made to perform it for one quarter in the evening;
for a Kṣatriya, however, it is prescribed as unasked food (ayācita) for three nights; and for a Brāhmaṇa, it is traditionally taught [as a full penance].
He also states the nature of the Ardhakṛcchra and Pādonakṛcchra:
"In the evening and in the morning for half a day, it is three-quarters [of a kṛcchra] when the *nakta* is excluded.

This is the meaning: by performing two sets of three days consisting of *ayācita* and fasting (*upavāsa*), one achieves an *ardhakṛcchra*. By performing three sets of three days excluding the *nakta*, one achieves a *pādona-kṛcchra*. The method for the *ardhakṛcchra* has also been stated by that same author: "In the evening and in the morning likewise, and two days of *ayācita* have been declared."
One should not eat for two days; that is prescribed as the half-kṛcchra penance.

[174] Thus it is said. Here too, the determination should be understood as depending upon one's capacity. As for the *prājāpatya-kṛcchra* prescribed by Gautama, which is accompanied by many auxiliary elements such as recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*):

Having eaten sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) for breakfast, he shall not eat for three nights. Then, for another three days, he shall eat only at night. Then, for another three days, he shall not beg from anyone. Then, for another three days, he shall fast. He shall stand during the day and sit during the night, if he desires swift results. He shall speak the truth. He shall not converse with those who are not noble (*anārya*). He shall constantly recite the *Raurava* and *Yaudhājapa* hymns. At each pressing of the Soma, he shall touch water and purify himself with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, which contain the word "purifier" (*pavitra*). He shall also purify himself with the eight verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*. Then follows the water libation (*udakatarpaṇa*): *Oṃ, obeisance to Hamā, Mohama, Saṃhama, Dhunvanta, Tāpama, and Punarvasu. Obeisance, obeisance to Mauñja, Urmya, Vasuvinda, and Sarvavinda; obeisance, obeisance to Pāra, Supāra, Mahāpāra, Pāradā, and Pārayiṣṇu. Obeisance, obeisance to Rudra, Paśupati, the Great God, Tryambaka, Ekacara, Adhipati, Hara, Śarva, Īśāna, Ugra, Vajrin, Ghṛṇin, and Kapardin. Obeisance, obeisance to Sūrya and Āditya. Obeisance, obeisance to Nīlagrīva and Śitikaṇṭha. Obeisance, obeisance to Kṛṣṇa and Piṅgala. Obeisance, obeisance to Jyeṣṭha, Śreṣṭha, Vṛddha, Indra, Harikeśa, and Ūrdhvaretas. Obeisance, obeisance to Satya, Pāvaka, Pāvakavarṇa, Kāma, and Kāmarūpa. Obeisance, obeisance to Dīpta and Dīptarūpin. Obeisance, obeisance to Tīkṣṇa and Tīkṣṇarūpin. Obeisance, obeisance to Saumya, Supuruṣa, Mahāpuruṣa, Madhyamapuruṣa, Uttamapuruṣa, and Brahmacārin. Obeisance, obeisance to Candralalāṭa, Kṛttivāsas, and Pinākahasta; obeisance, obeisance.* This same formula is used for the worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*), and these same verses are used as oblations of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*). At the end of twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial porridge (*caru*), he shall offer it to these deities: *Svāhā to Agni; Svāhā to Soma; Svāhā to Agni-Soma; Svāhā to Indra-Agni; Svāhā to Indra; Svāhā to the Viśvedevas; Svāhā to Brahman; Svāhā to Prajāpati; Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.* At the conclusion, there is the feeding of Brāhmaṇas. Thus ends the section. (GDh 27.2–29)

The nature of the *prājāpatya* penance has been stated by the passage beginning with "haviṣyānnam" and ending with "upavaset. Its procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is then described by the passage beginning with "tiṣṭhet. By the phrase ending with "ahani tiṣṭhet," it is meant that during the day, at times not incompatible with eating and other activities, one should remain standing throughout the day. By the phrase ending with "rātrāv āsīta," since sleep is necessary, it is stated that one should resort to it only while remaining seated. "He should also be desirous of speed" means he should possess the desire, "May I become pure quickly. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Desiring quick purification, he should stand during the day and sit during the night."

[177] In this context, regarding the group of limbs beginning with "one should speak the truth," the qualification of the eligible person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), namely "desiring speed," must be supplied. By this, it is understood that this rule does not apply to one who thinks, "I shall become pure gradually. *Raurava* and *Yaudhājaya* are two *sāmans*. The thirteen mantras beginning with *namo hamāya* are to be seen as applicable to the libations (*tarpaṇa*), the worship of the Sun (*sūryopasthāna*), and the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*). Alternatively, there are fifty-six mantras ending in the dative case. The libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be performed at each of the three daily pressings (*anusavana*), because the libation is an ancillary part of the ritual bath (*snānāṅga*). And so says Bhṛgu.
"Bathing is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya).
Libation (tarpaṇa) is a constituent part of these three; this indeed is the rule always."

The worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*) and the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*), however, should be performed once each day. This is because, although one could have simply stated, "Now follows the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*), the worship of the Sun, and the oblation of clarified butter," the author instead provides separate rules by saying, "This alone is the worship of the Sun; these alone are the oblations of clarified butter. The remainder is clear. This [penance] is to be understood as standing in place of two *prājāpatya* penances that lack the ancillaries of recitation (*japa*) and oblation (*homa*) mentioned by Hārīta and others, since those are extremely heavy due to being accomplished through great effort. Alternatively, for those such as Śūdras who lack the entitlement to use mantras, the *prājāpatya* should be understood as being devoid of recitation, oblation, and so forth. For this very reason, it was stated by Aṅgiras:
"Therefore, having approached a Śūdra who always stands on the path of dharma,
penance should be prescribed that is devoid of recitation (japa) and burnt offerings (homa).
This [rule] is to be understood as applying to those Brāhmaṇas and others who possess the entitlement to perform recitations, burnt offerings, and so forth, as stated by Gautama.
Now follows the *atikṛcchra*;
its definition is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"One should eat a single morsel for three three-day periods as previously described."
"A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should always fast for three days.

This means that on each of the nine days—consisting of the days of eating one meal (*ekabhakta*), eating only at night (*nakta*), and eating food obtained unasked (*ayācita*)—he should consume only a single morsel, and he should fast for three days; in this manner, it becomes an *atikṛcchra*. As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"This very same [penance] would be an *atikṛcchra* when one eats a handful of food" (YDh 3.320).

[179] Thus—the meaning is that this very *prājāpatyakṛcchra*, when combined with eating a handful of food (*pāṇipūrānna*) on nine days consisting of one-meal days, night-meals, and unasked-for meals, becomes an *atikṛcchra*. This refers to those who are incapable [of more severe penance], because a handful of food is a larger quantity than food measured by mouthfuls (*grāsa*).
Now follows the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*;
its definition was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days" (YDh 3.321).

Viṣṇu also states: “The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days” (ViDh 46.13). As for Gautama’s rule: “Subsisting on water alone for the third [period] is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*” (GDh 27.32)—meaning that during the times of eating prescribed for the *ekabhakta*, *nakta*, and *ayācita* days, one subsists solely on water; this *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* applies to those who possess the physical capacity [to endure it]. Regarding the *atikṛcchra* and the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) declared for the *prājāpatyakṛcchra* should be understood to apply as well, because of Gautama’s traditional teaching: “By this very [procedure], the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* are explained” (GDh 27.31). Yama describes the definition of the *parāka*:

"Having fasted for twelve days, with his self disciplined according to his vow, this *prājāpatyakṛcchra* consisting of raw grain destroys all sins. Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya states the definition of the *parṇakṛcchra*:

"By drinking water boiled with the leaves of the *parṇa*, *udumbara*, *jātī*, and *bilva* trees, and *kuśa* grass, one leaf at a time for each day, it is declared to be the *parṇakṛcchra*. (YDh 3.317) [181].

Thus, one should drink water boiled with the leaves of the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aravinda*, and *bilva* trees, one by one, every day; and on one day, water boiled with *kuśa* grass. Yama states another definition of the *parṇakṛcchra*:
"Having fasted for three nights and being pure, one should boil all of these together and drink them with water; this is prescribed as the *parṇakṛcchra*.

The meaning is that when one has combined the leaves of the *palāśa* and other trees, boiled them in water, and drinks that decoction at the conclusion of the three-night fast, then it becomes a *parṇakṛcchra*. Mārkaṇḍeya describes the nature of the *phalakṛcchra* and other such penances:
The wise have declared that the *phala-kṛcchra* consists of [eating] fruits for one month;
the *śrī-kṛcchra* is said to consist of *bilva* fruits, and another is likewise described by the syllables of the word *pāda*.
In this manner, using only *āmalaka* fruits for a month, another [type of] *śrīkṛcchra* is recorded;
with leaves, it is considered a *patrakṛcchra*, and with flowers, that *kṛcchra* is so called.
"The *mūlakṛcchra* is prescribed as being performed with roots, while the *toyakṛcchra* is performed with water.

When one boils fruits such as *bilva* and others in water and drinks that water for one month, then it becomes the *phalakṛcchra*. When one drinks the decoction of any one of the roots of *bilva*, *padmākṣa*, and so forth, for one month, then the *patrakṛcchra*, *puṣpakṛcchra*, and *mūlakṛcchra* are accomplished. Yama states the characteristics of the *vāruṇakṛcchra* and the *strīkṛcchra*:
"A celibate student, having conquered anger, [should eat] barley-meal with water even for a month..."
And one should drink it while restricting one's food; this is called the Vāruṇa Kṛcchra.
"One should drink cow urine for three days and indeed drink cow dung for three days; for three days one should subsist on *yāvaka* alone—this is called the *strīkṛcchra*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 5.31).
Yājñavalkya describes the nature of the *saumyakṛcchra* as follows:
"Oil-cake, gruel, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal—consuming these one by one every day, followed by a fast for one night, this is called the *saumya-kṛcchra*.

(YDh 3.322) *Ācāma* is the liquid residue of boiled rice. Having consumed each of these five—oil-cake and the others—for one day respectively, one should fast on the sixth day; this is the *saumya-kṛcchra*. As for what was stated by Jābāla—that the *saumya-kṛcchra* extends over four days—[it refers to a different version].
"Oil-cake, barley-meal, buttermilk, and water-barley-meal, followed by a three-night fast—this is called the *tulāpuruṣa*. Thus it is said;
this [penance] is to be accomplished in eight days. However, Yājñavalkya states that it is to be accomplished in fifteen days.
"By practicing each of these for three nights in succession, that which lasts fifteen days is to be known as the Tulāpuruṣa. (YDh 3.323).
"Of these"—meaning of the five substances under discussion, such as oil-cake and the rest—Yama, however, has stated that [the penance] is to be accomplished in twenty-one days.
Then, consuming gruel, oil-cake, buttermilk,
and water-mixed barley-meal for three days at a time, he subsisted on air alone for two periods of three days.
The Tulāpuruṣa vow, however, is said to last for twenty-one nights.
Thus, these three [penances] are to be established according to the relative degree of the gravity of the sin. Regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) here, Hārīta says:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for the *tulāpuruṣa* as taught by the Three-eyed One (Śiva).
Having performed the officiating of sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice, or having consumed urine or feces..."
Having accepted what should not be accepted, having officiated at sacrifices for those who should not be served, and having censured those who are blameless.
For one afflicted by Vināyaka or struck down by a great disease,
this Tulāpuruṣa penance is the destroyer of even the most heinous sins.
This meritorious gateway to heaven was fashioned by Mahādeva;
[it consists of] sipping water, oil-cake, buttermilk, and barley-meal mixed with water.
Practicing this for three days at a time, subsisting on air for two such periods of three days,
one purifies various misdeeds committed through speech, body, and mind.
Rinsing with water (ācamana) destroys those [impurities], as does a newly performed śrāddha rite and the impurity of birth (sūtaka).
So too does pungency, that which is harsh, and what has been defiled by hair or insects.
It destroys the urine and feces of a dog, as well as anything touched by a killer of a Brahmin;
it expels even that which remains after piercing through the bone, such as oil-cake.

Whatever defects there are in foods, and whatever defects of unctuousness exist anywhere, as well as that which has been touched by the mouth of a donkey or a camel, or even that which has been touched by a fierce person— [all these are to be avoided].
One removes those [sins] and whatever else has been looked upon by a dog by means of buttermilk;
likewise, gold, horses, sesame, cows, land, clothing, and women [remove other sins].
A righteous soul purifies everything, even that which is hidden, by means of water and barley-meal.

One who subsists on air purifies the sins of killing a Brahmin, killing an embryo, stealing gold, drinking liquor, violating the teacher’s bed, defiling a maiden, approaching a eunuch, or approaching a woman in her courses.
[186] Two male figures should be made of sandalwood and ushira-grass, each weighing one pala;
or alternatively, one should have two male figures made from river clay.
Having had an iron arrow well-fashioned according to that great beast by which it was pierced, or the weapon [used], and the target on both sides;
It should be one span in length, with loops formed at both ends.
One should have a golden or silver scale fashioned for the goddess;
if these are unavailable, the scale should be made in whatever manner is possible.

I invoke that tawny one, the brownish-red man who holds the plow, mace, and discus in his hands—[that] tawny one who holds the discus, plow, mace, trident, and thunderbolt in his hands. Come of your own accord! O Charioteer, come! O Svayāma, come! O Nāga, come! O Kṛṣṇājina, come! Welcome; most welcome! O Blessed One, Tulāpuruṣa, Great God, accept this seat, this water for the feet, this water for rinsing the mouth, and these perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and food offerings. Be gracious, O Lord; salutations to you! Be free from anger and well-disposed. Then, one should consecrate the scale with the mantra: "By the truth of the Ṛṣis, the truth of Brahman, the truth of the Gods, and the inner truth—by that truth, O speaker of truth!"
Tell me of the excellence of lands: which land will you cause to flourish?
Tell me of the excellence of seeds: which seed will you cause to grow? And tell me of the excellence of kings: which king will you cause to prosper?
Tell us of our prosperity; what will become of us?
But when one has repeatedly weighed oneself against the teacher on a scale and considers oneself light while the other is heavy, then one may begin the ritual action.

Svāhā to Agni, lord of the earth! Svāhā to Vāyu, lord of the intermediate space! Svāhā to Sūrya, lord of heaven! Svāhā to Soma, lord of the stars! Svāhā to Vāsuki, lord of the *nāgas*! Svāhā to Kubera, lord of the *yakṣas*! Svāhā to Indra, lord of the gods! Svāhā to Brahmā, lord of the three worlds! Svāhā to Devī, mistress of fortune (*bhaga*)! Svāhā to Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa! Svāhā to Kūṣmāṇḍarājaputra! Svāhā to Vināyaka! Svāhā to Mahāvināyaka! Svāhā to Mahāmahāvināyaka! Svāhā to Vakratuṇḍa, lord of the hosts (*gaṇa*)! Svāhā to Dharma! Svāhā to Adharma! Svāhā to the Balance (*tulā*)! Svāhā to Tulāpuruṣa! Svāhā to the Goddess for her return! Having performed it once, one becomes pure, fit for his sons, and capable of ritual action; having performed it a second time, one attains the state of a leader of the hosts (*gāṇapatya*); having performed it three times, one attains the abode of Mahādeva. This is the prescribed dharma for the full moon of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Phālguna, or under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the *kṛcchra* penances: the *vāruṇakṛcchra*.
Regarding that, Yama describes the Vāruṇa-kṛcchra:
"A celibate student, having conquered anger, should drink barley-meal with water for a month while maintaining a restricted diet; this is called the Vāruṇa-kṛcchra. Thus it is said.

Now, regarding the *aghamarṣaṇa-kṛcchra*: Viṣṇu states the *aghamarṣaṇa-kṛcchra* as follows: “Now there are the *kṛcchra* penances. One should not eat for three days. Every day, one should perform the ritual bath at the three periods of the day (*triṣavaṇa*). Submerged in water, one should mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra three times. During the day one should remain standing; at night one should remain seated. At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow as a gift. This is the *aghamarṣaṇa*” (ViDh 46.1–9). Śaṅkha, however, describes the *aghamarṣaṇa-kṛcchra* in another manner:
“For three days, bathing at the three periods of the day, one should observe silence while muttering the *aghamarṣaṇa*.”
One should recite it three times mentally in the water and not eat for three days.
"One should always remain in the *vīrāsana* posture and give away a milch cow;
this vow known as the *aghamarṣaṇa* is the destroyer of all sins. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 18.1–2).
Now follows the *yajñakṛcchra*.
Regarding this, Aṅgiras says: "Disciplined, bathing at the three sessions of the day, self-controlled, and observing silence,
he should undertake the morning bath and perform his daily recitation."
One should recite the Sāvitrī and the Vyāhṛtis eight thousand times,
placing the syllable Oṃ at the beginning and likewise at the end of each form.
Seated on the ground in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), well-restrained, one should perform the recitation;
whether sitting or standing, one should drink cow’s milk once.
In the absence of cow’s milk, there should be cow’s curd;
in the absence of curd, there should be buttermilk; and in the absence of buttermilk, there should be barley gruel.
Whichever one among these may be appropriate, that he should drink;
and he should also consume barley-gruel mixed with cow’s urine.
This Kṛcchra penance, which destroys all sins and is divine, was taught by Aṅgiras himself as being completed in a single day; it is traditionally known by the name Yajña.

"This auspicious expiation is for those joined with mortal sins (*pātaka*), as well as for those with minor sins (*upapātaka*), and even for those joined with great sins. Now follows the *devakṛcchra*.
Yama demonstrates the hardship created by the gods:
"One should eat gruel, barley-meal, vegetables, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter for three days each; then for the final three days, one should subsist on air alone."
[192] This vow, known as Kṛcchra-devakṛta, which destroys all impurities,
was practiced by the Maruts, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.

"Indeed, by the power of this vow, they became free from passion. Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the barley-gruel penance (*yāvakakṛcchra*): Śaṅkha states [the following] concerning the barley-gruel penance.
"One who is composed should practice eating cow dung and barley for one month;
he should perform the *yāvaka* vow for the removal of all sins" (Śaṅkha-Smṛti 18.10).

Devala also says: "The consumption of barley grains boiled in water for seven nights, a fortnight, or a month is called *yāvaka*. By this, *yāvaka*, *pāyasa*, and *udaka* [vows] are explained. These—*yāvaka*, *pāyasa*, and *udaka*—are explained according to the procedure of the *Prājāpatya*."
Now, the *prasṛtiyāvakakṛcchra*;
now, the *prasṛtiyāvaka*. Regarding this, Hārīta says:

"He who perceives himself as heavy with deeds committed by himself should cook a *prasṛti* measure of barley-gruel for his own sake. Then he should offer it into the fire; that itself is the *bali* offering. And he should consecrate the cooked gruel with mantras."
"You are barley, the king of grains, belonging to Varuṇa and mixed with honey;
you are the cleanser of all sins, declared a purifier by the seers."
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, and barley is the nectar of the waters;
may they purify all my evil, whatever misdeed has been committed by me.
Whatever deed has been done by speech, whatever deed has been done by action, and whatever was ill-conceived by the mind—
may the barley grains purify all that misfortune and Kālakarṇī for me.
Likewise, [one should avoid] the failure to serve one's mother and father committed during youth,
as well as that which has been licked by a dog or a pig, and that which is defiled by food-leavings.
The theft of gold, the state of being a *vrātya*, and likewise my own childhood, as well as all slander against Brahmins— may the barley grains purify all of this for me.

While it is being cooked, one should perform a protection ritual. Having poured it three times into the vessel with the mantra: “Homage to Rudra, the lord of beings! O Heaven, Sāvitrī, and Mānasa-ukti! one should offer it into oneself with the mantra: “Those gods who are born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, and whose fathers are skillful—may they protect us, may they favor us; homage to them, svāhā to them. One seeking wealth should do this for three nights. A doer of evil becomes purified after drinking it for six nights. One guilty of a great sin (*mahāpātakin*) [is purified] after seven nights. By drinking it for twelve nights, one burns away all sins committed by a person. By drinking it for twenty-one nights using barley grains that have been washed, one sees the *gaṇas*, one sees the Lord of the *gaṇas*, one sees Knowledge (*vidyā*), and one sees the Lord of Knowledge. He who eats boiled barley-gruel once a day, along with cow’s urine, curds, milk, and ghee, is instantly liberated from sin; “I am he,” says the Blessed One Maitrāvaruṇi. Thus [ends the section]. (HārSm 28.32–48)
Thus have the Prājāpatya and other vows been described. Now follows the method for undertaking these vows; regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
I shall now fully explain the formal undertaking of all vows according to the prescribed rules for all sins, when one intends to perform an act of expiation.
[195] At the end of the day, having removed the nails, body hair, and so forth, one should perform a bath prepared with ashes,
cow dung, earth, water, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and other such substances.
The removal of impurities must be performed for the sake of accomplishing external purification,
preceded by the cleansing of the teeth and accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The vow should be undertaken at the beginning of night when the stars are visible outside;
thereafter, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should remain silent while reflecting upon one's own misdeeds.
"One should ultimately bear intense grief that torments the mind" (ViDh 3.21–25).

The meaning is: having gone outside the village; on the previous day at the beginning of the night, having formally resolved (*saṃkalpya*) the vow according to the manner prescribed by the assembly (*pariṣad*), one should begin to perform the vow on the following day together with its constituent parts, such as bathing three times a day (*triṣavaṇa*) and the morning fire-oblation (*prātarhoma*). The constituent parts, including the morning fire-oblation and so forth, have been shown by Jābāla:
"At the commencement of all *kṛcchra* penances, and especially at their conclusion..."
For he should indeed offer separate oblations with clarified butter alone into the domestic fire.

"And at the conclusion of the vow, one should perform a *śrāddha* and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of cows, gold, and so forth. Yama also says: "Remorse, tranquility, and bathing are declared to be constituent parts [of the rite]."
Of all the occasional vows, according to the prescribed ritual.
[196] “One observing a vow should avoid anointing the limbs, anointing the head, betel, ointments, and whatever else causes strength or passion” (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.14).
Chāgaleya states the transgression incurred by one who has undertaken a vow but fails to complete it:
"Indeed, he who, having previously taken a vow, does not practice it intentionally, becomes a Cāṇḍāla while living and is reborn as a dog after death. Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*):

Next, when it is impossible to perform the previously mentioned vows due to some cause, the appropriate substitutes are stated. Among those, the substitutes for the *prājāpatya* penance are shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"A *kṛcchra*, ten thousand recitations of the *Devī*, and two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*)."
A thousand oblations of sesame seeds, as well as the complete recitation of the Vedas.
"Twelve Brahmins should be fed, as well as the Pāvakeṣṭi;
or else the Pāvamāneṣṭi—thus the wise have declared them to be equal.
This is also stated in another Smṛti.
[197] “A *kṛcchra* penance, ten thousand recitations of the *gāyatrī*, likewise a water-fast, and the gift of a cow to a Brahmin—these four are equal.
Thus it is said; and also in another *smṛti*:
"If the performance of the *prājāpatya* rite is impossible, the best of the twice-born should give a cow;
in the absence of a cow, its equivalent value must be given—of this there is no doubt.
And that value should be given according to one's capacity. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"In the absence of cows, there shall be a gold *niṣka*, or half of that, or even a quarter.
Wherever a certain number of *prājāpatya* penances are to be repeated, there that same number of gifts of cows (*godāna*) must be repeated. This too has been shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"From birth onwards, there are many various sins..."
But for a crime short of killing an embryo, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six years.
"In substitution for cows, one hundred and eighty [cows] should be given by the wealthy;
or, the wise man should mutter the Gāyatrī eighteen lakhs.

Now, according to the aforementioned method, thirty-six lakhs of Gāyatrī recitations would result as the substitute for a twelve-year Prājāpatya penance; however, a count of ten million (koṭi) is recorded specifically in the Caturviṃśatimata.
By reciting the Gāyatrī ten million times, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
he who recites it eighty lakh times is liberated from the drinking of liquor.
"Seventy lakhs of the Gāyatrī purify the goldsmith;
by sixty lakhs of the Gāyatrī, one who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated.
If this were the case, there would be a mutual contradiction between these two statements. Thus it may be argued.

If that is the case, then by this very same reasoning, even the recitation of ten million [mantras] cannot serve as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*). Rather, it must be understood that it is presented as an alternative because it covers the same scope as the twelve-year vow (*dvādaśavārṣika-vrata*). The substitutes for the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and other such penances have been shown in that very same context:
"The *Cāndrāyaṇa*, the *Mṛgāreṣṭi*, the *Pavitreṣṭi*, likewise the *Mitravindā*, the animal sacrifice, and the three-month *Kṛcchra*."
Bṛhaspati has declared that ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds, two *parāka* penances, and one hundred thousand recitations of the *gāyatrī* mantra are equal.

In the absence of regular (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, as well as of iṣṭi sacrifices and animal sacrifices (paśubandha), oblations of cooked grain (caru) are prescribed.
In place of the *parāka*, *taptakṛcchra*, and other such penances, one should perform three *kṛcchras*;
or else, one may arrange for vows, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth, according to the previous rules.

[199] Thus it is said. However, one who is incapable of performing ascetic penance (*tapas*) but possesses an abundance of grain should fulfill the *kṛcchra* and other vows by means of feeding Brāhmaṇas. That too has been stated in that very same work:
"In the *kṛcchra*, there are five; in the *atikṛcchra*, three times that; in the third [the *parāka*], thirty each day; and in the *taptakṛcchra*, forty; in the *parāka*, twenty multiplied by three."
"In the *kṛcchra* penance known as *santāpana*, there are twenty-six [mouthfuls]; that same number, reduced by two, constitutes the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
During this austerity, one whose strength is diminished should feed the foremost of the Brahmins. Thus it is said.

The phrase "day after day" (*ahar ahar*) is connected to every [penance] mentioned. The third is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. As for what was previously cited—"twelve Brahmins should be fed"—as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the *prājāpatya*, that refers to one who lacks wealth; for it prescribes feeding sixty Brahmins over twelve days at the rate of five per day for a wealthy person. For this very reason, another *smṛti* states: "If a Brahmin is somehow unable to perform the *prājāpatya*, he should properly feed five eminent Brahmins [per day] as desired."
The substitution of the gift of a cow for the *sāntapana* and other penances is shown in that very same *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"For a *prājāpatya*, one should give one cow; for a *sāntapana*, two;
and likewise three cows each for a *parāka* and a *taptakṛcchra*."
"In the rule for the substitute (pratyāmnāya) of the Cāndrāyaṇa, eight cows should always be given;
one should give a gift according to the extent of one's wealth for the sake of purification.
As for that which is stated in another Smṛti regarding three gifts of cows for the Cāndrāyaṇa:
In the Prājāpatya penance, one cow is prescribed; for the Atikṛcchra, two are recorded;
and for the Cāndrāyaṇa and the Parāka, three cows are likewise the sacrificial fees.
This refers to the case of one who possesses no wealth; for it is said that one who is unable to perform the gift of a cow (*godāna*) and other such rites should give grass to cows. Thus says Kaṇva:
"One should perform a single study [of the Veda], or else a *prājāpatya* penance;
or, being desirous of purification, one should give ten thousand handfuls of grass to cows."
The specific application of recitation (*adhyayana*), muttered prayer (*japa*), and other such rites according to particular types of persons is shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Those devoted to dharma and those devoted to austerity may at times fall into sin;
for them, the performance of muttered prayer, burnt offerings (*homa*), and so forth, is specifically prescribed."
One should especially give the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances to those Brahmins who merely bear the name, being fools devoid of righteousness.
"A wealthy person should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that has been prepared with great effort;
in this manner, one should cause penances to be administered according to the specific status of the individual.
Following this very direction, the substitutes for pilgrimages and other such acts well-known in other Smṛtis are to be inferred as appropriate. For this very reason, Devala says:
By visiting sacred fords and holy shrines,
a man is liberated from evil through the ascetic power of brahmins.
All rivers flowing to the ocean are meritorious; all excellent mountains are meritorious;
every sacred site is meritorious; and all forest retreats are meritorious.
