Now, the following are the most meritorious great rivers: the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Yamunā, Narmadā, Vipāśā, Vitastā, Kauśikī, Nandā, Virajā, Candrabhāgā, Sarayū, Utpathavartinī, Sindhu, Kṛṣṇā, Veṇī, Śoṇā, Tāpī, Pārāvatī, Pāṣāṇakī, Gomatī, Gaṇḍakī, Bāhudā, Pampā, Devikā, Kāverī, Tāmraparṇī, Carmaṇvatī, Vetravatī, Godāvarī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Sucakṣus, and Aruṇā. Gaṅgādvāra, Kanakhala, Śakrāvatāra, Saukara, Prayāga, and Gaṅgāsāgara—these are the *tīrthas* of the Gaṅgā. Plākṣa, Prasravaṇa, Vṛddhakanyaka, Sārasvata, Ādityatīrtha, Badarīpāñcāla, Vaijayanta, Pṛthūdaka, Naimiṣa, Vinaśana, Camasodbheda, and Prabhāsa—these are the *tīrthas* of the Sarasvatī. The confluence of the Kāverī, the confluence of the Sarasvatī, and Gandhamādana—these are the most meritorious *tīrthas* of the ocean. Puṣkara, Mūrdhaka, Gayāśiras, and Kurukṣetra—these are the meritorious sacred fields (*puṇyakṣetra*). Vārāṇasī, Mahābhairava, Devadāruvana, Prācīnabarhis, Kedāra, Madhyamamahālaya, Kumāramahālaya, Rudrāvatāra, Vaṅgala, Viṣṇuśiva, Mahākāla, Puruṣottama, and Jambumārga—these are the sacred shrines (*āyatana*). The Himavat, Udaya, Mahendra, Vidura, Śataśṛṅga, Śrīparvata, Devaparvata, Nīlaparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra—these are the most meritorious mountains that destroy sin. Other sacred fields, shrines, mountains, hermitages, and *tīrthas* are also exceedingly meritorious. Thus says Viśvāmitra.
Austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* are the causes of purification and prosperity,
whether the offense is public or secret, unmentioned, doubtful, or unclear.
"The Prājāpatya, the Sāntapana, the Śiśukṛcchra, and the Parāka. Thus says Jamadagni:
"At a sacred ford (tīrtha), the penance is one quarter of a Kṛcchra; at a river, one obtains half the fruit."
"But it is double on the Mahānadī, and triple at a confluence.
Likewise, Nārada says:
"The Atikṛcchra, the Parṇakṛcchra, the Saumya, and the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra..."
The Mahāsāntapana is for purification; the Taptakṛcchra is purifying;
the Japopavāsakṛcchra and the Brahmakūrca are likewise purifiers.
These [penances], whether taken individually, collectively, or even by twos or ones,
should be applied with effort to all major sins (pātaka) and minor offenses (upapātaka).
For the sake of purification, one should perform rites consisting of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance either combined with other acts or alone;
or alternatively, a fast for three nights, a month, a fortnight, or half of that.

For those who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka) and for those regarding whom no specific penance has been prescribed, purification should be performed with fruits for six days or twelve days, excluding the consumption of rewards.
Having observed the powers, classes, and qualities, one should quickly form a single comprehensive cognition;
then, having observed the continuities and so forth, everything should be conceptualized in accordance with the scriptures.
"Whatever has been stated in the *Prakāśa*, in the *Rahasyaka* it is prescribed that one-twentieth,
one-thirtieth, or one-sixtieth [of the penance] should be assigned, depending on factors such as caste and so forth. Thus,
the substitutes for *kṛcchra* penances have been described.

Thus ends [the section] in the commentary on the Parāśara-smṛti composed by the minister Mādhava, who bore the burden of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the Great King of Kings, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
The Section on Expiatory Rites in the Twelfth Chapter.
[205] Now, the ripening of karma is examined.

Although in common usage the word *karman* applies equally to both good and evil deeds, here—because expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is the subject at hand—it refers specifically to evil deeds, since it is the latter alone that is present to the mind as that which is to be removed by such means. The specific ripening (*vipāka*) is the state of yielding fruit. The ripening of actions is "karmic ripening" (*karmavipāka*). This ripening is threefold: birth, lifespan, and experience. Patañjali codified all of this in the *Yoga Sūtra*: "When the root exists, its ripening consists of birth, lifespan, and experience" (YS 2.13). The meaning of this sūtra is as follows: the five afflictions (*kleśa*)—namely ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live—are the root of actions, because it has been sūtrized: "The latent deposit of action (*karmāśaya*) has the afflictions as its root" (YS 2.12). When that root consisting of the five afflictions exists, those actions ripen. However, for one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), whose seeds of affliction have been burnt, accumulated actions do not initiate their fruit, because they have been reduced to ashes by the fire of knowledge. Just as rice devoid of its husk does not sprout, so it is with these actions. It is only by depending upon the five afflictions, which stand in the place of the husk, that actions ripen into the forms of birth and so forth. Among these, "birth" refers to existence as a worm and the like.

For there is a traditional legal text (*smṛti*) stating: "Having performed a sacrifice for one who has fallen [from his caste], one is born in the womb of a worm" (BrPurāṇa 217.40). Regarding the lifespan: "In that state, the twice-born lives for fifteen years or the like;
therein, the twice-born lives for ten or five years" (BrPurāṇa 217.40).

Because of this statement; and because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) beginning with: "Experience (*bhoga*) consists of the torments of Yama and so forth; for in the world of Yama, they undergo terrible suffering" (Brahma Purāṇa 125.137).
We shall elaborate in many ways upon this maturation (*vipāka*), characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience, by means of examples from both general and specialized treatises.

Now, one might object: "This maturation cannot be enjoined nor prohibited, because it is not something to be performed and because it is unavoidable; for this very reason, its definition within a scripture devoted to injunctions and prohibitions is inappropriate."

This is not a fault, because it serves that purpose by way of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning penance (*prāyaścitta*). For it is the established rule of those who know the logic [of Mīmāṃsā] that an explanatory passage attains syntactic unity with an injunction or a prohibition—acting as an incitement toward what is enjoined and as a deterrent from what is prohibited. And in this case, since penance consisting of the performance of the *prājāpatya* and other rites is of the nature of suffering, engagement in it cannot occur through mere passion; therefore, an incentive (*prarocanā*) must be provided to ensure such engagement.

Now, an objection may be raised: while one can be incited toward prescribed rites such as the *agniṣṭoma* by describing the ripening of results such as heaven—since heaven and the like are favorable fruits—the description of diseases such as consumption (*kṣayaroga*) is not useful for incitement, because they have undesirable results. This is an unequal comparison. For in that case, incitement must be produced toward the means for attaining heaven and so forth; but here, incitement does not arise toward the means for producing consumption and the like, but rather toward the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) which brings about the cessation of that consumption. And the cessation of that [disease] is indeed a favorable result.

Now, one might object: even so, it must be stated that the ripening (*vipāka*) of the ritual action consisting of expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—as that which inspires one to perform it—is precisely the cessation of diseases such as consumption, and not the ripening of [the sin of] killing a Brahmin and so forth, because the latter does not inspire one to act.

Not so. For acts such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) are of two kinds: those already accumulated and those yet to be accumulated. Among these, regarding the acts yet to be accumulated—which are the objects of prohibition—the mention of diseases such as consumption (*kṣayaroga*) functions as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) intended to deter one from them, just as the mention of "a hundred torments" serves to deter one from threatening a Brahmin. Having heard of the adverse fruit resulting from acts already accumulated, one becomes terrified and desires a means for their cessation. Therefore, because it serves to induce a sense of dread, it also functions as an incentive toward expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Thus, this presentation of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*) is useful as an *arthavāda* that is both inciting and deterrent.

Thus, in this way, there is the application of both that which has been accumulated and that which is being accumulated. Regarding those [karmas] whose fruit has already begun to manifest, agitation is established simply through the direct perception of an adverse result. However, the motivator is the description of the ripening of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) in the form of the cessation of disease and so forth. Therefore, the ripening (result) here is defined as having the form of diseases such as consumption (*kṣaya*), as well as the form of their cessation. In that regard, the ripening of sinful karma is stated in general terms in the *Śivadharmottara*: "Now, therefore, the demerit of men who are falling [into lower states] is fully described."
"Because it causes one to fall into the most terrible ocean of hell, it is called 'sin' (pāpa).
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Bhārgava, there exists a body known as the *ativāhika* (conveying body)."
This occurs only for human beings when the time of death has arrived.
O best of the Bhṛgus, O twice-born one, that body of human beings is led by the messengers of Yama along the path of Yama; it is not so for other living creatures.
Human beings attain either heaven or hell, but no other living beings do so; all of them are merely consumers of the fruits [of their actions].
O descendant of Bhṛgu, it is human beings alone in this world who accumulate a store of both auspicious and inauspicious karmas.
Therefore, O illustrious one, it is a human being who, upon death, enters the world of Yama; no other living creature is established in that state of fruition.
"Likewise, for a person who has reached the world of Yama, Yama determines their wombs and hells according to their karma. Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
Those men who are averse to the Dharma through their actions, thoughts, and speech,
undergo terrible suffering in the world of Yama.

"Even by performing a small deed here that is evil in nature, a man attains a terrible hell and undergoes torment in the worlds of Yama. Thus [it is said] in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* as well. (BrPu 125.136–42)
A doer of evil goes to hell unless he is first intent upon expiation;
for expiations must correspond to the specific sins, each according to its nature.
"Having recollected each [case] exactly as it was declared by the supreme sages. Thus [it is stated].
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Sin committed undoubtedly goes to destruction through expiations (*prāyaścitta*)."
Those who have not undergone the prescribed penances and have not been punished by kings fall into hell, as well as into the wombs of animals.
"Even having reached human birth, they become marked in this world in such a way;
therefore, an expiation must be performed for the removal of that defilement. (ViDhU 2.70.3–5).
Also, in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
For gods, animals, and humans whose minds are devoted to unrighteousness,
Dharmarāja is remembered as the teacher who [punishes] with various most terrible executions.

For those who are devoted to the practice of restrictive observances but whose selves have stumbled through negligence, the Guru is the teacher through expiations; Yama, however, is not desired by them.
The king is declared to be the punisher of adulterers, thieves, and those who act unjustly; and he is the King of Dharma for those who are concealed.
"Therefore, one should perform atonement for the evil committed. Thus it is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa*.
And consequently, one undergoes a body of torment with great suffering.
Born from that karma for the sake of torment, it does not arise from a mother or a father.
Just as before, by means of its dimensions, age, state, and configuration,
it leaves behind that previously well-guarded body composed of the five elements.
He assumes another body, born of his own karma, for the sake of experiencing retribution;
it is composed of the qualities of the subtle elements, is not his own [permanent] self, and is produced by his own karma.
One obtains a firm body for the experience of pleasure and pain;
by means of that, the man who has committed evil, having experienced his own karmas, suffers intensely.
"Happy is the righteous one, free from malice, who has been brought here from the abode of Yama. Thus [it is said].
Manu, however, describes the specific results of maturation according to the specific nature of actions such as those performed mentally:
"O sinless one, this entire dharma of the four castes has been declared by you."
Tell us, in truth, the supreme completion of the fruits of karmas.
The righteous Bhṛgu, son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen to the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action."
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, yields auspicious and inauspicious fruits;
the destinies of humans—whether superior, inferior, or middling—are born of action.
One should know that for this embodied being— who possesses these three kinds [of action], who has three bases, and who is endowed with ten characteristics— it is the mind that is the instigator.
Coveting the wealth of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind,
and adherence to falsehoods— this is the threefold mental action.
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form,
and idle chatter— these constitute the fourfold nature of speech.
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the rules,
and consorting with another's wife— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action].
This person experiences the mental [karma], whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of the mind alone;
verbal action by means of speech alone, and bodily action by means of the body alone.
"Through defects of action born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of birds or wild animals; and through those of the mind, to the status of a low-born caste. (Manu Dharmaśāstra 12.9). Hārīta also says:

Eating all that is not to be eaten, consuming what is unfit for consumption, drinking what is not to be drunk, approaching those who should not be approached, officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate, accepting gifts from the unworthy, adultery with another’s wife, the misappropriation of property, and violence toward living beings—these are the bodily [transgressions]. Harshness, falsehood, quarreling, and the selling of the Vedas—these are the vocal [transgressions]. Afflicting others, malice toward others, anger, greed, delusion, and egoism—these are the mental [transgressions]. Thus, these eighteen hells-like actions, in whichever stage of life a person commits them, he shall experience their bodily, vocal, and mental consequences in that very same stage of life. For thus it is said:
In whatever state one performs a virtuous or non-virtuous deed,
in that very same state one shall obtain its respective fruit.
"By means of the body alone one experiences the physical [karma], by means of speech the verbal,
and by means of the mind alone this [being] experiences the mental— whether auspicious or inauspicious. (Hārīta Smṛti 32.13–18)
Having established that the self has the nature of the Lord, Yājñavalkya says:
"If this is so, O Brahmin, how is it that he is born in sinful wombs?
How is it that the Lord is joined with undesirable states?"
And why does one endowed with the sense organs not perceive prior cognition?
Furthermore, why does the all-pervading self, though itself omnipresent, not perceive [the sensations of] others?
Through the defects born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, this living being goes to the state of the lowest animals and plants, as well as through hundreds of wombs of existence.
Just as the fortunes of embodied beings are infinite according to their states of existence,
so too are the forms of those possessing bodies here in all wombs.
The ripening of karmas for some occurs after death, while for others it arises in this very life;
for yet others it occurs both here and hereafter—such is the nature of things, and therein lies the purpose.
Coveting material goods, dwelling upon what is undesirable,
and being intent on false attachments, one is born in the lowest wombs.
A person who speaks untruth, as well as one who is slanderous, harsh,
or a prattler of idle chatter, is born among beasts and birds.
"One who delights in taking what is not given, one who consorts with the wives of others, and one who is injurious toward immobile beings by improper means, is born among them. Thus [it is said].
He himself has stated the specific nature of the maturation [of karma] according to the specific qualities such as *sattva* and the rest: [YDh 3.129–36].
One who knows the self, is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has conquered the senses, performs dharma, and is learned in the Vedas— such a person of sattvic nature attains the state of divine birth.
The steadfast man who delights in the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause, who is enterprising and sensual, being of a rajasic nature among men, attains birth after death.
One who is drowsy, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar,
as well as one who is negligent and of broken conduct— such a person characterized by tamas is reborn among the animals.
"Thus, possessed by passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), wandering here, and joined with undesirable states, he enters into *saṃsāra*. (YDh 3.137–40). Manu also says:
One should know that sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities of the self,
by which the Great One (mahat) remains pervading all these states without exception.
Whichever of these qualities is predominant throughout the body,
it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality.
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is known as attachment and aversion;
this is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings.
In that regard, whatever one perceives within oneself as conjoined with joy—
tranquil and radiant as if pure— one should understand that to be the quality of sattva.
But that which is conjoined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, know that to be *rajas*, which is always carrying away embodied beings against their will.
But that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense objects,
inconceivable, and unknowable— one should understand that to be *tamas*.
Furthermore, I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities— the foremost, the intermediate, and the lowest.
Study of the Vedas, purity, knowledge of that [Brahman], restraint of the senses,
performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self— these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva.
Delight in undertaking tasks, fortitude, engagement in noble deeds,
performance of dharma, and reflection on the Self— these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva.
Delight in undertaking tasks, persistence, embracing what is not beneficial,
and constant indulgence in sense objects— these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa).
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct,
a habit of begging, and negligence— these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Furthermore, for these three qualities residing in the three [states],
this should be known as the summary definition of their characteristics in their respective order.
Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even when intending to do it—
all that should be known by the wise as characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas).
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve over failure to achieve it— that should be known as rajasic.
That which one desires to know in its entirety, that which one does not feel shame in practicing,
and that by which one’s own self is satisfied— this is the characteristic of the quality of a virtuous being.
Lust is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
righteousness is the characteristic of *sattva*. Their superiority follows this sequence.
I shall now briefly explain, in their proper order, those qualities by which one enters into these various states of cyclic existence for all of them.
Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas indeed attain the state of humans;
and those characterized by tamas always attain the state of animals—such is this threefold destiny.
This secondary course of existence is to be understood as threefold and of three kinds:
inferior, middling, and superior, according to the distinctions of action and knowledge.
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes, reptiles,
domestic animals, and jackals constitute the lowest state of darkness.
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas;
lions, tigers, and boars—these constitute the middling state of darkness (tāmasī gati).
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and deceitful men,
as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas— these are the highest destinies among those in the realm of darkness (tāmasa).
Jhallas, Mallas, and actors, men who live by the sword,
and those addicted to gambling and drinking— this is the lowest state belonging to the quality of passion (rājasa).
Kings, kṣatriyas, the domestic priests of kings,
and those whose primary concern is the science of war— this is the intermediate rājasī path.
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are attendants of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases, find their highest state among the royal lineages.
Ascetics, renunciants, brahmins, and the hosts of celestial beings in their vimānas,
as well as the lunar mansions and the daityas— this is the first, the sāttvika destination.
Ascetics, renunciants, brahmins, and the hosts of celestial chariot-dwellers;
the lunar mansions and the Daityas—this is the first, the Sāttvika state.
Sacrificers, seers, Vedas, gods, luminaries,
years, ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, sattvic goal.
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, and the Great One (Mahat), as well as the Unmanifest (Avyakta)—
the wise declare these to be the highest state characterized by goodness (sāttvikī gati).
"Thus has been fully described the entire threefold, threefold cycle of rebirth consisting of all living beings, resulting from the three types of action. (MDh 12.24–51).
Now, various specific wombs resulting from diverse specific sins that cause states such as being a *preta* (ghost) and so forth are declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Due to his intolerance of another's virtues without cause, a great evil arose; that is the reason for his state as a preta.
These sinners, who seized the property of Brahmins, have come to the state of ghosts;
some were devoted to the wives of others, and others were intent on betraying their masters.
"In this exceedingly dreadful land, some who delight in betraying their friends,
having fallen away from their own duties, are all born into the womb of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Thus [it is said] in the *Padmapurāṇa*.
One who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, one who abandons those for whom he ought to sacrifice,
and one who has desisted from the sacred sciences of Viṣṇu— that man is born as a preta.
"Having received the general sacrificial fee, one who is deluded takes it alone;
that man, devoted to the disposition of nihilism (*nāstikya*), is born as a *preta*. Thus [it is said] in the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Any man who is base and likewise a slanderer,
or one born of a Brahmin lineage who eats meat in vain;
A man who constantly harms living beings is born as a preta.
He who eats without having performed the rites for the gods and likewise the libations for the ancestors,
and without having given to his circle of dependents, is born as a *preta*.
A man who is devoted to another's wife, a stealer of others' wealth,
and one who finds satisfaction in slandering others, is born as a preta.
The man who gives his daughter to an old man, to a low-born man out of a desire for wealth,
or to one who is ugly or of bad character, is born as a preta.
A man who, having taken the wealth of gods, women, or teachers, does not restore it—
especially that of eminent Brahmins— is born as a preta.
But that evildoer who creates an obstacle to wealth being given to Brahmins is born as a preta.
If a Brāhmaṇa dies from food provided by a Śūdra,
even if he is a knower of the three times, a master of the Vedas, a knower of Dharma, or a scholar of the six Vedāṅgas;
Even a Brahmin who is a knower of the four Vedas is born as a preta,
as is a man who composes scriptures, composes books, or is learned in the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga).
That man who, out of desire or delusion, abandons the duties appropriate to his family and country and practices something else, is born as a preta.
Especially for one who is impure from remnants of food, and likewise for one who has died in the intermediate space.
"The state of a preta certainly arises for those who die by poison, fire, water, or death at their own hands; this is the truth, there is no doubt. Thus it is stated in the Agni Purāṇa.
That man who, out of greed, abandons his mother, father, elders, kinsmen, and virtuous people, is born as a preta.
A man who is a base womb-born being, a contemptible physician, one of inferior knowledge, a bad teacher,
and one who bestows favor upon Śūdras, is born as a preta.

He who reviles the twice-born and the gods, who is always devoted to song and instrumental music, and who eats while showing contempt for the elderly, children, teachers, and Brahmins— indeed, he is such a one.
The man who gives a maiden for a bride-price is born as a preta;
so too is one who misappropriates a deposit, a betrayer of friends, or one who is always intent on cooking for others.
That man who does not approach his blameless wife during her fertile period,
or who does not tolerate [the presence of] his friends at a sacrifice, is born as a preta.
If a twice-born man, when not in a time of distress, takes elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, couches, seats, or even a black antelope skin, he incurs sin.
Likewise, the twice-born man [obtains merit from] a swing facing both ways, the earth together with its mountains,
the gift given at Kurukṣetra, and likewise [from giving] to a Cāṇḍāla or one who has fallen from his caste.

"One who eats at the monthly *navaśrāddha* feast partakes only of the food of a *preta*; likewise, one who seizes the daughter of a noble family is born as a *preta*. Thus [it is stated] in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara (AgPu 201.41–48).
Having stolen all one's possessions, as well as the property of the gods,
and because of giving what has been stolen, a man indeed goes to the state of a Piśāca.
And that man, O Goddess, who causes the work of the temple to be performed by one who has been entrusted with it,
he too goes to the state of a piśāca through his betrayal of his master.
Having taken the property of his master, if he neither performs sacrifice nor gives it away,
that fool who sustains only himself goes to the state of a piśāca.
O Goddess, he who, deluded by pride, exercises authority over a monastery,
or he who destroys the property of the monastery and consumes the consecrated offerings (nirmālya), [is a sinner].
Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin,
one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa in a waterless region of the forest.
But those who have fallen under the power of delusion declare unrighteousness to be righteousness—
those who seize the wives of others, whether by theft or by force.
"In a forest or a waterless region, they become *brahmarākṣasas*. Thus says Manu:
"Having entered into association with outcasts, or having gone to another man's wife..."
And by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.
By addressing a teacher with "thou," by uttering "hum" to a Brahmin, or by defeating him in debate,
one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa in a waterless region of the forest.
Those who hate Brahmins and revile them are indeed Rākṣasas; so too are those who revile their teacher, the officiating priest, their preceptor, or an ascetic.
"And those who also show contempt for sages become Rākṣasas in this world.
Thus [it is said]. And in the Vāmana Purāṇa: "He who accepts a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) even from a Caṇḍāla or an Antyaja..."
But that officiating priest who accepts payment for his services becomes an earthworm dwelling within a stone. (Vāyu Purāṇa 61.27).
In the Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"That man who eats alone while his servants are hungry..."
Having entered the womb of a dog, that man is born as a Caṇḍāla.
He who abandons the dharma declared in the Vedas and practices another dharma will certainly be born in the womb of a dog for ten thousand years.

"Those who revile the meaning of the Vedas and those who revile Brahmins are Śūdras in this very life; indeed, upon death, they become dogs. Thus it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa* (Revākhaṇḍa 30.37–39).
If a teacher should abandon a disciple who is like a son without cause,
acting out of his own caprice, he too becomes a violent person.
That son who treats his father and mother with contempt—
even if he is a Brahmin— shall, after death, first be born as a donkey.
Having attained the state of a donkey, he lives for ten years;
then, after one year as a crocodile, he is born as a human being.
He who treats with contempt his eldest brother, who is equal to a father, [is reborn as a worm].
He too meets with death and is born in the womb of a crane;
but a man who steals another's hopes is born in the womb of a worm.
But a man who destroys trust, being evil-minded, is born as a fish;
this occurs when a marriage, a sacrifice, a gift-giving, or a great festival is at hand.
He who, out of delusion, creates an obstacle, is born as a worm after death;
that ungrateful Brahmin, having gone to the realm of Yama, is likewise reborn as such.
O twice-born ones, having undergone many tortures there for many years, he meets with a terrible execution through Yama’s cruel punishments while remaining in that state.
Then the stingy person and the ungrateful one enter into cyclic existence;
but he who should break the downpour of water becomes a fish.

One who approaches his wife through an improper channel becomes a wolf; one who deceives by means of false weights and measures becomes an owl; and one who, having promised gifts to the twice-born, fails to give them, becomes a *madhūka* tree.
"O King, the *devalaka* shall obtain the womb known as that of a *caṇḍāla*;
and by eating on the eleventh day after [the donor] has died, he is born as a dog. Thus [it is stated] in the *Garuḍapurāṇa* (BrPu 218.48–83).
Those wicked ones who give false testimony become worms in impure matter for a long time;
after that, they become serpents, and immediately thereafter, they become piśācas.
Those wicked people who betray their gurus and friends, those who betray their masters,
as well as those who betray their twice-born teachers and disciples, the ungrateful, and likewise the atheists;
Those who abandon their kinsmen and those who abandon those seeking refuge become sinful worms in excrement or hunters of deer.
"Endowed with a multitude of urinary diseases, they are born as *śambuka* insects in the water.
Having eaten during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a man is born as an elephant. Thus it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*.
The Brahmin who eats food without having performed the five great sacrifices shall eternally become a village pig, a carnivorous beast, and even a hunter.
"But a twice-born man, by selling single-hoofed animals, is born as a wild beast;
by being envious, he becomes a worm in excrement, and by practicing contempt, he becomes a worm. Thus it is said in the Vāyusaṃhitā.
Indeed, because he has performed many sacrifices, he becomes a donkey; because he eats without having had them consecrated by mantras, he becomes a crow;
and because he eats without prior examination, he becomes a monkey in the lonely forest.
"He who bestows ignorance shall become an ox;
by giving stale food to a Brahmin, one indeed goes to a state of hunchbackedness.
Thus it is said in the *Umāmaheśvara-saṃvāda*.
If one possesses the Agnihotra fire but fails to maintain its protection,
that Brahmin who neglects the sacred festival days (parvan) shall be reborn as a deer.
Those who subsist on the Vedas, who are wicked, and who are constantly lustful for women,
become crows in this world and remain feeders of excrement for a long time.

"By eating milk-rice (*pāyasa*), rice mixed with sesame (*kṛsara*), and sweet sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) without first giving them to the fire and the Brahmins, one becomes a serpent after death. Thus it is said in the *Nāradapurāṇa*.
O King, that woman who does not become endowed with happiness through the happiness of her husband is born as a female hawk for three and five years.
But that sinful woman who, having restrained her husband out of shame, addresses him with abusive words and compels him to do what ought not to be done, shall become a flying fox.
For she who, out of regard for her husband, does not give away existing wealth or even her own life,
O fair-limbed one, is born as a worm in excrement.
Released from the womb of worms, she becomes a wood-worm;
those who are senseless accomplish the tasks of their masters.
"Having become enjoyers of sensations, they are indeed born as roots [of plants]. Thus [says] Vṛddha-Gautama:
"And a man who teaches the Veda for a fee becomes a tiger."
A living being who recites [the Veda] without permission is born as a jackal.
From a Śūdra he reads as a Caṇḍāla, subsisting on the property of a Brāhmaṇa.

[229] Thus it is said. Yājñavalkya also states: "One who covets the property of others, likewise one who contemplates undesirable things, and one who is intent upon what is false, is born in the lowest wombs."
A person who speaks untruth, as well as one who is malicious and a speaker of idle chatter,
is born among beasts and birds.
"One who delights in taking what is not given, who consorts with another's wife,
and who is a violent injurer of stationary beings by improper means, is born among them. Now, [follow] the fruits of the remnants of various kinds of prohibited actions.
In that regard, from the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara:
"Those who show disrespect toward their gurus and elders are born into the families of outcasts such as *śvapākas* and *pulkasas*, who are contemptible and devoid of intelligence."
For he who practices the study of the Vedas without being authorized by his teacher is born on earth as a human being among those deprived of their caste; likewise,
those who have fallen under the sway of delusion declare what is unrighteous to be righteous.
And those who exert themselves for the sake of death are born here as humans;
they become the lowest of men, devoid of burnt offerings and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
[230] Thus it is said in the *Skānda-purāṇa*, in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*: "Those who are proponents of [false] causal theories obtain birth in an evil land;
and those who are intent on betraying their masters obtain birth in a lowly family."
Those who eat in such a manner without having first given to the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born,
shall obtain birth in a time of famine, during a plague among people, or in a wretched land.
And those who incite quarrels between a loving husband and wife become deformed,
wander about aimlessly, and are shunned by all the world.
Those who create obstacles to the giving away of a daughter, or those who sell her, become impoverished, separated from their wives, and deprived of their lifespan.
"She gives birth only to daughters and never to a son alone;
moreover, those [daughters] are born as prostitutes, widows, or likewise unfortunate.
Thus it is said, and also in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
For those by whom nothing was given, poverty is the mark;
they are born as fierce, violent, humpbacked, and dwarfed, and indeed as diseased.
Childless, overcome by quarrels, and serving the wives of others; engaged in the work of dyers, they wear tattered clothes and possess wretched fortune.
"Those who are deceitful, fickle, greedy, foolish, harsh-speakers,
and devoid of charity— these become devourers of the property of the gods and Brahmins.
Thus it is stated in the Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Those by whom the father, mother, teacher, brother, or any other person with impaired faculties are not honored, they are the lowest of men.
In this world of mortals, those fools who consider themselves wise become wretched and blind, for they abandon their own wives.
They go to the terrible Tāmisra hell; of this there is no doubt.
There, at the end of a hundred years, having attained human status in this world, they are born again.
He is born with diseased skin, ill-favored, and impoverished;
he who consorts with another's wife is born afflicted with sciatica.
One who gives false testimony shall become stammering, and one who speaks falsely except for the sake of cows shall become mute;
indeed, by giving stale food to a Brahmin, one shall go to the state of being hunchbacked.
"Due to stinginess one becomes blind from birth, and due to hatred one becomes deaf;
by eating food without having given it away, one shall be childless. Thus it is said in the Gauḍa Purāṇa.
And those men who go about disregarding the glorification of the Blessed One quickly incur deafness in birth after birth.
Those lowest of men who, seeing the gate of the Blessed One and his attendants, pass by without offering salutations and other marks of respect to them, are possessed by darkness (tamas).

Those men on earth who are born blind from birth, those who are physically deformed and without protectors, those who are lame, those who lack feet, and those who suffer from leprosy— all these are born as such because they did not accept [the teachings].
The shadow of Viṣṇu has certainly been transgressed by them; of this there is no doubt.
And likewise, whoever steps upon the shadow of the Lord’s abode [commits a grave offense].
"He is born lame in the forest, indeed afflicted by diseases and the like.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The backbiter shall have a putrid nose; the informer shall have a putrid mouth."
O Rāma, he was bald-headed, envious, an atheist, and a reviler of the Vedas.
In the same way, O twice-born one, a man who is an atheist incurs further [rebirth];
likewise, a person who is a churner of oil becomes blind.
He who acts contrary to his guru is born as one afflicted by epilepsy;
and he who eats sweets alone, O fortunate one, is born with a wind-tumor (vātagulma).
One who eats from a sacrificial pit becomes a consumer of excrement, suffers from chronic disease, and is afflicted by pain. Furthermore,
having heard insults directed at one’s guru, master, or parents, as well as the reviling of the Vedas,
one becomes dull-witted, deaf, or the lowest of men.
By performing the act of lighting a lamp for Devadatta, the evil-minded person is born with eyes like bubbles or is afflicted with eye disease.
In that very same way, by virtue of that sinful karma, he becomes wretched in appearance,
of low caste in the world, and utterly dull-witted.
One who sells what ought not to be sold becomes deformed;
likewise, one who causes his wife to be superseded by another without fault incurs the same fate.
He incurs fear of the king, and likewise in legal proceedings,
for having performed root-rites for the purpose of subjugation.
He becomes hateful in this world; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise, the one who marries before his elder brother is born in this world afflicted by all manner of diseases.
One who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice is born as one who causes the intermixture of castes;
likewise, a fool who sells the Vedas is born as a gambler.
An atheist shall be poor and excluded from all ritual acts;
one who is given over to excessive pride is born into a contemptible family.
Those who revile their gurus and elders are reborn in the families of outcasts such as Śvapākas and Pulkasas— despised and devoid of intelligence.
Death may come from a precipice, or from poisons— both vegetable and animal—
or from fanged creatures, or from outcastes, or likewise from a brahmin.

[235] Furthermore, death from falling from a house, as well as from falling from a tree, and death caused by cattle in this world should be understood as the lot of those who have committed evil deeds.
In this world, one who has been struck is struck in turn; likewise, one who has been robbed is robbed.
Having killed, one incurs death; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whatever one practices toward another, that very thing arises for oneself;
whatever kind of affliction one undergoes through the action performed by one's own hand, that same result comes back to oneself.
"Such an affliction should be understood to exist for him as well, birth after birth;
therefore, with every effort, one should avoid such affliction. Thus [it is said in] Viṣṇudharmottara 2.107.6–30. Also in the Mahābhārata:
Those who are nihilists, inactive, and transgressors of their teachers and scriptures; those ignorant of dharma and devoid of proper conduct—they become short-lived.
Those who are of bad character, who have broken the bounds of propriety, and who are constantly engaged in indiscriminate sexual intercourse,
become short-lived men in this world and goers to hell.
The man who plays with clods of earth, who cuts grass, who bites his nails, who is constantly impure, and who is a slanderer— such a person does not attain a long life in this world.

I cut short his life-span and likewise seize his wisdom: [236] that twice-born man who recites the Veda while still impure from food, who undertakes the study of sacred texts while soiled, and who, out of delusion, practices his recitations even at an improper time.
"Those who urinate facing the sun, facing fire, facing a cow, or facing a twice-born,
as well as those who do so on a path, become short-lived. Thus it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara*.
And he who subsists on the property of the gods shall become armless;
for by him, the property of the gods has always been consumed by his own hand.
Deprived of the sense of taste, hunchbacked, itchy, and suffering in all his limbs,
a man becomes thus after making physical contact with a deity for the sake of convincing others.
If one should later practice sexual misconduct, that person will become a bubble-mouthed being;
and by eating the food of a temple servant, he will gradually become afflicted with a large goiter.
Through sin, a man becomes afflicted with leprosy on all his limbs and suffers from blindness;
by taking a lamp from a temple, a man becomes lame and deaf; one who hates the gods becomes fainting and dizzy, while one who takes sides [with them] becomes feverish.
He becomes a scorner of the gods, always addicted to sexual intercourse;
his entire wealth is constantly plundered, and he is despised, deluded by lust.
[237] Thus says Vṛddhagautama.

One who lives off the property of the gods suffers from heart disease. By failing to give what was promised to a Brahmin, one becomes short-lived. Having many wives yet finding pleasure in only one, one becomes impotent. Being appointed by a master to a duty but being unable to perform it, one suffers from dropsy. When the weak are oppressed and the strong remain indifferent, one becomes deficient in limbs. One who takes sides in legal disputes suffers from diseases of the tongue. Having undertaken the performance of a religious rite initiated by oneself and then abandoning it, one suffers separation from beloved ones. Eating before others have eaten, one suffers from colic. One who insults friends, kinsmen, masters, and relatives leads a life of humiliation. Seeing a guest eating while remaining silent, one receives only a skull-fragment as alms. By providing shelter in a place where the sun does not shine, one suffers separation from beloved ones. Serving a teacher, a master, or a friend through deceit, one loses the wealth already acquired. A thief of trust becomes the abode of all miseries. One who causes suffering to cows becomes a snub-nosed person. One who is merciless toward cows has a flat nose. One who destroys paths lacks luster in the assembly. One who utters great insults suffers from goiter. One who obstructs merit has a crooked nose. One who defiles the dharma practiced by the virtuous has squinting eyes. One who hates holy men, gods, ascetics, twice-born ones, teachers, knowledge, and yoga has a distorted face. One who destroys tanks and gardens is deficient in eyes and limbs. An ungrateful person is crippled in all undertakings. One who covets the property of others shall suffer from consumption. A guard of thieves—
He who is not impartial in legal disputes and is intent on the conduct of a thief,
nor does he gain profit from trade when traveling to foreign lands.
"There shall be disease, danger to life, and death for that sinner right there. Thus, in the *Umāmaheśvara-saṃvāda*:
"But he who, without having performed the sacrifice for the wicked, should cause grain to enter [his house]..."
In the Maru desert, there may be a tree devoid of both fruit and flowers.
For a thousand divine years, that evil-minded person shall be a plowman;
at the end of that time, having become human through the passage of time, he may occasionally [attain a better state].
He who, out of a base disposition, causes the severance of affection is born indeed poor, diseased, foolish, and of low birth.
Those men who do not listen to the words of their teacher nor to the words of the Vedas incur childlessness as a result of that sin.
And because of that atheism of all of them, they fall into a state of muteness;
for he who, having made a request, [refuses] a cow together with her calf and filled with milk—
If one drinks milk by means of oneself, one thereby falls into blindness.

"The lowest of men, having discharged urine or spittle into fire, suffers from a burning sensation in all his limbs and is afflicted with pain in the stomach. Thus it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara*.
One who gives poison shall have black sores on the face, leprosy, and be intoxicated;
indeed, a man who causes suffering to others shall have sores on the tongue and in the mouth.
But that man who should do harm to one who has helped him will suffer from asthma,
cough, fever, and diseases of all his limbs, and his offspring will die.
Even one whose son has died may become friendless if he hates the lineage of others;
he who acts for the destruction of another's wealth is possessed by a spreading malady.
One who abandons his lawful wife without cause shall suffer from dropsy;
and that lowest of men who, having made a prostitute his wife, lives with her as if she were a woman of noble family.
A man who is unable to eat food and instead subsists on the remains of others' meals becomes a source of mental distress for those around him.

One who suffers from consumption, fever, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, burning sensations, or fistula-in-ano; one who is menstruating; and those who associate with outcasts, Cāṇḍālas, the most sinful, or the fallen—[these are excluded].
A litigant who eats at Puṣpavatī becomes afflicted with leprosy and fever;
he shall be childless and poor, for he has administered poison to one who trusted him.
A man who deludes others by enjoying prohibited things may even become insane through the knowledge imparted by another.
That man who, having lent money, takes an excessive rate of interest in this world,
will be born into a family of wealthy men and thereafter go to another land.
Even there, that man indeed finds no profit from trade;
he who acts improperly toward what is important suffers from fever, asthma, and cough.
"One who suffers from diseases of all the limbs, a sinful soul, a hater, and one whose body is like that of the dead"—
thus [it is said] in the *Umāmaheśvara-saṃvāda*:
"Those lowest of men who nourish themselves with choice food..."
While children look on, he eats without attachment, giving nothing away.
No oblation was offered, no austerity was practiced, and nothing whatsoever was given to a brahmin by him who nourished only his own self; that sin I shall now declare.
"In whatever region there is drought, or wherever there is the arising of violent winds,
in that region those who perform evil deeds are born afflicted by hunger. Thus it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
But he who, having abandoned the state of a Brahmin, devotes himself to the dharma of a Kshatriya,
falls away from Brahminhood and is born from a Kshatriya womb.
That Brahmin who, resorting to greed and delusion, performs the work of a Vaiśya, that twice-born man attains the status of a Vaiśya; likewise, he who performs the work of a Śūdra.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from his own duty indeed attains the status of a Śūdra;
so too, O mighty-armed one, do a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who fail to practice their dharma.
Having abandoned his own duties and resorting to the work of a Śūdra,
he falls from his own station and becomes one of mixed caste (varṇasaṃkara).
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, he goes to such a state;
O son, if one dies with the food of a Śūdra still within his belly.

"A Brāhmaṇa falls to the state of a Śūdra; there is no deliberation on this matter. Thus [it is said] in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* (5.26.7–13): "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya [who takes] the grasping of hands within his own caste..."
But if one does not perform the recitation for another's hand, O King, they fall through the act of grasping.
And whoever takes the hand of a woman of lower caste without regard for the union of castes, he too shall partake of that same caste.
[242] Thus.
Now, regarding the specific maturation of karma: therein, from a specific act of violence arises a specific birth. On this point, Manu says:
Learn now all that manner of birth into which this living soul enters in this world, and by whatever specific karma, in due succession.
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) enter these transmigrations upon the exhaustion of that [karmic residue].

"A killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; and of a Caṇḍāla or a Pulkasa. Thus [it is said] in the *Nandipurāṇa*. (MDh 12.53–55)
The man who has killed a Brahmin is cast down into the hells one after another;
for an eon after eon, and at the end of that time, he is born as an immobile being.
Due to the distinctions of grasses, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and trees,
the varieties of grass are considered innumerable, as are the varieties of shrubs;
the varieties of creepers are beyond counting, and the same is true for the varieties of climbing plants.
The varieties of creepers are indeed innumerable, as are the species of trees;
moreover, their harmfulness is further considered according to the differences in location.
[243] Then, after some time, having experienced their karma in succession from various stationary wombs, they become reptiles.
Whether by the distinction of tree-bark, or by the distinction of region,
or even by the distinction of reptiles and the like— having there consumed that which is sinful.
Thereafter, the mortal is born among deer in countless varieties;
having experienced the fruits of his own karma even there, he is born in the wombs of beasts.
Even there, having enjoyed material enjoyment and finally attained the state of a cow,
one is released from that animal birth and is thereafter born as a human.

"Even there, no fixed rule exists; such a sinner may be born among dog-cookers and the like, or he may be born among men ending with the Brahmins. Thus it is said, and likewise in the *Śivadharmottara*:
Thus, with their sins purified yet by means of residual karma,
embodied beings then reach the earth and are born again.
Having experienced sufferings there, they are born among the species of insects;
having emerged from the insect species, they are gradually born as birds.
Those who are defiled are born as birds in the wombs of wild animals;
having transcended the suffering of wild animals, they are born in the wombs of domestic livestock.
Having entered the womb of an animal, they are born again as humans;
thus, after wandering through all the wombs in succession, they eventually attain human birth.
By the power of the passage of time, they attain the human state, which is exceedingly difficult to find;
and by the weight of their merit, they even attain the most excellent form of human existence.
The various destinies have been declared according to the gravity or lightness of karmas;
therefore, having attained human status, one is there afflicted by diseases.
"By causing a terrible skin disease (kuṣṭha), one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus [it is said] in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Having killed a man unarmed, a person is born as a donkey."
One who kills a woman is born as a worm, and one who kills a child is likewise reborn as such.
Having cut off the testicles of a bull, a man shall incur impotence;
thereafter, he shall further pass through twenty-one births.
Having entered among worms, insects, and moths, as well as among those who practice theft,
and having attained a despised lineage such as that of the Caṇḍālas and Pulakas;
Lame, blind, deaf, afflicted with leprosy, and tormented by consumption;
or else oppressed by diseases of the mouth, diseases of the eyes, or by other ailments.
He becomes epileptic and indeed falls into the state of a Śūdra;
this very sequence is observed for those who steal cows, gold, and other such things.
"And likewise for those who steal knowledge, and those who disobey the instructions of their guru. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 15.18–36).
In the Brahmapurāṇa:
"But he whose conduct is fierce, who causes fear to all beings..."
Whether with the hands, or with the feet, or again with a rope, or with a staff;
Seeking to cause harm, his intellect base, he constantly strikes living beings with clods of earth, pillars, or various means; he is always a source of terror.
[246] One who thus conducts themselves with such moral discipline falls into hell;
yet, if by a reversal of time they should attain human birth, [they will still suffer].
"Afflicted by killing and bondage, he will be born into a low family;
despised by the world, he is the lowest among men due to the fruits produced by his own actions. Now, the remaining fruits of the act of violence:

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita have shown the specific fruits of violent actions: "Thereafter, having experienced sufferings for many thousands of years in places such as Kumbhīpāka and Raurava within the domain of Yama, these characteristics appear among those born here [in this world]. For example: the killer of a Brahmin becomes leprous; the killer of a cow becomes blind; and others become afflicted with various diseases. Thus says Yama:
"But for those who are impure due to their sins, and for those who have fallen from their status through their deeds..."
And for those who have transcended the state of animals, there is a characteristic mark upon the body.
In this world, certain wicked-souled men undergo a transformation of their physical form due to their own misdeeds, as well as those committed in previous lives.
One should know that the killer of a twice-born becomes afflicted with leprosy, and the stealer of gold has deformed nails;
those who injure living beings are born with physical defects and are devoid of righteousness.

[247] Thus says Hārīta: “One who destroys an embryo in the womb becomes one with deformed nails; a killer of a Brāhmaṇa becomes a leper; those who inflict suffering upon others become eternally blind; those who delight in the distress of others become chronically ill; those who steal sight become blind; those who steal hearing become deaf; those who steal speech become mute. For thus it has been said:
‘By whatever limb one causes pain to another, one is born deficient in that very limb.
One does not obtain anything—whether auspicious or inauspicious—without having performed [the corresponding action]. (HārSm 24.73–80)
Kāśyapa says: One who seizes another's field shall suffer from consumption; one who kills a man shall suffer from hemorrhoids;
and one who harms his own wives shall be afflicted with dropsy.
One who pierces the ears will suffer from earaches; one who destroys the lips will have lip diseases;
and one who causes teeth to fall out will always suffer from dental ailments.
From stiffness of the chest he becomes one with a stiff chest; from injury to the eyes he becomes one who destroys his sight;
and by striking with the foot, that man becomes afflicted with erysipelas (visarpa).
One who causes pain and does what is unpleasant becomes afflicted by the disease of the bow from grasping the bow;
and he who strikes with the feet becomes one whose feet are like stakes.
He who tears down vast trees becomes one whose speech is faltering;
he who, being armed with a spear, slaughters sturdy beasts becomes possessed of a spear-like pain in his own body;
and he who [strikes] the two eyes of cows becomes afflicted with night-blindness.
"Driven by his past conduct, he hurls the trident. Thus [it is said]. Vyāsa also says:
"The killer of a father goes to the state of a Piśāca; the murderer of a mother is born blind."
Having killed a limb of a living being or a young deer, one becomes barren or has offspring that die.

One becomes afflicted with an incurable disease, a killer of children, or consumptive; one who destroys all living beings, suffers bodily distress, is wounded, has leprosy, suffers from erysipelas, or becomes a murderer of others.
He who destroys the sight of others shall become afflicted with eye disease;
he who cuts the tongues of others shall have a sore upon his own tongue.
One who is ungrateful, or has burst eyes, or is afflicted by tertian fever,
or suffers from quartan fever characterized by alternating heat and cold, or has constant fever— [these are those who do not attain liberation].
He who causes fear to living beings with dogs, whether in a village or a forest;
he who causes alarm and distress to others, or who strikes them with a stone.
"And a man born as a *talaghātī* (a floor-beater) among wealthy families, having gone to another country, shall suffer a great disease there. Thus [says Vyāsa Smṛti 6.17–22]. Vṛddha-Gautama says:
"He who cuts down trees in vain shall have a sinus ulcer," so it is said in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"He who destroys lordly trees (vanaspati) shall have cracked feet."
One intent on harming living beings, a killer of creatures, or one whose lineage has perished.
A man who, subsisting on air alone, digs up an anthill and destroys it, shall become either black-scabbed, white-leprotic, barren, or afflicted with erysipelas.
One who wore an elephant hide shall suffer from fever due to the command of past karma;
a killer of an embryo shall have perspiring hands, and one who kills offspring shall suffer from chronic dysentery.

[250] Thus, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O descendant of Bhṛgu, O knower of dharma, having caused any living being whatsoever to be killed and having eaten its flesh, one becomes afflicted by disease in this world. (ViDhU 2.108.4)

Thus [have been described] the fruits of all karmas resulting from violence; now, regarding the specific birth-realm resulting from the particular karma of drinking what should not be drunk and eating what should not be eaten, it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"A drinker of intoxicants attains the womb of worms, insects, moths, and birds that feed on excrement, in accordance with their prior karma. Thus it is said in the *Umāmaheśvara-saṃvāda*.
Those who are addicted to liquor, those who consume liquor,
he who causes a tavern to be built, and he who provides the drinking of liquor;
O Goddess, those who sell liquor, those who cause it to be purchased, and those men who drink it— all of them share an equal portion of the karmic result.
O woman of beautiful hips, those lowest of men are born into servitude as vintners, outcastes, hunters, or fishers.
[251] Even animals, once born, meet with death;
hear now, O auspicious one, the destiny of those who are addicted to drinking intoxicants.
Having become a worm on the surface of the earth for sixty thousand years,
once that existence as a worm has come to an end, I shall now describe the sin.
Those who are devoted to drinking intoxicants go to a hundred births as dogs and twenty-five as jackals; O lady of excellent vows, what destination do they reach?
I shall describe the sin of a wicked-souled, liquor-drinking Brāhmaṇa who drinks wine and eats its dregs, such as that which belongs to a Śūdra.
O Goddess, having become a crow, that doer of evil deeds lives for a long time subsisting on excrement;
at the end of twelve years, he may live [to see] his destined end.
That embodied being who desires growth by means of another's flesh through his own flesh, having passed through a hundred wombs, shall have a diseased body.
In whatever wombs those men who eat meat are born,
they are born into them through their karma, afflicted by hundreds of diseases and ailments.
[252] Thus says Manu: "A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor shall go [to the state] of worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed of predatory creatures" (MDh 12.56).

Viṣṇu also says: "One who eats the food of those whose food should not be eaten, and one who eats what is forbidden to eat, becomes a worm" (ViDh 44.11). Vṛddhagautama states: "By obstructing the livelihood of a Brahmin, one becomes a frog for seven births;
but he who eats forbidden food is born as a tortoise."
"One who eats insects, one who eats cold food, one who eats fish, one who eats food obtained by begging,
or one who eats another's food without being invited, shall become a crow. Now, the results of the remaining actions such as drinking what should not be drunk:
Regarding this, Hārīta states: “A drinker of *surā* has a protruding tongue; one who eats what is forbidden has black teeth” (HārSm 24.68–69). In the Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa:
“Due to the residue of sin, one becomes a drinker of *surā* and one with black teeth.

In the Śivadharmottara: “One who eats what is forbidden suffers from goitre (*gaṇḍamālā*). Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One who eats what is forbidden suffers from goitre. Kāśyapa says: “A drinker of *surā* has a flickering tongue” (KāśSm 13.19).
Now, regarding the specific wombs resulting from particular acts of theft, Manu says:
"And [one becomes] a spider, a snake, a lizard, or among animals that move in water."
And among the predatory Piśācas, that Brahmin was a thief by the thousands.
By entering into union with outcasts, by violating another man’s wife,
and by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa.
Having stolen gems, pearls, corals, and various other jewels out of greed, a man is born among the workers in iron.
Having stolen grain, one becomes a rat; bell-metal, a swan; water, a water-fowl;
honey, a gadfly; milk, a crow; savory broth, a dog; and ghee, a mongoose.
A vulture [eats] meat, a cormorant fat, a *tailapaka* bird oil,
a cricket salt, and a crane curd.
Having stolen silk, a partridge [is reborn as such]; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; having stolen a cow, an iguana; and having stolen molasses, a guḍa-insect.
The Cuccundarī [is the deity of] auspicious fragrances; the peacock, of leafy vegetables;
the porcupine, of various kinds of prepared food; and the hedgehog, of unprepared food.
By stealing fire, one becomes a crane; by stealing household utensils, a house-builder bird;
and by stealing red garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.
A wolf [dreaming of] a deer or an elephant, a tiger an horse, a monkey fruit or flowers,
a bear a woman, a water-hen water, a camel vehicles, and a goat livestock.
Having stolen any kind of another's property by force, or having consumed an offering that was not consecrated by the fire, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal.
"Women also, by stealing in this same manner, incur guilt;
they become wives of those very same creatures. (MDh 12.57–69).
Yājñavalkya says:
One who steals the jewels of others will be born into a low caste;
having stolen leaf-vegetables, one becomes a peacock; and having stolen beautiful fragrances, one becomes a *cucchundarī* [musk-rat].
A mouse indicates the theft of grain; a camel, a vehicle; a monkey, fruit;
a water-fowl, water; a crow, milk; and a house-wasp, household utensils.

A honey-thief becomes a gadfly; a stealer of meat, a vulture; a stealer of a cow, a monitor lizard; likewise, a stealer of fire, a crane; a stealer of clothing, one afflicted with leprosy; a stealer of liquids, a dog; and a stealer of salt, a cricket.
"This which I have stated regarding the act of theft is for the sake of illustration;
for just as there are various kinds of property, so too are there species of living beings. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.213–16, cited in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa).
One who steals a deposit is released from hell only to be born as a worm;
[so too for one who steals] grain, barley, sesame, mung beans, horse gram, mustard seeds, and chickpeas.
Having stolen other grains or crops out of delusion, an insentient creature is reborn as a rat with a massive mouth and a body as hard as a diamond.
Having stolen food, a man is born as a fly;
having stolen milk, he is born as a cat after falling from hell;
and having stolen food mixed with sesame and oil-cake, he becomes a mouse.
By stealing clarified butter one becomes a mongoose; by stealing meat repeatedly, a crow; by stealing deer-meat, a hawk; and by stealing salt, a cricket.
By stealing milk, one is reborn as a crane;
he who steals oil is born as an oil-drinking insect;
having taken honey, a man becomes a gadfly, and having stolen clarified butter, an ant.
Having stolen niṣpāva beans, one is born as a house-lizard;
having stolen a seat, one attains the state of a partridge.
Having stolen iron, that evil-souled one is born as a crow;
having stolen bell-metal, he becomes a *hārīta* bird, and having stolen silver, a pigeon.
One who steals a red garment becomes a jīvañjīvaka bird.
Having stolen auspicious perfumes, one becomes a muskrat;
having stolen grain, one becomes a hare; by stealing straw, one becomes a eunuch; and by stealing wood, one becomes a wood-boring insect.
One who steals flowers becomes a leper; one who steals a cart becomes poor and lame;
one who steals vegetables becomes a partridge; and one who steals water becomes a cātaka bird.

"Having gone to the most dreadful hells, such as Raurava and others, the stealer of land [becomes] in due order a blade of grass, a shrub, a creeper, a vine, a bast-fiber plant, or a tree. Thus [it is said].
Gautama says:

One who speaks untruth becomes one with a stammering tongue and whose speech falters repeatedly; [258] one who abandons his wife becomes one with dropsy; a false witness becomes one with elephantiasis, having swollen shanks and feet; one who obstructs a marriage becomes one with a cleft lip; one who threatens with violence becomes one with severed hands; a matricide becomes blind; one who violates his daughter-in-law becomes one with testicles like those of a dog; one who voids excrement or urine at a crossroads suffers from dysuria; a defiler of virgins becomes a eunuch; one who eats stale food becomes a worm; an envious person becomes a mosquito; one who quarrels with his parents becomes epileptic; a stealer of deposits becomes childless; a stealer of gems becomes extremely poor; a seller of knowledge becomes a beast of burden for men; a seller of the Vedas becomes a leopard; a priest who officiates for many clients becomes a water-fowl; a priest who officiates for those unfit to sacrifice becomes a boar; one who eats without being invited becomes a crow; one who eats only delicacies becomes a monkey; one who eats here and there becomes a cat; one who burns a forest thicket becomes a firefly; a teacher of children becomes foul-mouthed; a taker of what is not given becomes an ox; a miser becomes a bee; one who extinguishes a fire becomes afflicted with ringworm; an Āryan who behaves like a Śūdra becomes a dog-cooker; a stealer of cows becomes a snake; a stealer of oil becomes consumptive; a stealer of food becomes indigestible; a stealer of knowledge becomes mute; a stealer of water becomes a fish; a stealer of milk becomes a heron; a stealer of another’s property becomes a servant to others. Thus [it is said]. (GDh 20.4–38)
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One who steals a prostitute becomes a snake that creeps upon mountains; one who steals another’s water, a porpoise; one who steals grain, a pigeon; one who steals offerings for the ancestors, a crow; one who steals copper, a *valgula* bird; one who steals cakes, a ghost; one who steals sacred scriptures, a fool; one who steals a parasol, a *kāraṇḍava* duck; one who steals perfumes, a moth; one who steals a banner, a chameleon; one who steals vegetables, a beast; one who steals a bed, one who has no bed; one who steals flowers, one with a foul odor; one who steals fruit, one who bears no fruit; one who steals a lamp, an owl; and one who steals land, any one of the following: a mongoose, a snake, a cat, or a rat.

"Whatever belongs to another—be it small or be it large—one certainly attains a corresponding womb after stealing it, in accordance with the nature of that enjoyment. Thus [ends the section on the results of theft]. Now, the remaining fruits of the act of stealing:
In that regard, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states: "O Rāma, men who, having stolen gems such as jewels, pearls, corals, and various other precious stones, are born among goldsmiths."
O tiger among men, having forcibly seized whatever another's property it may be, a man incurs the state of being a beast of burden in human existence.
A thief of grain shall be deficient in limbs; one who steals mixed grains shall have redundant limbs;
a stealer of cooked food shall be diseased; and a stealer of speech shall be mute.
One who steals clothing shall become afflicted with vitiligo; one who steals a horse shall become lame;
one who steals a lamp shall become blind; and one who extinguishes a light shall become one-eyed.
One who is impoverished, one who steals the wealth of others, one who is insane, and likewise one who sets fire [to a dwelling].
Likewise, one who steals all [the cattle] should be known as being lame;
and by stealing a cow, that lowest of men is born blind in this world.
"Those who steal clothing or food likewise become naked and hungry; the lowest of men who steals gems becomes a leper. Thus [it is said] in the Vāyupurāṇa (ViDhU 2.107.2–9).
A man who steals becomes afflicted with wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) and likewise suffers from leprosy;
furthermore, a man who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa is born as one suffering from urinary disorders (prameha).
He who takes away juices and other such things will have perspiring hands and feet; he who is a thief of food will suddenly become emaciated.
"And a mortal who steals speech is born with a damaged voice. (Vāyu Purāṇa 2.31.25–27), in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara;
furthermore, "one who steals grain is born with deficient limbs, or likewise one who steals grass."
One who steals the property of others and one who deprives his dependents of their means of livelihood.
Those who seize the food, fields, or houses of others,
as well as gold, jewels, pearls, garments, and ornaments;
Those men who, deluded by ignorance, constantly seize the various seats, wealth, grain, and household utensils belonging to others;
And for those who have died in this world, this rule is prescribed:
they are always naked, wretched, afflicted by hunger, clad in rags, and miserable.
Treated with contempt by their kinsmen and deprived of the enjoyment of wealth,
they seek them out here, having fallen into the state of servitude.
And those men who steal musical instruments and various kinds of percussion instruments, O Goddess, go to the state of animals because of that sin.
Having stolen musical instruments such as the *anaddha* and others, as well as the *jhallarī* and *paṭaha* drums,
those foolish men go deaf because of that sin.
Those who, out of wickedness, steal a bell-metal vessel, a drum, a flute, a lute, or a tumburu lute, become piśācas.
Those who steal a drum, a plaster, or likewise small boxes,
and those who steal a lotus, go thereby to the state of being mute.
"And those men who, O Goddess, steal lamps from palaces or even from the houses of Brahmins, by that act they go to the state of blindness.
Thus [state] Śaṅkha and Likhita.

A thief of gold has deformed nails; a stealer of clothing suffers from vitiligo; a stealer of silver has ringworm; a stealer of metallic objects has circular skin spots; a stealer of oils suffers from consumption; a stealer of food suffers from indigestion; a stealer of speech is mute; one who lives off the property of the gods becomes a vulture; a stealer of lamps suffers from jaundice; and one who destroys the livelihood of a Brahmin becomes impoverished. Furthermore, by the specific nature of their actions, people are born hunchbacked, impotent, lame, or poor. Thus says Yama: "And a stealer of goods or medicinal herbs shall incur chronic illness."
A thief of grain shall be afflicted with sores, and one who steals food shall suffer from coughing.
"A man who steals the property of the community suffers from goiter;
one who seizes strength suffers from consumption; and one who steals meat becomes a hawk. Thus [it is said in] the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Revākhaṇḍa*. (YaSm 5.3–5)
O lord of men, those who speak with false measures, false weights, or give false testimony are cooked in the Andhatāmisra hell.
Having dwelt there for a period of one hundred thousand years,
those men wander here in the house of their enemy, bound, for as long as they desire.
"One who steals gold becomes a man with deformed nails; one who steals books becomes mute;
for one who steals fruits, offspring die—of this there is no doubt.
Now, the specific nature of the womb [of rebirth] results from the specific karma of approaching those who should not be approached.
In that regard, in the Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa: "One who violates the wife of his guru will certainly become a chameleon;
one who approaches the queen becomes a camel, and the husband of a low-caste woman becomes a scorpion."

[265] Thus says Gautama: "By having intercourse with a *cāṇḍālī* or a *pulkasī*, one becomes a python; by having intercourse with a female ascetic (*pravrajitā*), a desert-demon (*marupiśāca*); by having intercourse with a *śūdra* woman, a long worm; one who approaches a woman of his own caste becomes poor; and one who approaches a cow becomes a frog. In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"By approaching another's wife, however, one is born as a red water-jug (*raktadroṇa*)."
He is born successively among the species of dogs, jackals, pigs, and vultures.
That evil-minded evildoer who violates his brother’s wife,
that sinner, having fallen from hell, attains the state of a male cuckoo.
A sinful man, driven by lust, who violates the wife of a friend, the wife of a teacher, or the wife of a king, is born as a pig.
A Śūdra who has approached a Brāhmaṇa woman is born from a womb of worms;
having produced offspring in her, he becomes an insect within wood.
"He is born as a pig, a worm, a water-fowl, and a *caṇḍāla*. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 15.9–16) [266].
Thus it is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The wife of a friend, the wife of a teacher, and likewise the wife of a king..."
He who, out of lust, commits an assault shall be born as a pig after death.
He becomes a pig for five years, a wolf for ten years,
an ant for three months, and a worm for exactly one month.
Having undergone these transmigrations, one is born in the womb of a worm;
there, in the womb of a worm, one lives for fourteen months.
Then, having committed an unrighteous act, one will indeed be born as a wolf;
thereafter as a dog, a jackal, a vulture, a serpent, a crow, and likewise a crane.
But that evil-souled man who, deluded, takes pleasure in his brother’s wife,
O twice-born one, shall become a cuckoo for one year.
That sinful disciple who, even in his mind, approaches the wife of his teacher,
goes to fierce transmigrations because of his unrighteous mind in this world.
Having been born in the womb of a dog, he lives for three years;
having experienced hell even there, he is then born in the womb of a worm.
Having attained the state of a worm, he lives for one year;
thereafter, having reached hell, he is born into a Brahmin womb.
A low-caste man who has approached a Brāhmaṇa woman is born in the womb of a worm;
then, upon meeting his death, he is born again as a pig.
O twice-born ones, by that karma, the fool is then born as a dog.
"Having become a dog, one is then born as a lizard;
thereafter, having produced offspring there, one is then born as a mouse. Thus [it is stated] in the Nārada Purāṇa (BrPu 217.66–80).
One should not think of or even look upon one’s mother,
daughter, daughter-in-law, a brother’s wife, a teacher’s wife, or the wife of a king.
[268] That man who, upon seeing these women, falls into agitation— even if they are outcaste women— goes to a terrible hell as a result of his intentional thought.
"All the merit performed by him becomes futile, and not otherwise;
through the exhaustion of his merit, he certainly becomes a sinner and a stone," thus [it is stated] in the Varāha Purāṇa regarding an unchaste woman.
Thereafter she becomes a bitch, and after that a sow;
once her karma is exhausted, she thereafter becomes a despised human being.

"And she does not obtain happiness, being tormented by that suffering. (VāmPu 20.71–72) "The violator of the Guru's bed [undergoes the fate] of grass, shrubs, and creepers, as well as of carnivorous beasts with fangs, and of those devoted to cruel deeds, respectively."

"Those who have intercourse with women who should not be approached become, after death, carnivorous beasts of prey that gradually eat what is forbidden to eat; those who devour one another become fish; and those who serve the lowest women become [beings] in the final [rebirth]. Thus, according to the *Padmapurāṇa*, there is a specific result corresponding to the specific act of approaching those who should not be approached.
One who approaches the wife of a teacher will suffer from abdominal disease; likewise, by approaching another's wife, one will be afflicted with fistula.
