"Likewise, through great sin, one may become a sufferer of glandular swellings upon approaching an outcaste woman. Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"And he who violates his wife's chastity is born in this world as a eunuch."
And his wife likewise becomes one who is attached to another man.
O knower of dharma, one who has stolen a woman becomes afflicted with leprosy;
one who takes pleasure in sexual intercourse with those of improper species incurs a disease of the genitals.
O best of the twice-born, having gone to Gāṃ, a man who,
with a wicked mind, beholds another's wife naked shall incur the loss of his virility.
He attains blindness from birth in the next world, without a doubt;
he becomes one who has broken his vow of chastity and is afflicted with a disease of the genitals.
"A creature who engages in promiscuous sexual intercourse indeed becomes a eunuch, O twice-born one. (ViDhU 2.70.41–46)

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One who engages in sexual intercourse on sacred festival days (parvan) becomes a sufferer of urinary disease (pramehin). One afflicted by a virile disease, one who approaches the wives of others, and one whose own wife is unprotected [from such advances], become so. One who spills his seed upon cows becomes one with diseased skin (duścarmā). One who approaches a female donkey becomes a sufferer of urinary disorders involving urine (mūtramehī). One who approaches a woman of the same lineage (sagotra), one who approaches a woman who drinks liquor, and one who approaches a woman, become one with elephantiasis (ślīpadī). One who approaches his mother, father, or sister becomes one who lacks seed (abījī). For one who gambles with anyone other than his own wife, there is a thinning of the hair. One who violates the bed of his teacher (gurutalpagah) becomes one with diseased skin. One who spills his seed upon a Caṇḍāla woman, one who defiles a maiden, one who approaches a woman of the same lineage, and one who lacks seed, [become so]. One who directs [his seed] into the mouth of his lawful wife becomes bald (khalvāṭaḥ). One who approaches his mother’s sister becomes one who spills his seed, one with elephantiasis, one with a severed organ (vadhrī), and a sufferer of diabetes (madhumehī). Thus says Vṛddha-Baudhāyana.
By approaching a cow, one becomes a sufferer of madhumeha; by approaching a four-footed animal, one suffers from dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
A human who approaches a donkey, a horse, or other such animals becomes a madhumehin.

"One who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the same caste becomes afflicted with blood-disease; a killer of a father suffers from jaundice; and by having intercourse with a woman of the lowest castes, a mortal is born [with such ailments]—of this there is no doubt. Thus says Vṛddha-Gautama.
Having approached the wife of his guru, he becomes a scorpion, a snake, or likewise a bird,
a fanged beast, a wild animal, a predator, or even a carnivore, and that repeatedly.
Likewise, having attained human birth, one may become subject to wasting diseases, leprosy, abdominal dropsy, urinary disorders, skin diseases, or fistula-in-ano.

One who has intercourse with his mother’s sister suffers from fever, diarrhea, burning sensations, burning of the feet, and worm-infested sores; one who does so with his own wife suffers from urinary diabetes.
One who violates a maiden suffers from urinary stones, colic, urinary disorders, and difficulty in urination;
furthermore, by approaching a maiden born of his own lineage, a man becomes deprived of arms.
By approaching a woman of the same lineage or the same caste, a man shall become afflicted with elephantiasis;
by approaching his mother or his sister, he shall become an elephantiasis-stricken beggar.

One who has sexual intercourse with a mother-in-law will have feet devoid of bones; one who has intercourse with a female friend or a wife's sister will suffer from painful urination; likewise, one who has intercourse with a daughter-in-law will be tongueless and suffer from enlargement of the scrotum.
A mortal who approaches a woman during her menses, or who delights in approaching a Caṇḍālī woman,
shall suffer from burning fever and, in future births, be afflicted with abdominal tumors.

By approaching an ascetic woman who is pregnant, one suffers from difficulty in urination; by approaching a sick woman, one becomes afflicted with disease; and by approaching a widow, one is beset by urinary stones.
A mortal who approaches the wives of others becomes afflicted with urinary disorders (prameha), difficulty in urination (mūtrakṛcchra), and colic;
likewise, one who violates the wife of his teacher becomes afflicted with urinary disorders.
One who approaches female slaves, who performs cruel deeds, and who is always devoted to sensual pleasure,
is born as a leper among mortals, having sexual relations with women of his own caste or those of others.
A man who engages in sexual intercourse with his own mother is born bald;
moreover, a person who approaches the queen of a king becomes a eunuch.
By looking excessively at the wives of others, one becomes afflicted with eye disease;
if there are many women, one who goes to but a single wife shall become lame.
A man who gambles with anyone other than his own wife shall have scanty hair; likewise, women who gamble with such men shall become prostitutes, child-widows, or deaf.
"Or they become female slaves, long-term invalids, or blind. Thus it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"And he who employs his eyes even to look upon the wives of others..."
Indeed, by that evil nature, they truly fall into impotence.

"Those men who abandon their cattle, those who violate the bed of their guru, and those who engage in promiscuous sexual intercourse, are born as eunuchs. (BrP 217.64–65) Thus, having cited certain scriptures in this manner, a portion of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*) has been described. In this same direction, other forms of ripening are to be inferred; for it is not possible for anyone to cite them in their entirety. This has been stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
I have thus described to you these births among animals and their characteristics;
however, it is not possible for me to describe them in their entirety.
And those wombs which belong to the lowest of men.

[273] Thus, there is also an incapacity [to enumerate them] due to the infinity of karma. Even though Viṣṇu has compiled the sins beginning with the *atipātaka* (grave transgressions) and ending with the *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous sins) into ten categories, that compilation is nonetheless made only under the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the classes such as *atipātaka*. However, as for the individual instances of sin, there is no limit to their number, owing to differences in their essential nature, as well as place, time, agent, state, and so forth. When there is no limit even to the actions themselves, then the limit of their ripenings (*vipāka*) is all the more remote; for it is recorded in tradition that each single action possesses manifold types of ripening. And many Smṛti texts have been cited that declare such manifold ripenings, such as those beginning with "a dog, a pig," and so on. Nevertheless, a complete enumeration of these is impossible to conceive even with the mind. Therefore, only a mere indication in the direction of the matter has been shown.

It has been stated previously that this description of the ripening [of karma], by turning a person away from what is being accumulated and generating a sense of urgency regarding what has already accumulated, functions as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in connection with prohibitions and the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Among those, the prohibitions have been detailed in the section on conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*), and the rules for expiation in the section on expiation (*prāyaścittakāṇḍa*). Furthermore, those expiations concern accumulated [karma]. However, in the case of [karma] that has already begun to take effect, it must be investigated whether an expiation exists or not. On this point, some say that there is indeed one, and they cite the following scriptural statement:
Sin committed in a previous birth afflicts one in the form of disease;
its pacification is achieved through medicines, gifts, recitations, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth.
[274] Thus it is said.

But surely—this cannot withstand logical scrutiny. For instance, it is established that a prohibited action is to be removed by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). However, once its fruit has begun to manifest, the action has already transcended the state of being an "action" and entered the state of being a "fruit. And nowhere is there any well-known instance of an expiation for a fruit.

This is not a fault, because even at the stage when the fruit has manifested, there is no absolute cessation of its status as karma; otherwise, the conventional usage "the fruit of an evil deed" would be untenable. Alternatively, the existence or non-existence of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is to be understood solely through the scriptures (*śāstra*). If the scripture prescribes an expiation even for the fruit itself, what is lost for you? And scripture has indeed been cited: "Its pacification is by means of medicines," and so forth. Therefore, there certainly exists an expiation even for that whose fruit has already begun to manifest.

Others, however, hold that there is no expiation at all for one whose fruit has already begun (*ārabdhaphala*). This is because we do not observe the cessation of conditions such as having deformed nails (*kunakhitva*) through expiation. If the fruit that has begun were to cease through expiation, then innate conditions such as having deformed nails would also cease through expiation; yet we do not perceive this to be so. Just as the hitting of a target by a released arrow cannot be rectified, so too the fruit that has begun cannot be remedied. With this very intention, the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa composed the Sūtra: "But only those prior [works] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is the limit" (BrSū 4.1.15). The meaning of this is as follows: those good and evil deeds which were under discussion in the two preceding sections as being removable by the knowledge of reality, only those are "whose effects have not yet begun. There is no removal of good and evil deeds whose fruits have already begun. Why? "For that is the limit" (*tadavadheḥ*). Because in the Śruti text, "For him there is delay only so long," it is heard that even for one in whom knowledge has arisen, the limit regarding liberation is the falling away of the body. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of passages such as 'the pacification of that'?"—[the answer follows].

It is said: For an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is not being taught here, because it is not recited within that specific context. Indeed, this is recited in the section on medical treatment (*cikitsā*). And so, just as medical treatment is a visible means for the cessation of disease, so too are giving gifts (*dāna*) and other such acts invisible means. This being the case, giving gifts and the like do not constitute expiation here in the same way that medical treatment does; rather, giving gifts and the like produce a certain powerful merit (*apuṇya*—here referring to *puṇya*, "merit") from a single performance. And that [merit], having obstructed the fruits of other well-performed deeds, yields its own fruit. The remainder of the obstructed fruit is then experienced in dreams or in another birth. All of this has been explained in detail by Parāśara in the *Upapurāṇa*.
The karma that initiates the body— whether of a yogi or even one who is not a yogi—
undoubtedly does not perish without the experience of its fruit.
O Śuka, the karma accumulated by an embodied being through his present body yields its own fruit for the ignorant one, either in this world or in the next.
O sinless one, even in this very life, karma that has begun to bear fruit may obstruct its own commencement and instead yield its result either in a dream or during the waking state.
But O best of men, when the obstruction has ceased, the commenced karma yields its stable and supreme fruit,
having its portion of results restrained, even within a dream.
Just as experience arises in the waking state equal to the portion that has ceased,
so too does it deliver karma, together with that very [experience], once it has ceased.
Thus, whether in a dream or while awake, the embodied soul undoubtedly experiences the fruit of that which has been obstructed,
in accordance with what has already begun.
However, by means of extremely intense merits and demerits acquired in this world,
the wise embodied being, having severed the *prārabdha* karma, experiences its respective fruits.
The embodied soul experiences the remainder of its *prārabdha* karma, which was interrupted, through another body;
therefore, what man can transcend that?
O Śuka, actions must necessarily be experienced, whether simultaneously or sequentially,
even through incompatible bodies such as those of dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, and so forth;
for it is the fruits that are to be experienced which follow from actions in due order.
In this world, causes revolve like a wheel;
they begin in a specific sequence, and their destruction occurs through experience.
When all accumulated actions have gathered together, the powerful karma of the embodied being initiates its fruit— the body as well as the means for its attainment— so says the wise one.
"Everything that is difficult to accomplish, the insentient Māyā, the power of Maheśvara, brings about; there is no doubt in this, for such is its nature. Thus [it is said].

If it is argued that by accepting the obstruction of a result already set in motion (*prārabdha-phala*) by a powerful karma, even natural defects such as deformed nails (*kunakhitva*) and the like might occasionally be obstructed—[we reply: let them indeed be obstructed. However, where no such obstruction is observed, one must infer a weakness [in the karma]. As for powerful karma, it is recorded in tradition that even the state of birth can be altered by boons or curses; thus, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, it is stated that a tiger attained the status of a lord of the Gaṇas (*gaṇeśvaratva*) through the Lord (*Īśvara*). If even the body of one already born can undergo alteration due to a powerful cause, what need is there to mention the alteration of conditions such as having deformed nails?

This being the case, all the treatises that prescribe the pacification of diseases and so forth will be rendered supportive without contradicting the experience of the *prārabdha* (fruits of past actions already underway). The pacification of disease is accomplished through medicines and the like; therein, the medicines are those well-known in the *Āyurveda*. As for gifts (*dāna*), they are to be understood from the *Baudhāyanakalpa*, the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*, and other sources. Recitation (*japa*), however, has been explained in many ways in the *Ṛgvidhāna*, *Sāmavidhāna*, and other works proclaimed by Śaunaka and others. Thus it is recorded in the *Ṛgvidhāna*: "One should recite the hymn beginning with 'ṛtasya' thirty thousand times in the temple of Viṣṇu."
In the month of Māgha, by [worshipping] the Aśvattha tree, urinary disease is destroyed.
If one recites the *Śukra-sūkta* three times ten thousand times at an *aśvattha* tree,
various types of wind-diseases (*vātaroga*) will undoubtedly perish.
Or one should recite the Vāruṇa Sūkta ten thousand times at the root of a Dhātrī tree;
then, for the destruction of diseases caused by heat and the like, one stands happily upon the earth thereafter.
The wise man should recite the *sūkta* beginning with "kadrudrāya," which destroys cold-fever;
by touching the *liṅga* ten thousand times, he likewise quickly attains health.
One should recite this hymn to the powerful Rudra in a temple of Śiva ten thousand times for the destruction of fever; of this there is no doubt.
If one should recite this hymn to Rudra ten thousand times in a temple of Śiva, it destroys diseases such as cough and pain; of this there is no doubt.
Swinging [the vessel], one should recite the hymn one hundred thousand times using either *bilva* or *śivā* fruits;
leprosy will be swiftly destroyed during the month of Māgha, without a doubt.
The wise person suffering from leprosy should recite the Haṃsa-mantra thirty thousand times in the temple of Viṣṇu and offer water for honor; thus he shall attain equality with gold.
By reciting the mantra of Citradeva, diseases of the head are destroyed;
thereafter, by reciting it ten thousand times in the temple of Viṣṇu, there is an increase in lifespan and other benefits.
One who suffers from leprosy should recite the *Amīvahā* hymn, composed by Svapna, three times ten thousand times in a temple of Śiva; he shall then attain a golden complexion.
One should recite the hymn beginning with "mitrasya"; epilepsy will be destroyed, and even one burdened by great sins shall remain free from disease upon the earth.
But one suffering from colic should recite this hymn in a temple of Śiva for ten thousand times during the month of Māgha; he shall be liberated, of this there is no doubt.
Every day, one should recite ten times the hymn "sūryo no divaḥ."
"And at Badarī for three years, there is the destruction of wasting diseases and other ailments. (ṚgVi 101–51).
These recitations (*japa*) have been taught by Śaunaka in the *Ṛgvidhāna*. Regarding the fire-oblation (*homa*), he says the same therein:
"Then one should perform a thousand-fold oblation with the *citramantra*."
By performing the Trimadhuka rite with the Arka hymn, disease of the head is destroyed.
When the seventh lunar day falls on a Sunday, one should perform a thousand oblations of oleander flowers with the Gāyatrī mantra while standing in the midst of water.
"Disease shall be swiftly destroyed; that man conquers death. Thus [it is said in ṚgVidhāna 169–71]. Baudhāyana also says:
"One who is seized by an incurable disease, fierce and life-taking..."
With the hymn beginning "ā te rudra," being pure and restrained in speech, he should offer oblations verse by verse.
Having first offered oblations of clarified butter and worshipped Śaṅkara,
he should diligently subsist on the remnants of the sacrificial offering, increasing it by one portion each day.
When a month has been completed, one conquers death and is liberated from diseases;
for those unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), the recitation (japa) shall be double that amount.
[282] Thus it is said; and in the second book (kāṇḍa) of the Taittirīyaka branch, oblations for the purpose of removing disease are described in many ways.

In that regard, first, in the section on the animal sacrifice for specific desires (*kāmyapaśu*) within the first *anuvāka* of the first question, following the injunction “One should immolate a white animal dedicated to Vāyu” (*vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta*, TS 2.1.1.1), it is heard: “One who has been ill for a long time should immolate [an animal] for Vāyu accompanied by his team (*niyutvate vāyave ālabheta*)” (TS 2.1.1.3). “One who has been ill for a long time” (*jyogāmayāvī*) means one suffering from a chronic disease. The horses of Vāyu are called *niyuts*; thus, he is “accompanied by them” (*niyutvān*). And the fruit is heard in the supplementary portion of the passage: “He indeed bestows upon him out-breathing and in-breathing; even if his life-force has departed, he lives indeed” (TS 2.1.1.4). “He indeed” refers to Vāyu accompanied by his team (*niyutvān*). “Upon him” refers to the one suffering from a chronic disease. “Life-force has departed” (*itāsuḥ*) means whose vital breaths have gone.

In the second section, it is heard: "He who is seized by Varuṇa should sacrifice a black animal with one white hoof to Varuṇa" (TS 2.1.2.1). Some say that "seized by Varuṇa" means afflicted by the disease known as dropsy; others say it means afflicted by some unknown ailment. "One whose foot is white" is *ekaśitipāt*. The result is stated: "He indeed releases him from the noose of Varuṇa" (TS 2.1.2.2). "He indeed" refers to Varuṇa himself. "From the noose of Varuṇa" means from the aforementioned disease.

In that very same section [of the Veda], it is said: “One who has been ill for a long time should sacrifice a black-necked animal to Agni and a tawny one to Soma” (TS 2.1.2.7). *Babhru* means tawny-colored. As for its fruit: “He ransoms his body from Agni and his vital essence from Soma; even if his life-breath has departed, he indeed lives” (TS 2.1.2.7).

In the fourth section, it is stated: “If one should fear, ‘I shall become afflicted with skin disease,’ he should sacrifice a dark-colored animal to Soma and Pūṣan” (TS 2.1.4.3). For one who has ascertained a future illness through signs such as itching and the like, fear certainly arises. However, the result of that rite is: “He does not become afflicted with skin disease” (TS 2.1.4.3).

In the sixth section [of the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā*], it is stated: “One whose illness has been long-standing and neglected should sacrifice a hornless goat to Prajāpati” (*TS* 2.1.6.3). A hornless animal (*tūpara*) is one devoid of horns. As for its fruit, it says: “He indeed releases him from that wasting disease” (*TS* 2.1.6.5). “He” refers to Prajāpati himself. “From that wasting disease” means from a chronic, debilitating illness.

In the ninth Anuvāka, it is stated: “One who has suffered from chronic illness for a long time should sacrifice a white animal to Mitra and a black one to Varuṇa” (TS 2.1.9.3). Its fruit is declared thus: “Verily, he releases him from the noose of Varuṇa; even if his life-breath has departed, he lives on” (TS 2.1.9.3). Thus, these animals that remove disease have been described in the first Praśna. Likewise, in the second Praśna, in the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), it is heard in the first Anuvāka: “He whose cattle or men have perished, or who is afraid, should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni Surabhimat” (TS 2.2.2.3–4). The object of fear here should be understood as the foul odor (*pūtigandha*) consisting of disease, because its fruit is proclaimed in the supplementary passage: “For the removal of foul odor” (TS 2.2.2.4). In the third Anuvāka: “One who has suffered from chronic illness for a long time should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni Pavamāna, to Agni Pāvaka, and to Agni Śuci” (TS 2.2.4.2). Its fruit is declared: “When he offers to Agni Pavamāna, he thereby bestows breath upon him. When he offers to Agni Pāvaka, he thereby bestows speech upon him. When he offers to Agni Śuci, he thereby bestows life-span upon him. Even if his life-breath has departed, he lives on” (TS 2.2.4.2–3). Likewise, it is heard in that very same place: “One desiring sight should offer this very sacrifice” (TS 2.2.4.3). “One desiring sight” refers to one afflicted by eye disease, because its fruit is heard: “When he offers to Agni Śuci, he thereby bestows sight upon him; even if he is blind, he sees clearly” (TS 2.2.4.3–4).

In this same manner, other passages may also be cited as examples. Recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*) based on the *Ṛgveda* and *Yajurveda* have been demonstrated; those based on the *Sāmaveda* should likewise be demonstrated through a close examination of that Veda.

As for acts of worship (*arcana*), they are well known from the *Āgamas* of the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, and others. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "by worship and so forth," one should understand the visible and invisible means—such as the offering of water (*arghya*), meditation (*dhyāna*), yoga, and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)—which remove disease. These are well known from the *Yogaśāstra* and other such works; however, we do not write them here for fear of making the book too voluminous.

Nor should it be suspected that because no correspondence with the result is observed even when the recitations and other rites prescribed have been performed, one should not proceed with confidence; for this same logic applies equally to medicinal herbs. If you say that confidence should likewise be absent in those cases too, then alas, Āyurveda would be as good as consigned to the depths.

Now, if you think that when medicines are being administered, because some defects persist or because the defects are powerful, the repeated application of the remedial medicine is required—then this same answer applies equally to recitations (*japa*) and the like. The principle that "once a scriptural injunction has been performed, its purpose is fulfilled" is to be understood as applying only to those acts whose fruits are unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), not to those whose fruits are seen (*dṛṣṭa*). For this very reason, repetition is prescribed for acts such as threshing. Indeed, the Mīmāṃsakas do not consider the injunction for threshing to have fulfilled its purpose with a single blow of the pestle while the rice grains remain unhusked. In that case, just as the repetition of threshing continues until the production of rice is complete, so too here the repetition of recitation and other such acts should be understood to continue until the cessation of the disease is achieved.

As for the fact that in some instances a small number [of recitations] is heard for *japa* and so forth, that should be established as referring to cases involving minor faults. This being the case, there is no contradiction anywhere. Furthermore, this principle of treating a disease should be applied to all undesirable *prārabdha* (commenced) fruits of karma. Whether one accepts that *japa* and so forth constitute expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and thus admits the cessation of *prārabdha* karma, or whether one does not accept that and holds instead to the mere obstruction of the fruit—under either view, engagement in the prescribed *japa* and other rites with confidence is established.

If such confidence in this remedy exists even regarding those actions whose fruits have already begun (prārabdhaphala), despite the suspicion that they might be averted solely by experience, then what need is there to mention the confidence one should have in engaging in expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) for actions whose fruits have not yet begun? Therefore, one must engage in the aforementioned expiations with absolute certainty; may all be entirely auspicious.
Thus, having expounded this detailed exposition of conduct and penance, accompanied by an indication of legal procedure, in two sections, the venerable teacher Parāśara concludes the treatise:
"This is the Pārāśara Śāstra, consisting of five hundred verses. (12.81)
This compendium of the Dharmaśāstra consists of ninety-two [chapters]. Thus it is said.

Since Parāśara composed a certain *upapurāṇa* as well, and because that work is primarily concerned with knowledge (*jñāna*), the word "this" (*etad*) is used to distinguish his present work from it. The collection of twelve chapters composed beginning with "Now, therefore, on the peak of the snowy mountain" (PārSm 1.1) is referred to by the word "this," as it is the subject under discussion. The description of the connection with Parāśara is intended to remind one of the exceptional authority of this treatise regarding the laws of the Kali age, as previously stated. Here, the word "treatise" (*śāstra*) denotes an injunctive statement, based on its etymological derivation: "it is a *śāstra* because it instructs" (*śāsanāt*).

Now, an objection: there is also the etymological derivation of "śāstra" from the root *śās*, as in "it is called a śāstra because it instructs (*śāsana*) and praises (*śaṃsana*). As it is said in the Purāṇa:
"It is designated a śāstra because of its instruction and its praise."

"Certainly. That proficiency concerns the treatises on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*), because they consist of the exposition of the established reality of Brahman (*siddha-brahma-tattva*). But here, since there is the statement of matters to be practiced (*anuṣṭheya-artha*), it is precisely as previously stated. To manifest that very point, the phrase 'of the Dharmaśāstra' was used. The mention of the number [of verses] is for the purpose of precluding the insertion or deletion of other statements. Because there is no great bulk of text—as in the case of the *smṛtis* of Manu and others—one might suspect that some duties (*dharma*) have been omitted; therefore, the word 'compendium' (*saṅgraha*) was used to exclude such a possibility."

Since this treatise has the practice of its meaning as its primary purpose, one might suspect that its mere recitation is of no consequence for attaining heaven; therefore, he states that it is a means to attain heaven, just like the study of the Vedas:
"Just as the acts of Vedic study [lead to merit], so too is this treatise on Dharma. (12.82)
"It must be studied with effort by one who is certain of going to heaven.
This has been explained by the very words used.

Now, one might object: since Vyāsa inquired about the characteristics of the Kali age and Parāśara replied, “In the Kali age, the Smṛtis are those of Parāśara” (ParSm 1.24), it must be said that all [rules] spoken by Parāśara concern only the laws of the Kali age. Furthermore, the phrase “the rest is declared by the Sage” (ParSm 1.34) clearly indicates the acceptance even of prohibitions against practices of other sages during the Kali age. Consequently, there arises a persistent contradiction regarding whether or not the sins mentioned in the root text—such as the contraction of debts—and the long journeys inferred from the root text are to be practiced in this age. Nor should it be argued: “Why should the Smṛti not have as its subject matter the laws of the Kali age simply because of their abundance? For there is no differentiating cause for such a restriction; if prohibitory statements were the sole basis, it would follow that agriculture and similar activities should also not be performed. Moreover, it would follow that long journeys other than the pilgrimage to Setubandhu, and livelihoods other than agriculture and so forth—specifically those distinct from the stages of life such as renunciation—would be inadmissible. If custom were the criterion, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and it would result in the Smṛti becoming redundant. [The author continues: This objection is not valid. Why? Because the Smṛti itself provides the differentiation. It is stated: “In the Kṛta age, the Dharma was based on the Vedas; in the Tretā, on the Vedas and sacrifices; in the Dvāpara, on the Vedas, sacrifices, and gifts; in the Kali, O King, it is based solely on the Smṛti. Furthermore, the Smṛti states: “Whatever is not prohibited by the Smṛti and is consistent with the Veda—that is Dharma; the rest is non-Dharma. (ParSm 1.25). Thus, the Smṛti is the source for both injunctions and prohibitions. Since the Smṛti is the source, it is reasonable to conclude that the prohibitions apply to the Kali age. To this it is replied: [290] In the Kali age, everything spoken by Parāśara and that which is inferred from his words must indeed be performed; there is nothing whatsoever that is not to be performed. However, a distinction regarding their performance is understood through the force of systematic consistency (*samanvaya*). For instance, prohibitions are rooted in the impossibility of their application in the current age; otherwise, the origin of the injunctions would be rendered meaningless. This impossibility is twofold: based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and what is unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). Regarding those rooted in perceived impossibility, both performance and non-performance are blameless. Where an injunction of counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) is inferred because no other explanation is possible (*ananyathāsiddha*), there a perceived impossibility is postulated. For example: "One who has come from a long journey and is exhausted" (ParSm 1.41); "One should give water into the hand of an ascetic" (ParSm 1.53); "When the Vaiśvadeva rite is present" (ParSm 1.41); "Those belonging to the four castes and stages of life" (ParSm 2.1); "Heirs who share a single funeral ball" (ParSm 3.7); "Someone deceased in another land" (ParSm 3.10); "Those in whose house a student dwells" (ParSm 3.18); "One who is observant of vows and purified by a sacrificial session" (ParSm 3.21); [291] "And the twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires" (ParSm 3.21); "There is no impurity for a king" (ParSm 3.22); "Whomsoever the king desires" (ParSm 3.22); "Those led forth to the cremation grounds" (ParSm 8.22); "Slaves, barbers, cowherds, family friends, and half-share plowmen" (ParSm 11.21); "Or one should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice" (ParSm 12.71)—from such perceived impossibilities, the injunction for long journeys is to be inferred. The rule for the contraction of impurity, "A Brahmin is purified in one day" (ParSm 3.4), is explained away as being either for the sake of *yāyāvara* (wandering) Brahmins, or as a counter-exception to the prohibitions mentioned regarding the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). The rule for remarriage, "When he is lost, dead, or has gone forth" (ParSm 4.28), is explained away as referring to cases of marriage where the order of seniority is violated, such as marrying before an elder brother (*pariveda*). The enumeration of types of sons beginning with "And the son born of the wife" (ParSm 4.22) [292] is explained away as being for the purpose of penance (*prāyaścitta*), just like the mention of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* sons.

Nor should it be said that the same [penance] would apply even to the *datta* (adopted) and *aurasa* (legitimate) sons; for by praising intercourse during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and censuring its opposite, and by formulating the definition as if for the *aurasa* son alone, it is established that the *datta* son is also within the scope of the injunction. Thus, it is made clear that the mention of the *datta* and *aurasa* sons does not refer to penance. The penance for association (*saṃsarga-prāyaścitta*) mentioned in passages such as "A Brahmin should practice association" (Parāśara-smṛti) is otherwise explained as referring to cases such as officiating at sacrifices for those outside the community (*lokavilakṣaṇa-yājana*). However, the rule "from sitting, from lying down, and from traveling" (Parāśara-smṛti 12.79) is otherwise explained as resulting merely in loss of caste (*pātitya*).

In other cases, such as the killing of a cow and the like, the impossibility of the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated; their performance is censured. Where a direct injunction for the unseen is observed, as in agriculture and so forth, its non-performance is censured, because prohibitions function precisely with regard to what is other than that. The same should be understood for the subjects of the previously mentioned injunctions that cannot be established otherwise, since even those possess the character of direct injunctions for the unseen within their respective domains. It is with this very intention that the entire explanation is consistent; thus, everything is coherent.

In this twelfth chapter, the sinless lord of sages, the son of Śakti, has described the various types of conduct not mentioned in the first section on student life, as well as certain specific varieties of expiations that were left unmentioned even within the eight chapters of the second section.
The eminent teacher Mādhavācārya has clearly explained that [text] for the sake of favoring the learned. || 1 ||
In this chapter, the remaining portion of both sections combined shall be in the twelfth [chapter],
concerning the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for secret sins and the like which he has mentioned here step by step;
as well as other rites such as the *saumya-kṛcchra* which bestow well-ordained fruits— the ripening of one's actions.
Mādhava, who knows the heart of mindfulness, has explained everything that can be characterized as an existent entity.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Mādhavīyā, the commentary on the Parāśara [Smṛti], composed by the minister Mādhava, who was the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the Great King of Kings, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
This section on penance is completed.
